title: Claude Code capture skill: visual checks without Playwright
text: Blog / Posts / Claude Code capture skill Agents · Tutorial Claude Code capture skill: visual checks without writing Playwright scripts A downloadable Claude Code skill and billing-card fixture. Route app capture to SnapEye, visual review to SnapDiff and browser interaction to SnapSurf. Capture before editing, compare afterward The skill below tells Claude Code which component to capture, when to save the baseline and how to read the comparison. SnapEye handles local app capture, SnapDiff visual review, SnapSurf browser interaction. None of this needs a Playwright test script. SnapSurf uses Playwright internally to control its browser; SnapEye captures through the running app; SnapDiff compares captures inside the page. SnapEye, SnapDiff and SnapSurf have different roles SnapEye: capture your app and compare before and after Claude runs a command to capture a component in your local app. After a code change, another command compares it with the saved image and reports whether the pixels changed. Good for checking a CSS refactor or finding a visual regression. SnapEye captures and records the app; it does not click through the interface. SnapDiff: review visual differences inside the browser SnapDiff captures components, compares them with saved images and shows the differences in the page, where you inspect and approve changes through its reporter. Use it for interactive review. Its basic browser workflow saves references in that browser’s storage; blocking a CI build needs the separate test setup. SnapSurf: let the agent operate the browser SnapSurf lets Claude open a page, find a control, click or type, and check what changed: open a settings form, verify that a dialog appeared. Use it when the task needs interaction. It starts its own browser session, without the logins from your open Chrome tabs. Semantic verification says whether the interface changed state; visual comparison says whether captured pixels changed. A “saved” message can be correct while a button overlaps it, so check pixels when the task concerns appearance. Set up local capture in a Vite app npm install --save-dev @zumer/snapeye @zumer/snapdom@3 import { defineConfig } from 'vite'; import { snapeye } from '@zumer/snapeye/vite'; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [snapeye()] }); Start the dev server, then capture the component before editing it, with a stable viewport, fixed fixture data and a specific target rather than the whole application. npx snapeye capture billing-card-desktop --target '#billing-card' # Close the capture-trigger tab before editing, then: npx snapeye diff billing-card-desktop --target '#billing-card' --fail-on-change Read status first. A successful run with diff.changed: false passes an appearance-preserving refactor. If it changed, inspect the reported regions and artifacts. An environment failure is not a passing comparison. Download a Claude Code capture skill Save this complete SKILL.md as .claude/skills/visual-capture/SKILL.md in the project. The skill supplies the routing instructions; the tools, installed separately, perform the capture. The official skill guide documents the directory and frontmatter. --- name: visual-capture description: Capture and verify local UI changes with SnapEye; use SnapSurf for browser interactions and SnapDiff for in-page review. --- Capture the baseline before editing. Keep the viewport and fixture data fixed. Use SnapEye for a selector-level capture and read status before diff.changed. Never replace a baseline simply to hide a regression. Use SnapSurf for navigation and verify after every action. Report the target, artifacts, tool versions and what was actually verified. The downloadable version also covers errors, intentional visual changes and signed-in sessions, and keeps publication and baseline approval subject to the user’s instructions. A reproducible billing-card exercise Open the fixture or download its HTML : a static card with synthetic data and a button that deliberately changes its border, so baseline and regression are easy to tell apart. npm install --save-dev vite @zumer/snapeye @zumer/snapdom@3 npx snapeye serve billing-card.html # In another terminal, using the URL printed by serve: npx snapeye capture billing-card --url <printed-url> --target '#billing-card' # Close the capture-trigger tab, edit the CSS, then compare: npx snapeye diff billing-card --url <printed-url> --target '#billing-card' --fail-on-change For an interaction-only state, a fresh trigger URL reloads the page. Reach the state with a browser tool and use SnapEye's documented in-page API; the CLI will not have captured an already-open modal. The SnapDiff live demos show an in-page review workflow with deliberate visual drift. Add browser interaction through MCP SnapSurf is published in the official MCP Registry as io.github.zumerlab/snapsurf and listed in Glama . The registry entry checked on October 5, 2026 is version 0.1.2, distributed as the npm package @zumer/snapsurf . claude mcp add --scope user snapsurf -- npx -y -p @zumer/snapsurf@latest snapsurf-mcp Then ask Claude to open the app, find a named control, act, verify and assert the intended transition. Read structuredContent , get fresh target ids after new observations, and escalate to pixels when the semantic report cannot answer the question. A semantic diff does not prove a SnapDOM image has the right pixels. For a workflow that needs the user's existing signed-in tab, use an authorized integration for that tab. A useful task to give Claude “Refactor the billing card CSS without changing its appearance. Capture #billing-card before editing, keep the fixture and viewport fixed, compare afterward, and report the JSON verdict and artifact paths. If verification fails, explain the failure; do not overwrite the reference.” For an intentional redesign, specify which region may change and inspect it before approving a new reference. Keep the original reference until that review is done. Related: element capture , recapture and invalidation , React lifecycle timing . Sources checked October 5, 2026: SnapEye setup and CLI , SnapDiff workflows , SnapSurf MCP integration , and the Claude Code skill guide above. Playwright MCP, for comparison Microsoft’s Playwright MCP also lets an agent operate a browser without a standalone test script; its documented approach uses structured accessibility snapshots. SnapSurf adds a digest-and-diff workflow with assertions over retained transitions. Both control a browser, so compare their observation and verification APIs against the task at hand. Keep Playwright tests for an established end-to-end suite, multi-browser automation or a CI workflow your team already maintains. Add selector-level DOM capture when the immediate question is what changed in a running component. Protect the baseline during hot reload After a CLI capture finishes, close its trigger tab or navigate to the ordinary app URL before editing. In our local SnapEye 0.4.0 fixture, leaving the capture query open during Vite hot reload triggered another capture and replaced the baseline, which would turn a real change into a misleading no-change verdict. With the capture URL removed before editing, the deliberate border change produced changed: true and exit code 3. The fixture was checked in Chromium at 320 × 240 captured CSS pixels. An unchanged run reported zero changed pixels; the border regression reported a change. The check covered this fixture in Chromium only.

title: DOM Capture Boundaries and Integration Patterns — SnapDOM
text: Blog / Posts / DOM capture boundaries SnapDOM Blog DOM capture boundaries and integration patterns SnapDOM needs a readable DOM and leaves navigation to browser tooling. Browser control connects it to Node, cross-origin documents and automated application flows. Juan Martin Muda · August 22, 2026 TL;DR Let Playwright or Puppeteer create the browser state. Run SnapDOM inside that page and return result.url or a raster data URL to Node. A same-origin iframe can be captured from its parent; a cross-origin document must be served from the same origin or captured from its own page or frame context. useProxy fetches assets; it cannot grant access to iframe DOM. Run the capture where the DOM lives SnapDOM starts from an Element . It reads layout, computed styles, fonts and image state, then asks the browser to paint the styled clone inside an SVG <foreignObject> . A Node process, server renderer or worker without a document has none of those APIs. The process that receives an HTTP request can still own the job: launch a browser, prepare the page, save the output. The call to snapdom() stays inside the page that owns the element. Situation Capture context Route SSR app after hydration The client page Capture after mount and after the DOM is ready Backend Node job A controlled browser page Launch Playwright or Puppeteer and inject SnapDOM Web Worker The page's main thread Send a capture request with postMessage Service Worker or edge worker A separate browser service Forward the job to a real browser runtime Cross-origin document Its own page or frame context Run the capture where that document is readable Navigation or E2E flow The final, stable page state Let the browser driver navigate, interact and wait first jsdom and similar DOM implementations parse markup but do not replace browser layout and paint: no geometry, font rendering, SVG decode or canvas behavior. Give Node a real browser This Playwright script loads the installed IIFE bundle, opens a report, waits for an application-owned ready signal and makes two files from one SnapDOM capture. Node manages the process and filesystem; the page creates the SVG and PNG. npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest playwright npx playwright install chromium import { chromium } from 'playwright' import { writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises' import { createRequire } from 'node:module' import { dirname, join } from 'node:path' const require = createRequire(import.meta.url) const snapdomPackagePath = require.resolve('@zumer/snapdom/package.json') const snapdomBundlePath = join(dirname(snapdomPackagePath), 'dist', 'snapdom.js') const browser = await chromium.launch() try { const context = await browser.newContext({ bypassCSP: true, viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 }, deviceScaleFactor: 1 }) const page = await context.newPage() await page.goto('https://example.com/report', { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' }) await page.locator('#report[data-export-ready="true"]').waitFor() await page.addScriptTag({ path: snapdomBundlePath }) const output = await page.evaluate(async () => { await document.fonts.ready const report = document.querySelector('#report') if (!report) throw new Error('Report element not found') const capture = await window.snapdom(report, { embedFonts: true, dpr: 1 }) const png = await capture.toPng() return { svg: capture.url, png: png.src } }) const svgBody = output.svg.slice(output.svg.indexOf(',') + 1) const pngBody = output.png.slice(output.png.indexOf(',') + 1) await Promise.all([ writeFile('report.svg', decodeURIComponent(svgBody)), writeFile('report.png', Buffer.from(pngBody, 'base64')) ]) } finally { await browser.close() } The installed package includes an IIFE at dist/snapdom.js that exposes window.snapdom . Resolve package.json first to locate that bundle, since the package entry point can resolve to an ES module. Resolving the installed package works across hoisted and standalone installs, keeps CI output reproducible and works offline. In Playwright, CSP bypass belongs to the browser context; Puppeteer uses page.setBypassCSP(true) before navigation. CaptureResult , Blob , Canvas and HTMLImageElement instances stay in the browser process. Strings cross page.evaluate() cleanly, so produce every format from the reusable capture and return data URLs or encoded text. page.screenshot() is the direct tool for a single pixel-based screenshot. SnapDOM inside the browser earns its place when the application also exports client-side, when you need SVG, when a plugin edits the captured DOM, or when one frozen capture must feed several formats. Capture cross-origin documents from their own context When an iframe is same-origin, SnapDOM reads its document and places a PNG of the iframe's visible viewport into the parent capture. A sandboxed frame without allow-same-origin may still be inaccessible even when its URL looks local. For a cross-origin iframe, the parent page cannot read iframe.contentDocument . SnapDOM leaves a striped placeholder by default and emits a warning; placeholders: false keeps an invisible spacer of the same box size. This follows the browser's same-origin policy. If you control the deployment, serve or reverse-proxy the document under the same origin. For an authorized third-party page, navigate a controlled browser to that URL, inject SnapDOM after navigation and capture document.documentElement . Playwright and Puppeteer can also run code in an individual cross-origin frame context: const frame = page.frames().find(candidate => candidate.url().startsWith('https://partner.example/') ) if (!frame) throw new Error('Partner frame not found') await frame.addScriptTag({ path: snapdomBundlePath }) const framePng = await frame.evaluate(async () => { await document.fonts.ready const image = await window.snapdom.toPng( document.documentElement, { clip: 'viewport', dpr: 1 } ) return image.src }) The driver reaches the frame through the automation protocol; SnapDOM still runs inside the document it reads. If the artifact needs both parent and child, capture the child separately, provide its data URL as an image in a controlled render state, then capture the parent. If all you need is one PNG of the complete parent page, page.screenshot() is shorter and already composites the cross-origin frame's pixels. useProxy solves a different problem: fetching cross-origin images, fonts and backgrounds that allow proxying. It does not make iframe DOM same-origin, and an open proxy brings its own authentication and server-side request risks. Navigation stays with the browser driver SnapDOM captures the state it receives. It does not open URLs, authenticate, click controls, wait for application data, manage test baselines or compare pixels. Playwright or Puppeteer owns those steps and calls SnapDOM once the target state is stable. await page.goto(appURL, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' }) await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Generate report' }).click() await page.locator('#report[data-export-ready="true"]').waitFor() await page.addScriptTag({ path: snapdomBundlePath }) const captureURL = await page.evaluate(async () => { await document.fonts.ready const report = document.querySelector('#report') return (await window.snapdom(report, { dpr: 1 })).url }) An explicit application signal beats a fixed delay or network-idle heuristic. A page can finish its requests while fonts, transitions, charts or asynchronous rendering are still changing what the user sees. For visual regression, the runner should also pin the browser build, viewport, DPR, fonts, locale and timezone, and disable animations. SnapDOM supplies the artifact; the test system owns baselines, thresholds and assertions. Account for the browser service A backend capture still pays for a browser process. Reuse a browser when jobs are frequent, isolate work in fresh contexts, cap concurrency and apply timeouts. A public endpoint that accepts arbitrary URLs also needs URL allowlists and network isolation so it cannot become a route into private services. Every full navigation replaces the page's JavaScript context. Inject the bundle again after navigation and wait for the application's export-ready state before capturing. title: HTML to editable SVG and Figma with SnapDOM Vector
text: Blog / Posts / Editable SVG and Figma Vector · Figma HTML to editable SVG and Figma with SnapDOM Vector Turn a live component into editable SVG artwork and Figma clipboard output. Try a product card and review fonts, layers and conversion limits. From a shipped component to editable artwork To edit a captured component in a design tool, its labels need to stay text and its shapes need to stay shapes. PNG exports keep pixels. Core SVG captures embed HTML in a foreignObject. SnapDOM's Vector plugin reads the rendered DOM to measure text and shapes and reconstructs the supported parts as standalone SVG artwork. Its Figma clipboard export is a second destination for the same capture. Three outputs with different jobs PNG: a picture of the component PNG shows someone how the component looks. They cannot edit its labels as text or move its shapes separately. SnapDOM’s regular SVG: HTML stored inside an SVG file toSvg() keeps the captured HTML inside an SVG container, using foreignObject . Good for displaying the capture in a compatible browser; a design tool may not support that HTML content. The .svg extension alone does not make the component’s text and shapes editable in Figma. Vector plugin: text and shapes you can edit toVector() converts supported parts of the component into SVG text and shapes, for when someone needs to change a label or edit the artwork in a vector editor. For Figma, use the plugin’s separate toFigma() clipboard export and check the pasted result: fonts and some visual effects may differ from the browser. Check how an SVG stores its content before sending it to a vector editor. The HTML-to-SVG recipe covers the capture route; Vector is a separate plugin with a different output contract. Try a product card, then inspect the SVG Edit the product name, export the card and download its SVG. Open it in your vector editor, find the title and change it. The demo reports how many SVG text elements and foreignObject elements the exported file contains; check the imported result in your own editor. For charts and inline illustrations, use the Vector playground . Start with ordinary text, borders and gradients before effects your destination may approximate. Install and capture once npm install @zumer/snapdom@3 @zumer/snapdom-vector import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { vector } from '@zumer/snapdom-vector'; const card = document.querySelector('#product-card'); const result = await snapdom(card, { plugins: [vector()] }); const svg = await result.toVector(); // Wire this after capture has finished, on HTTPS or localhost: copyButton.addEventListener('click', () => result.toFigma()); toVector() returns an SVG string. toFigma() writes the clipboard and resolves without returning artwork. Keep the source connected through export, and register the plugin only on the captures that need it. The public plugin option is exclude ; do not copy historical internal engine settings into your application. The Figma handoff Generate first, click Copy to Figma , then paste into a Figma design file. Clipboard access needs HTTPS or localhost and browser permission. title: Tiled Rasterization for Large DOM Captures — SnapDOM
text: Blog / Posts / Tiled rasterization SnapDOM Blog Tiled rasterization for large DOM captures Capture a document once, then rasterize it through small SVG windows. The crop is applied before image decode, so each tile fits the browser's raster limits. Juan Martin Muda · August 11, 2026 For a single large PNG or JPEG file, use download() or toBlob() : SnapDOM assembles the file automatically. Use the crop API below when your output needs separate tiles or pages. TL;DR A very tall DOM capture can serialize to SVG and still fail when the browser decodes that SVG into one enormous bitmap. toCanvas({ crop }) windows the SVG before image decode. Capture once, move the window across result.meta , and each tile keeps the requested resolution while fitting the browser's raster limits, with no full-page canvas ever allocated. It solves the raster ceiling; it does not make cloning an enormous DOM free. The screenshot was fine. The bitmap wasn't. A “full-page screenshot” has two sizes. One is the serialized capture: an SVG with a styled DOM clone inside <foreignObject> . The other is the bitmap the browser creates when that SVG is decoded for PNG, Canvas, JPEG or WebP. The SVG can describe a page tens of thousands of pixels tall. The bitmap is where browsers push back. SnapDOM budgets 16,384 pixels per side on WebKit, 32,767 elsewhere, and about 268 million pixels of area (16,384 × 16,384). Actual allocation and decode limits depend on the browser and device. dpr counts toward the limit and defaults to devicePixelRatio , so on a Retina screen a scale: 2 capture is 4× wide and tall. Past the limit, img.decode() may reject with EncodingError: The source image cannot be decoded , or the canvas allocation fails later. Canvas-sized exports are proportionally downscaled when they exceed these budgets. For a deep-zoom viewer, tiled upload or print pipeline, separate crop windows preserve the requested resolution without a full-size canvas. Cut the SVG, not the canvas The obvious mosaic algorithm is the broken one: render one giant canvas, then cut it into smaller canvases with drawImage() . By the time the slicing loop starts, the browser has already decoded and allocated the giant bitmap. toCanvas({ crop }) moves the cut earlier. SnapDOM rewrites the serialized SVG's root width , height and viewBox to describe only the requested window, then hands it to Image.decode() . The browser never sees a full-height raster source. Capture once Clone, style and serialize one canonical SVG. Move the window Rewrite the viewBox to one tile's coordinates. Decode small Rasterize only that tile, consume it, repeat. All of this lives in the exporter. The capture path still walks and clones the DOM once; ten tiles do not repeat style collection, font embedding or image inlining ten times. Try the mosaic The report below is 640 × 2,400 CSS pixels, well under any browser limit so the demo stays polite, but it takes the same path as a 40,000-pixel document: one SVG capture, ten 320 × 480 crop windows, ten independent canvases. Scroll the source, then build the mosaic. Northstar / Annual report 2026 Revenue, retention and regional growth. One continuous DOM document: metrics, charts, regions and a timeline. N Build 10-tile mosaic One capture · no full-page canvas The gaps, borders and responsive scaling make the tiles visible here. At their native 320 × 480 size with no decoration, the ten canvases reconstruct the source. The whole implementation is a loop crop uses SVG viewBox coordinates, so the reliable bounds come from the capture, not from rereading the live element. Each canvas goes to a callback right away, so a production exporter can encode, upload or write the tile before requesting the next one. async function tileCapture(capture, options, consume) { const { tileWidth = 2048, tileHeight = 2048, scale = 1, dpr = 1 } = options const { contentX, contentY, w0, h0 } = capture.meta for (let y = 0, row = 0; y < h0; y += tileHeight, row++) { for (let x = 0, col = 0; x < w0; x += tileWidth, col++) { const width = Math.min(tileWidth, w0 - x) const height = Math.min(tileHeight, h0 - y) const crop = { x: contentX + x, y: contentY + y, width, height } const canvas = await capture.toCanvas({ crop, scale, dpr }) await consume({ canvas, crop, row, col }) } } } const capture = await snapdom(document.documentElement, { dpr: 1 }) await tileCapture(capture, {}, async ({ canvas, row, col }) => { const blob = await new Promise(resolve => canvas.toBlob(resolve, 'image/png')) if (!blob) throw new Error('PNG encoding failed') try { await uploadTile(blob, { row, col }) } finally { canvas.width = canvas.height = 0 } }) Exports on one capture are queued, so tiles rasterize in order instead of competing for decode and canvas memory. A visual mosaic like the demo can keep every canvas. For a huge page, process a tile and release it before moving on. The geometry is half the feature A naïve tiler starts at 0, 0 , which only works while the serialized content starts there too. Root transforms, asymmetric shadows, outlines and clip windows can move the logical page inside the SVG viewBox. SnapDOM exposes the final, immutable geometry as result.meta , after those effects are resolved. Geometry What it measures Use it for w0 / h0 The logical capture box Tile only page content contentX / contentY Its exact origin inside the viewBox Place the first content tile vbW / vbH The complete serialized artifact Include bleed and outer effects The loop above tiles the logical page from contentX, contentY over w0 × h0 . To keep every pixel of shadow or transformed bleed, tile from 0, 0 over vbW × vbH instead. Crop windows partly outside are clipped to the viewBox; empty, non-finite or fully outside windows reject rather than quietly returning the whole image. What tiling does not solve Tiling removes the full-bitmap allocation. It does not make capture a streaming DOM renderer: SnapDOM still clones the complete subtree, reads its styles, inlines assets and holds the serialized SVG. A 100,000-node document is still a 100,000-node capture. Virtualized or lazy sections must exist in the DOM before capture; no image library can serialize nodes the application has not rendered. tileWidth × scale × dpr and tileHeight × scale × dpr still need to fit the browser's raster limits. Keeping every tile alive holds the same pixels in aggregate. Encode or send each tile as you go when memory matters. Stitching the tiles back into one giant canvas recreates the original problem. The consumer has to understand pages, tiles or levels. If the initial DOM walk is the bottleneck, clip is the other tool: it prunes off-window subtrees before styling and inlining, but needs a separate capture per region. crop trades that pruning for one frozen artifact, so fonts, images, animation state and live data cannot change between tiles. Each crop also decodes and re-encodes the complete SVG data URL, and the browser still parses the full <foreignObject> payload. Tiling bounds bitmap allocation only. Where tile windows are useful We added crop and immutable geometry for document exporters, where a tall capture becomes PDF pages. The same mechanism fits map-style viewers, poster printing, zoomable archives and multipart uploads: one stable source, one rectangle at a time. In defineExports(ctx) , plugin authors can retain ctx.exports and call its canvas({ crop }) method from their custom exporter. This core-export facade reuses the canonical capture without recursively firing export hooks, so “mosaic” is a small custom export rather than a second rendering engine, and the extra work stays out of SnapDOM's capture hot path. Keep reading Capture a full page Canvas crop API Plugin export API Painting without canvas toCanvas({ crop }) and immutable capture geometry have been available since SnapDOM v2.24. See the crop reference .

title: Painting without a canvas, and other SnapDOM plugin tricks
text:
Blog / Posts / Painting without a canvas SnapDOM Blog Painting without a canvas element And a couple of other things that fell out of giving a screenshot library a plugin system with two hooks: afterClone and afterRender . Juan Martin Muda · July 21, 2026 · Examples updated for v3. The stateful plugins here request fresh captures; the default export URL is SVG. See the plugin guide for current hook contracts. TL;DR SnapDOM captures a DOM subtree by cloning it, serializing the clone to an SVG , and rasterizing that. Its plugin hooks fire on every capture from the same closure, so a plugin can hold state across calls that the library never persists. Three demos built on that: a paint app with no element , a contenteditable box rendering through WebGL , and a shooting gallery that uses the same trick as the paint app. The setup SnapDOM ( @zumer/snapdom ) is a browser library that clones a DOM element, inlines its computed styles, images and fonts, serializes the clone into an SVG data: URL, and exports it as SVG or rasterizes it to PNG, JPEG, WebP or canvas. Less common is the plugin system: lifecycle hooks ( beforeSnap , afterClone , afterRender , beforeExport , afterExport , plus defineExports for registering new output formats) that fire on every capture with a mutable context object. We added it for the boring reasons: watermarking, redaction, format conversion. Then we started poking at what else two of those hooks could do. A JavaScript closure keeps the drawing state between calls. SnapDOM 3 can reuse eligible captures, but the stateful hooks below request fresh work and restore the plugin's saved clone. Painting without a element The paint demo looks like a normal freehand painting widget, with no behind it. There is one hidden
holding an empty SVG layer, and an replaced on every stroke with a fresh snapdom.toPng() result. The "canvas" is a screenshot library capturing the same tiny element over and over, each time with one more stroke baked in. Two hooks and one closure variable: // Trimmed to the two hooks that matter — full version, with stroke // smoothing and SVG path bookkeeping, is at the link above. function createPaintPlugin () { let savedClone = null let pendingStroke = null return { name: 'paint', recordStroke (pathData) { pendingStroke = pathData }, afterClone (ctx) { // Instead of letting SnapDOM clone the pristine source, hand back // whatever we saved last time — with the new stroke appended. if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) if (pendingStroke) appendPath(ctx.clone, pendingStroke) }, afterRender (ctx) { // Checkpoint what was actually rendered as the new baseline. savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) pendingStroke = null } } } // on every point added while dragging: plugin.recordStroke(pathData) await snapdom.toPng(hiddenSource, { plugins: [plugin] }) Every stroke: append a point to an SVG path, call snapdom.toPng(el, { plugins: [plugin] }) again. afterClone swaps in last time's clone instead of a fresh one and adds the new bit of path; afterRender keeps the result. The live source element is never touched; the picture lives in the plugin's closure. Throttle to a capture every ~120ms while dragging (with a local, SnapDOM-free SVG path for cursor feedback) and it's a usable paint app that is, structurally, a loop of independent screenshots. A text field that's secretly WebGL The second demo looks and behaves like a normal editable text field: real caret, real selection, paste works, Enter inserts a newline. None of the visible text is painted by the browser's text engine. Underneath is a WebGL , and what you read is a texture. Two DOM elements make this work. A transparent contenteditable proxy sits on top of the canvas to give the browser somewhere to blink a caret and to receive keystrokes, so caret-color is set but the text is color: transparent . A second, hidden element mirrors what you typed and is the one SnapDOM captures. A plugin's defineExports adds a webgl export that feeds each capture into a double-buffered WebGL renderer, which cross-fades between old and new texture over about 110ms so nothing pops: function seamlessWebgl (renderer) { return { name: 'seamless-webgl', defineExports () { return { webgl: async ctx => renderer.update(ctx.export.url) } } } } // on every keystroke, against the hidden mirror element: const capture = await snapdom(hiddenSource, { plugins: [plugin] }) await capture.to('webgl') ctx.export.url is the capture's data URL, SVG with the default engine. defineExports hands the plugin the finished render and lets it decide what "exporting" means, here "upload as a GPU texture" instead of "hand back an ." A shader dropdown on the page (hologram scanlines, CRT, kaleidoscope, a datamosh effect, six more) never touches SnapDOM; it samples whichever texture is already on the GPU differently. Same capture pipeline, eight different-looking outputs. title: The setup
text: SnapDOM ( @zumer/snapdom ) is a browser library that clones a DOM element, inlines its computed styles, images and fonts, serializes the clone into an SVG data: URL, and exports it as SVG or rasterizes it to PNG, JPEG, WebP or canvas. Less common is the plugin system: lifecycle hooks ( beforeSnap , afterClone , afterRender , beforeExport , afterExport , plus defineExports for registering new output formats) that fire on every capture with a mutable context object. We added it for the boring reasons: watermarking, redaction, format conversion. Then we started poking at what else two of those hooks could do. A JavaScript closure keeps the drawing state between calls. SnapDOM 3 can reuse eligible captures, but the stateful hooks below request fresh work and restore the plugin's saved clone.

title: Painting without a <canvas> element
text:

holding an empty SVG layer, and an replaced on every stroke with a fresh snapdom.toPng() result. The live source element is never touched; the picture lives in the plugin's closure. Throttle to a capture every ~120ms while dragging (with a local, SnapDOM-free SVG path for cursor feedback) and it's a usable paint app that is, structurally, a loop of independent screenshots.

title: SnapDOM PDF vs html2canvas + jsPDF: searchable invoices
text: Blog / Posts / PDF vs html2canvas + jsPDF PDF · Comparison SnapDOM PDF vs html2canvas + jsPDF: searchable invoices from HTML Compare image PDFs, searchable DOM captures and programmatic jsPDF. Try one editable invoice across three real export routes. What the PDF contains An invoice PDF needs three things checked: the layout, whether the text can be selected, and whether payment links work. The three export routes below handle them differently. PDF export first shipped in the 4.0.0 plugin toolbox. It now installs separately as @zumer/snapdom-pdf . Its visible page is a captured image; an invisible PDF text layer adds selection and search. SnapDOM PDF vs html2canvas + jsPDF vs jsPDF SnapDOM + PDF plugin: capture the invoice you already have The PDF looks like the HTML invoice. The text layer lets the recipient search the invoice number and copy text, and links can stay clickable. Use this when your app already displays the document you want to export. The visible page is still an image; zooming in does not turn it into vector artwork. html2canvas + jsPDF: put a screenshot inside a PDF html2canvas turns the HTML into an image and jsPDF puts that image on a PDF page. The invoice text is part of the image: the recipient cannot select or search it. Use this when an image inside a PDF is enough. Selectable text or clickable links take more code. jsPDF directly: build a separate PDF layout You write the text and draw the document with jsPDF’s APIs. The text is selectable and you can add links; you also choose positions, fonts and page breaks yourself. Use this when the PDF should have its own layout. It does not copy the appearance of your HTML invoice. jsPDF writes text, graphics and links directly; its separate html() API depends on html2canvas. The table and demo compare the common addImage() recipe with programmatic jsPDF. See the jsPDF README and HTML API reference. html2canvas implements a documented subset of CSS rather than asking the browser for a native screenshot, and its feature list currently marks box-shadow and filter unsupported. Check the exported invoice against the source if it uses those styles. Try the same invoice three ways Change the client name below, generate each PDF, and search for that name in the files. Compare selection, link behavior and the visible header. The programmatic jsPDF version uses the same invoice data with its own layout. For a larger acceptance test, open the PDF playground , select A4 ledger , and check row breaks and repeated table headers. The multilingual and form examples cover other scripts and editable fields. Install and export npm install @zumer/snapdom@3 @zumer/snapdom-pdf import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { pdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-pdf'; await document.fonts.ready; const invoice = document.querySelector('#invoice'); const result = await snapdom(invoice, { plugins: [pdf()] }); const blob = await result.toPdf({ page: 'a4', margin: 36 }); // Upload the Blob, or opt into a download: await result.toPdf({ page: 'a4', download: 'invoice.pdf' }); Wait for the application's data and images as well as fonts. Capture options go on snapdom() or the plugin factory, paper options on toPdf() . Output options are in the PDF reference . Document checks before shipping Search for a unique invoice identifier, copy a full line item, click a known link, inspect page two, and open the file in the viewer your recipients use. The exporter supports pagination and repeated table headers, but a row taller than a page still has to split. Tagged output by itself does not establish PDF/UA conformance. Remove sensitive source content before capture. A painted rectangle hides pixels while leaving searchable text underneath. The downloadable document and the browser preview belong under the same redaction policy. Continue with the capture pipeline Start with choosing the capture element , then capture options and cache and recapture behavior . For editable SVG and Figma output, see the Vector and Figma workflow . title: SnapDOM v3 Is Out — SnapDOM Blog
text:
Blog / Posts / SnapDOM v3 is out Release · 3.0.0 SnapDOM v3 is out Automatic capture reuse, incremental recapture, fewer setup options and a live comparison you can run on your own machine. Juan Martin Muda · September 14, 2026 SnapDOM 3.0.0 is out, along with v3 of the official plugins. Most of the work went into making repeated captures cheaper without returning stale content. If you're new here: SnapDOM captures a DOM element with its styles and assets in the browser and exports SVG, PNG, JPG, WebP, canvas or blobs. The snapdom(element, options) entry point is unchanged in v3; the changes are underneath it. The second capture matters A share card gets exported several times unchanged. A dashboard updates one value between captures. Rebuilding everything each time repeats style reads, cloning and asset work that is still valid. In v3, the first successful capture of an eligible static element creates a memo, and a later capture reuses it if the relevant state is unchanged. For supported local mutations, the engine rebuilds the affected subtrees and splices them into the previous capture, automatically. Knowing when that is safe is the hard part. A local DOM edit can shift layout elsewhere. A scroll or focus change alters the image without changing the text. Canvas, video and iframe contents change with no DOM mutation at all. So the incremental path is conservative: it runs only when the engine can preserve the full capture's output. Anything else falls back to a full capture, and frame-driven content captures fresh. Direct stylesheet edits such as sheet.insertRule() still need invalidate: true , since they produce no DOM mutations for style invalidation. Details in the cache guide . Image exports from an existing result still use its captured state; if the page changes, call snapdom() again. PNG encoding and rasterization still cost time either way. Concurrent captures now keep their working state in separate sessions instead of one shared mutable session. Fonts by default, and a lot of small rendering fixes Web fonts now embed automatically when the captured content uses them. The default is embedFonts: 'auto' ; a capture using only system fonts skips that work. false leaves text fonts out, true forces discovery. A large part of the release went into rendering details: fractional widths adding a line wrap, misaligned pseudo-element boxes, scrolled containers and images, transformed and offscreen elements. Small defects, but visible in every export. V3 fixes those, preserves inherited fill colors in SVG icons, and corrects how slotted Shadow DOM content is cloned. Font handling preserves icon styles and keeps unrelated font families when an icon font shares their stylesheet. The changelog links to the individual fixes and reports. Two APIs for the work around a capture fromString() is for input that is HTML rather than an element on the page. It mounts the markup offscreen in the live document, captures it and removes the mount. Page CSS and fonts apply. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const capture = await snapdom.fromString( '

SnapDOM v3

' ) const image = await capture.toPng({ width: 1200, dpr: 1 }) document.body.append(image) The string goes into the real document through innerHTML , so use trusted markup or sanitize it first. A browser DOM is still required. preCapture() prepares eligible captures on user intent. Enable it once and keep the capture call in your control's handler. For a button and card already mounted in your app: const button = document.querySelector('#export-button') const card = document.querySelector('#card') snapdom.preCapture() button.addEventListener('click', () => snapdom.download(card, { format: 'png', filename: 'card.png' }) ) The first capture started during the control's press or click event teaches SnapDOM which element and options belong to that control. On later hover or focus it prepares the same capture before the next click. A capture deferred to an unrelated timer will not teach it. No arguments, no background polling. Official plugins and render engines At the v3 launch, the official @zumer/snapdom-plugins package also used version 3. Recording exports take new frames from the live element when recording starts. Current packages: the 5.x toolbox requires SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer. PDF , Vector and Stream now have their own packages. Check each package's core requirement; major versions no longer match. Plugins also receive capture geometry, the exact export options and canvas cropping support, for exports that must line up with the source interface or share a crop with a core exporter. Examples in the plugin gallery ; hooks and custom exports in the plugin reference . At launch, the native html-in-canvas engine needed a custom build. The default renderer remains SVG. Update, October 2026: Chrome 157 ships html-in-canvas without a flag, and the engine is now part of the default build. engine: 'html-in-canvas' paints the capture with Chrome's own renderer there and falls back to SVG everywhere else; the guide says when to use it. Run the comparison on your own machine The site got work too: the reference , capture recipes , framework guides , and the capture boundaries article on where SnapDOM runs when Node, browser automation or cross-origin frames are involved. The part I most want people to try is the live comparison . Pick a scene and the libraries (html2canvas, html-to-image, modern-screenshot and others) and run it in your own browser on your own hardware. Every library is timed through to a PNG data URL, with separate columns for first and repeat captures and the rendered output next to the timings. The regular scenes disable SnapDOM's capture memoization; the Polling scene exercises automatic reuse. Look at the images too: a fast result with missing content is a broken export. Pixel differences are measured against SnapDOM's output, a reference image rather than an independent correctness verdict. A capability matrix captures small fixtures and checks whether their marker colors survive: Shadow DOM, pseudo-elements, painted canvas content and more. Everything runs in your browser, so scene, browser and hardware all matter. Before upgrading from v2 This is a major release. Read the migration guide before bumping the version in an existing app. The changes that need a close look: width and height take precedence over scale . For a width of 400, use width: 400 instead of width: 200, scale: 2 . Raster dpr still applies; use dpr: 1 for that exact pixel width. Remove preCache and its subpath import. Capture reuse is automatic and preCapture() learns intent; it is not a rename. Remove burst , compress , resolvePicturePlaceholders and pictureResolver . fast: false remains supported and yields between work batches; see the current option . Handle custom image loading and timeouts in your app before capture. Core redaction masks password fields only. The redactInputs() plugin masks other visible fields. afterExport hooks observe the export result; their return values no longer feed the next hook. Use defineExports for custom output. filter and exclude still work together, each with its own hide/remove mode. Function-valued filter , exclude , excludeStyleProps and fallbackURL make each new capture run fresh so callbacks read current application state. The v2 branch stays available for projects staying on that release. npm install @zumer/snapdom@3 # If your app uses the official plugins: npm install @zumer/snapdom-plugins@5 Thanks to everyone who sent bug reports and small reproductions; several rendering fixes came from them. If a capture of your UI looks wrong on v3, open an issue with the browser, the source element and the exported result. title: SnapDOM vs dom-to-image — A Maintained Alternative
text: Compare / Head to head / vs dom-to-image Library Comparison SnapDOM vs dom-to-image The original dom-to-image API against SnapDOM: rendering approach, plugin exports and the return types that change in a migration. Feature matrix Migration snippet TL;DR dom-to-image captures the DOM through SVG foreignObject . SnapDOM takes the same approach and adds open Shadow DOM, CSS counters and a plugin lifecycle. Live benchmark: runs in your browser SnapDOM vs dom-to-image, head to head Each library exports the same element to PNG five times. The average includes fresh and repeated calls; SnapDOM can reuse the unchanged capture. The gap depends on your hardware, content and capture pattern. Test element to be captured by both libraries. Run benchmark SnapDOM Waiting to start… dom-to-image Waiting to start… A quick overview dom-to-image clones a node, inlines CSS and assets, and wraps it in a <foreignObject> for the browser to render. It returns image data URLs or a PNG Blob. Its repository lists current releases and supported browsers. SnapDOM is a from-scratch implementation of the same idea, actively developed, with a plugin system on top. Lifecycle hooks ( beforeClone , afterClone , beforeRender , afterRender , beforeExport , afterExport ) let you alter capture state, observe exports and add custom exporters without forking. title: SnapDOM vs modern-screenshot — Compared (2026)
text: Compare / Head to head / vs modern-screenshot Library Comparison SnapDOM vs modern-screenshot Two modern libraries, the same core idea: clone the DOM and let the browser render it inside an SVG <foreignObject> . Where they differ, and how to move between them. Feature matrix Migration map TL;DR Both render cloned DOM through foreignObject and export SVG, PNG, JPEG, WebP, Canvas and Blob. modern-screenshot has a TypeScript API. SnapDOM adds a plugin system for HTML, structured context and maps, searchable PDF, editable vector, GIF and video. Both are MIT-licensed. Live benchmark: runs in your browser SnapDOM vs modern-screenshot, head to head Each library exports the same element to PNG five times. The average includes fresh and repeated calls; SnapDOM can reuse the unchanged capture. The gap depends on your hardware, content and capture pattern. Test element to be captured by both libraries. Run benchmark SnapDOM Waiting to start… modern-screenshot Waiting to start… Same approach, different scope modern-screenshot and SnapDOM belong to the same family as html-to-image. Where html2canvas re-implements the CSS painter, they deep-clone the DOM, inline styles, fonts and images, and wrap the clone in an SVG <foreignObject> for the browser to render. A shared approach does not mean identical output or timing; test the content and browsers you use. Core output formats overlap. SnapDOM exposes a capture and export lifecycle, with official plugins for other representations and transformations. Both have browser-specific rendering behavior worth checking on complex pages. Feature matrix Feature SnapDOM modern-screenshot Rendering approach Clone + foreignObject Clone + foreignObject Output formats SVG · PNG · JPG · WebP · Canvas · Blob PNG · JPEG · WebP · SVG · Canvas · Blob Plugin system Yes No Web fonts ( @font-face ) Embedded Yes Pseudo-elements Yes Yes Shadow DOM Open roots Open roots TypeScript-first API Typed, JS core Yes Runtime dependencies 0 0 License MIT MIT Feature support in other libraries changes. For anything version-specific, check their docs , or run the live benchmark above and compare the output. When to use which Choose SnapDOM when… You need fast captures, including repeats of the same element ( live benchmark ). Your output depends on browser-rendered CSS, fonts or open Shadow DOM; test those elements in your target browsers. You need PDF, editable vector, HTML or agent context, through plugins or your own. Check your existing workflow… Decide whether post-processing or lifecycle hooks suit your transformations. Test your Web Components in the browsers you support. Check Safari output and complex @font-face setups with your assets. Image formats overlap; optional SnapDOM plugins add HTML, context, PDF and animation exports. Same task, side by side Capture #card as a PNG and add the image to the page: modern-screenshot import { domToPng } from 'modern-screenshot' ; const dataUrl = await domToPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); const img = new Image (); img.src = dataUrl; document.body. appendChild (img); SnapDOM import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); modern-screenshot's domToPng resolves to a data-URL string; SnapDOM's toPng resolves to a ready-to-append HTMLImageElement . For a PNG data URL, read (await snapdom.toPng(el)).src ; snapdom.toRaw(el) returns an SVG data URL. Migration map Check format and return type at each call site. SnapDOM image helpers return HTMLImageElement ; read .src for a data URL. Its default Blob format is SVG, so request PNG when migrating a PNG Blob export. modern-screenshot SnapDOM domToPng(node) (await snapdom.toPng(node)).src domToJpeg(node) (await snapdom.toJpg(node)).src domToWebp(node) (await snapdom.toWebp(node)).src domToSvg(node) snapdom.toRaw(node) domToCanvas(node) snapdom.toCanvas(node) domToBlob(node) snapdom.toBlob(node, { format: 'png' }) Frequently asked questions Is SnapDOM or modern-screenshot faster? It depends on the element, assets, browser and whether the capture is fresh or repeated. Run the live lab with its listed versions , then test both on your own content. What does SnapDOM offer that modern-screenshot doesn't? A plugin lifecycle and the official plugins listed above. The two share the core SVG, raster image, Canvas and Blob outputs. Can I migrate from modern-screenshot without rewriting everything? Common exports have equivalents; return types and options need review. See the migration map above for the PNG string, SVG and Blob cases. Are both libraries free for commercial use? Yes. Both are MIT-licensed. Neither charges per capture or needs a screenshot server. title: SnapDOM vs Playwright for Screenshots — Compared
text: Compare / Architecture / vs Playwright Architecture Comparison SnapDOM vs Playwright Compare SnapDOM’s in-app element export with Playwright Test’s automated screenshot assertions across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. TL;DR SnapDOM captures an element already rendered in the user's browser. Playwright is best for cross-browser automation, end-to-end tests and server-side screenshots. Different tools for different execution models Requirement SnapDOM Playwright Runs in an existing web app Yes Via automation Needs server infrastructure No Usually Capture arbitrary URLs No Yes You choose the rendering browser No, it renders in the visitor's browser Yes Element export button Direct Network workflow Choose SnapDOM when The element is already in the user’s DOM. The export must stay client-side, with no private UI uploaded. You need SVG, PNG, JPEG, WebP, Canvas or Blob from one capture. Choose Playwright when You render without an active user browser. You need navigation, authentication automation or full-page URL screenshots. Output must come from a controlled browser build. That needs a test/runtime environment and browser binaries, and it solves a broader automation problem. Example: compare a card in a test In a project using Playwright Test, a visual assertion checks the rendered card against a stored baseline. Replace the route and selector with your application’s: import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test' test('report card matches its baseline', async ({ page }) => { await page.goto('http://localhost:3000/report') await expect(page.locator('#report-card')).toHaveScreenshot('report-card.png') }) Playwright Test manages the browser fixture and screenshot assertion. Review the initial baseline, then compare later runs in the same browser and environment. Its visual comparison guide explains baseline handling. Use SnapDOM when the application needs an export button rather than a test assertion. Frequently asked questions Can SnapDOM replace every Playwright screenshot? No. It replaces client-side element capture, not remote-page rendering or browser automation. Can both be used together? Yes. Playwright can load a page that uses SnapDOM, though direct screenshots are often simpler in an automated workflow. title: SnapDOM API Reference — Methods, Exporters & Options
text:
Docs / API reference Documentation SnapDOM API Reference Create a reusable capture with snapdom(el) , export it in several formats, or use a shortcut for one output. This page documents the v3 API. Shortcut methods Capture options Usage patterns Reusable capture Keep the result to create a preview and a downloaded file from the same state: const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el); const img = await result.toPng(); document.body.appendChild(img); await result.download({ format: 'jpg', filename: 'my-capture.jpg' }); One-step shortcuts Direct export when you need a single format: const png = await snapdom.toPng(el); const blob = await snapdom.toBlob(el, { format: 'png' }); document.body.appendChild(png); snapdom(el, options?) Returns export methods, immutable capture geometry ( meta ) and diagnostics ( warnings ). Pass capture options here; later exports can change output size, format and quality. Set filter and exclude when capturing. Exporters keep that captured content. Function-valued policies run again on each new capture; see callback and cache behavior . { url: string; // SVG by default; PNG after native capture needs: 'clone' | 'render'; meta: Readonly; warnings: Array<{ code: string; message: string; detail?: unknown }>; toRaw(): string; to(type, options?): Promise; toImg(options?): Promise; // deprecated toSvg(options?): Promise; toCanvas(options?): Promise; toBlob(options?): Promise; toPng(options?): Promise; toJpeg(options?): Promise; toJpg(options?): Promise; toWebp(options?): Promise; download(options?): Promise; } With the default SVG engine, url and toRaw() return serialized SVG without drawing pixels. A successful native capture lazily encodes PNG instead. toImg() is deprecated; use toSvg() . Frozen meta records the viewBox size, output target, content origin and clip rectangle. A plugin capture that stops at needs: 'clone' has no rendered image or render metadata; image access throws. Shortcut methods Each shortcut captures and exports in one call, with the same element and the full set of capture options . The table describes the default SVG engine. Method Description snapdom.toRaw(el, options?) Returns the serialized SVG data URL without rasterizing it. snapdom.toImg(el, options?) Deprecated alias of toSvg snapdom.toSvg(el, options?) title: SnapDOM Cache & preCapture — Performance
text: Docs / Cache and preCapture Documentation SnapDOM Cache Behavior Reuse captured results, assets and styles across calls. snapdom.preCapture() can prepare an eligible capture when a user focuses or approaches its control. Cache control preCapture() Three kinds of reuse One result exports the same captured state many times. A later snapdom(el) call may reuse an unchanged capture. Resource and style caches cut the work of a fresh capture; the cache option controls them. Cache control Leave cache at its default. The other modes are for debugging or older callers: Mode Description "soft" Content-keyed persistent resource/style caches are enabled (default) . "disabled" / false Clears and bypasses those persistent caches. A debug and testing escape, not a tuning option. "auto" / "full" Accepted for v2 compatibility and silently mapped to "soft" . The policy applies when the capture pipeline runs. It does not disable automatic repeat memoization; a memo hit does no resource/style-cache work. Example: // Clear and bypass persistent resource/style caches (debugging) await snapdom.toPng(el, { cache: 'disabled' }); Eligible unchanged captures reuse the saved result. Observable changes invalidate it; supported local changes rebuild the affected subtree, while other changes trigger a full capture. Canvas, video and other frame-driven content capture fresh. After a CSSOM edit such as sheet.insertRule() or rule.style.color = 'red' , pass invalidate: true ; those edits fire no mutation event. It clears style snapshots and captures fresh, and that capture may become the next reusable result. Callbacks that read application state: function-valued filter , exclude , excludeStyleProps and fallbackURL suspend capture memoization. Each new capture re-runs them, including their style or fallback decisions; a changed closure needs no invalidate . let privateMode = false; const options = { exclude: node => privateMode && node.matches('[data-private]'), excludeMode: 'remove' }; const before = await snapdom(el, options); privateMode = true; const after = await snapdom(el, options); // current policy, no invalidate needed Exporting before again still gives the earlier content; use after once policy changes. Do not depend on an exact number of callback invocations. V2 migration: remove the public burst switch. Eligible repeat memoization is automatic in v3. Resource-cache settings and image exports remain separate from this reuse policy; cache: 'disabled' is not a replacement for burst: false . preCapture() Call snapdom.preCapture() once during setup. When an eligible capture starts in a press or click handler, SnapDOM remembers that control, target and a shallow copy of the call's options. Later pointer-enter, focus or press events on that control can prepare the same capture before the handler needs it. Normal invalidation still applies. The first intent event on an unknown control also warms the visible viewport once. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; snapdom.preCapture(); // The first click teaches the association; later intent can prepare the capture. button.onclick = () => snapdom.toPng(hero, { scale: 2 }); preCapture() takes no arguments and reacts to intent events, with no polling. Programmatic callers can capture early themselves. The old preCache() API was removed in v3. title: SnapDOM Documentation — API, Options, Plugins & Cache
text: Docs / Overview Documentation SnapDOM Documentation Capture a DOM element as an image. Plugins add PDF, editable vector and recordings. This reference covers SnapDOM 3. Quick start API reference Installation npm i @zumer/snapdom@latest Or use yarn add @zumer/snapdom@latest . Quick start Capture an element as a PNG image: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; const img = await snapdom.toPng(document.querySelector('#card')); document.body.appendChild(img); Use snapdom(el) when you need several exports from the same captured state: const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#card')); await result.toPng(); // → HTMLImageElement await result.toSvg(); // → SVG as Image await result.download({ format: 'jpg', filename: 'card.jpg' }); Documentation sections API reference: methods & exporters Options: every capture option Plugins: extend the pipeline Cache & preCapture: performance Browser and module builds CDN Choose the script tag for a global snapdom , or the module import: <!-- Minified build --> <script src="https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.js"></script> <!-- Minified ES Module build --> <script type="module"> import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs"; </script> Build outputs Variant File Use case ESM (tree-shakeable) dist/snapdom.mjs Bundlers (Vite, webpack), import IIFE (global) dist/snapdom.js Browser script tag; exposes window.snapdom . No CommonJS build. Plugin registry import. The subpath shares the core runtime and registry: import { registerPlugins } from '@zumer/snapdom/plugins'; Capture flow A capture freezes the subtree; exports read that state. With the default SVG engine: Stage What happens Clone Deep clone with styles, open Shadow DOM and same-origin iframes. Leave nodes out with exclude . Styles & Pseudo Inline ::before / ::after as elements, resolve counter() / counters() . Images & Backgrounds Fetch and inline external images/backgrounds as data URLs. Fonts Embed the webfonts the capture uses by default. Render icon-font glyphs through the icon path. SVG Wrap clone in <foreignObject> , serialize to data:image/svg+xml . Export Return the SVG, rasterize to PNG/JPG/WebP/canvas, create a blob, or run a plugin export. Plugins can use the clone without rendering by declaring needs: 'clone' . Image exports require 'render' , the default. Hooks and custom outputs: see the plugins guide . Choose a recipe for your output For a PNG preview, a downloaded file or a Blob to upload, use the HTML to PNG recipe . For a shareable report with several charts, use the dashboard export recipe . For framework state updates, the Angular guide waits for the next render, the Svelte guide waits for tick() , and the Lit guide selects a card inside its shadow root after updateComplete . title: SnapDOM Options — Every Capture Option Explained
text: Docs / Options Documentation SnapDOM Options Set output size, load capture assets, exclude private content and control clipping. These options describe SnapDOM 3. All options API reference All options All capture methods accept an options object. Option Type Default Description debug boolean false Log fallbacks and errors to the console. Off, SnapDOM logs nothing. scale number 1 Output scale, used only when neither width nor height is set. dpr number devicePixelRatio Device pixel ratio for raster output. download() always uses 1; use scale for a sharper file. width / height number null Absolute output size; one dimension preserves aspect ratio. format png | jpeg | jpg | webp | svg png Default for format-selecting exports; named helpers choose their codec. jpg resolves to jpeg . type png | jpeg | jpg | webp | svg undefined Deprecated alias kept synchronized with canonical format ; prefer format , though either name is honored. backgroundColor string | null null Background fill; defaults to #ffffff only for JPEG/WebP. quality number 0.92 JPEG/WebP quality from 0 to 1. filename string snapDOM Download filename base. embedFonts boolean | "auto" "auto" Embed used webfonts; skip the font phase on system-font-only pages. true forces discovery; false skips text-font embedding. localFonts array [] Local fonts { family, src, weight?, style?, stretchPct? } . iconFonts string | RegExp | Array [] Extra icon-font matchers. excludeFonts object undefined Exclude font families, domains or subsets. fontStylesheetDomains string[] [] Extra domains allowed for cross-origin font CSS. exclude string | function | Array [] Selectors and/or predicates; returning true excludes the node. excludeMode "hide" | "remove" "hide" Keep an invisible spacer or remove the node. filter function null Inclusion predicate; true keeps a node, false filters it out. Can be used together with exclude . filterMode "hide" | "remove" "hide" Independent layout mode for nodes rejected by filter . clip "viewport" | rect null Capture only a viewport or page-coordinate rectangle. useProxy string '' CORS proxy template/base. fallbackURL string | function undefined Fallback for a broken . A function reads current state when a new capture needs a fallback. placeholders boolean true Show placeholders for failed resources/CORS iframes. outerTransforms boolean true Keep the root's rotation and scale/skew. false removes rotation while preserving scale/skew; root translation is normalized. outerShadows boolean | "subtree" false Strip or bound root effects; "subtree" also bounds descendant shadow ink. Blur bleed is included unless clip fixes the edges. reconcile boolean false Measure and pin clone boxes that diverge from the live DOM. fast boolean | 'auto' true true captures in one task; false pauses about every frame to keep the page responsive. 'auto' is experimental. invalidate boolean false Force one fresh capture that is not served from the existing memo and clear style snapshots after unobservable application changes. A stable fresh result may become the new memo. captureSelection boolean false Render the live text or field selection. canvas HTMLCanvasElement null Reuse an existing raster target. excludeStyleProps RegExp | function null Skip matching computed-style properties. A function is evaluated afresh for each new capture. cache "soft" | "disabled" | "auto" | "full" | false "soft" Controls persistent resource/style caches only. disabled / false clears and bypasses them; legacy values map to soft . Repeat memoization is separate. plugins array undefined Per-capture plugin definitions. engine "svg" | "html-in-canvas" "svg" Select one of SnapDOM's two render engines. svg serializes the finished clone; html-in-canvas paints that same clone through the browser's native API (Chrome 157 and newer), with SVG fallback everywhere else. html-in-canvas runs where the browser exposes drawElementImage() : Chrome 157 and newer, without a flag. Firefox and Safari have no implementation. There, and on any capture the native engine cannot paint ( body and html roots, transformed or zoomed ancestors, clip , width / height , outerShadows , plugins with render hooks), SnapDOM runs the SVG engine on the same clone, so the option is safe to set without a feature check. SVG stays the default because it is faster: the native paint waits for a rendering update. The guide says when to pick which; the lab compares both engines and lists which plugins run on each. A successful native capture is a bitmap: url / toRaw() lazily encode PNG, toSvg() returns a PNG-backed image, and toBlob() defaults to PNG unless a format was set. Requesting an SVG Blob from it rejects. Use engine: 'svg' when you need serialized SVG. debug SnapDOM logs nothing to the console by default. Set debug: true to log fallbacks and errors with the [SnapDOM] prefix: failed fetches, cross-origin iframes, downscaled exports, invalid exclude selectors. Without it, result.warnings records capture fallbacks and limits. await snapdom.toPng(el, { debug: true }); Automatic image downsampling SnapDOM reduces oversized raster assets to the resolution the requested output needs, accounting for output size, transforms and DPR. It preserves aspect ratio and never upscales the source. This covers , captured canvas/video frames, non-repeating backgrounds and SVG . The benefit depends on the export: Raster exports decode smaller embedded images, which saves work when sources are much larger than their display size. SVG exports carry smaller image data. url and toRaw() return that serialized capture without rasterizing it. The SVG engine keeps the original asset data, so later exports at a larger resolution still have it. Images that already fit are left alone. A native-engine capture is a bitmap, so enlarging it scales the captured pixels. Fallback image on load failure Provide a default image for failed loads: a fixed URL, or a callback that receives measured dimensions and returns a URL (handy for dynamic placeholders). // 1) Fixed URL fallback await snapdom.toSvg(element, { fallbackURL: '/images/fallback.png' }); // 2) Dynamic placeholder via callback await snapdom.toSvg(element, { fallbackURL: ({ width = 300, height = 150 }) => `https://placehold.co/${width}x${height}` }); // 3) With proxy (if your fallback host has no CORS) await snapdom.toSvg(element, { fallbackURL: ({ width = 300, height = 150 }) => `https://dummyimage.com/${width}x${height}/cccccc/666.png&text=img`, useProxy: 'https://proxy.corsfix.com/?' }); Notes: If the fallback also fails, the keeps its box and shows a grey placeholder, and result.warnings lists its URL. The callback's width/height come from the original element (dataset, style/attrs, etc.) when available. The callback also gets src , so it can send only the images that failed through your own proxy: see Capture images without CORS . Dimensions (scale, width, height) width or height takes precedence over scale . dpr still multiplies raster pixels. Only width : height scales proportionally (and vice versa). Both width and height : exact size, may distort. Cross-Origin Images & Fonts (useProxy) Set useProxy to a proxy you trust for assets the browser cannot read directly: await snapdom.toPng(el, { useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example/?url=' }); When configured, the proxy handles cross-origin resource requests, including assets that already allow CORS. Same-origin and already-proxied URLs skip it. Fonts embedFonts The default, 'auto' , embeds webfonts used by the capture and skips font discovery for system-font-only content. Use true to force discovery or false to skip text-font embedding. Icon-font glyphs use a separate rendering path. localFonts Declare font files or data URLs when stylesheet discovery cannot supply them: await snapdom.toPng(el, { embedFonts: true, localFonts: [ { family: 'Inter', src: '/fonts/Inter-Variable.woff2', weight: 400, style: 'normal' }, { family: 'Inter', src: '/fonts/Inter-Italic.woff2', style: 'italic' } ] }); iconFonts Add custom icon families (names or regex matchers). Useful for private icon sets: await snapdom.toPng(el, { iconFonts: ['MyIcons', /^(Remix|Feather) Icons?$/i] }); excludeFonts Skip specific non-icon fonts to speed up capture or avoid downloads. await snapdom.toPng(el, { embedFonts: true, excludeFonts: { families: ['Noto Serif', 'SomeHeavyFont'], // skip by family name subsets: ['cyrillic-ext'] // skip by unicode-range subset tag } }); Notes excludeFonts applies to text-font embedding, not the icon-font rendering path. Matching is case-insensitive for families . Hosts are matched by substring against the resolved URL. Selecting content: filter and exclude Combine filter and exclude with independent layout modes. The CSS-effect filter plugin is a separate feature. filter : a synchronous predicate. True keeps a node; any falsy return filters it out. filterMode : hide keeps an invisible spacer for filtered nodes; remove drops them and allows reflow. Defaults to hide . exclude : a selector, a synchronous boolean predicate, or any mix of both in an array. A node is excluded if any rule matches. excludeMode : the separate hide/remove mode for exclusions; defaults to hide . Both modes omit the affected node's content. // Hide private fields while preserving space; remove the toolbar. await snapdom(el, { filter: node => !node.matches('[data-private]'), filterMode: 'hide', exclude: ['.toolbar'], excludeMode: 'remove' }); Per node, data-capture="exclude" is checked first, then exclude , then filter . The first match sets the mode and stops evaluation. The attribute uses excludeMode ; a matching exclude wins even if filter would reject the same node with a different mode. A true filter result never overrides an exclusion. Example: mixing selectors and a predicate: await snapdom.toPng(el, { exclude: ['.cookie-banner', (node) => node.dataset.secret === 'true'], excludeMode: 'remove' }); For selector-only exclusions, hide keeps the original space: await snapdom.toPng(el, { exclude: ['.cookie-banner', '.tooltip', '[data-test="debug"]'] }); Function-valued rules run on every new capture; an existing result keeps its content. See callbacks and memoization . Other v2 option changes When migrating from v2, remove these obsolete settings: burst : remove this switch. Eligible repeat memoization is automatic. Use invalidate: true for one fresh capture after an otherwise unobservable change. compress : remove the switch. Bitmap optimization is automatic; there is no public opt-out to embed the original resources verbatim. resolvePicturePlaceholders and pictureResolver : remove these settings. The clone resolves responsive images and common lazy-loading attributes. There is no replacement tuning object; handle custom loading, concurrency or timeouts in the application before capture. fast: false remains supported. It now pauses about every frame instead of using idle callbacks; see fast . For removed APIs, TypeScript names and plugin-hook changes, see the migration guide . outerTransforms outerTransforms: false removes the captured root's rotation while retaining its scale and skew. Root translation is normalized during capture. Descendant transforms keep their own layout. outerTransforms: true (default) keeps the root's rotation and scale/skew, including individual CSS transforms. outerShadows outerShadows: false (default) : strips root box-shadow , text-shadow , outline , and drop-shadow() . It preserves filter: blur() , whose bleed is included when the capture is not explicitly clipped. outerShadows: true : keeps root shadow/outline/filter effects and expands the bounds for their ink. outerShadows: "subtree" : also widens the capture for descendant shadow ink outside the root box, bounded by clipping ancestors. Note: outerShadows: false does not promise a bleed-free box. An explicit clip is the exception: its edges are exact and never expand for bleed. Example // Keep root transforms and include root shadow bleed await snapdom.toSvg(el, { outerTransforms: true, outerShadows: true }); reconcile With the SVG engine, captured HTML lays out inside . Inline text and table cells can wrap differently when font metrics or layout constraints differ from the live page. reconcile: true measures the styled clone offscreen against the live subtree and pins boxes that diverge. It adds a layout pass and can roughly double capture time. Use it when you see wrapping differences; SnapDOM also emits a one-time suggestion for captures that may benefit. await snapdom.toPng(el, { reconcile: true }); fast A capture reads the computed style of every node in one pass. On a large tree, such as a data table built from web components, that pass can hold the main thread for hundreds of milliseconds: the page stops painting and responding until it ends. fast: false lets the capture give the page a turn about every frame, so scrolling, typing and animations continue while it runs. true , the default, captures in one task. The pauses add little to the total time. fast: 'auto' is experimental and may change: it pauses only once a capture runs past 40 ms, so short captures never pause. If the captured element changes while a capture is paused, SnapDOM clones it again in one task, so the image shows a state the page really had. That check uses the watchers behind repeat-capture memoization, so a capture that is never memoized (frame-driven trees, function-valued callbacks, captureSelection ) keeps what it read. await snapdom.toPng(table, { fast: false }); Automatic repeat-capture memoization Capturing the same unchanged element repeatedly would re-walk the tree and re-read every computed style on each call. SnapDOM memoizes eligible static elements from their first capture. Observable DOM, style, media and interaction changes invalidate the result; frame-driven content that cannot be observed reliably is captured fresh. A mutation triggers a conservative full capture, or a differential rebuild when that rebuild is provably equivalent. At most 64 elements stay memoized; the least recently captured one is released. // Stable captures can reuse the result; the text mutation invalidates it. for (let i = 0; i Frame-driven canvas/video/iframe trees bypass the memo. Programmatic CSSOM edits ( stylesheet.insertRule/deleteRule , cssRule.style.* on a rule rather than an element) expose no browser signal, so pass invalidate: true on the next call. That call skips the existing memo and clears style snapshots; a stable fresh result may become the new memo: sheet.insertRule('.card { color: rebeccapurple }'); await snapdom(el, { invalidate: true }); Callbacks that read application state bypass this reuse; see the cache guide for the supported policies and an example. Firefox and Safari have no implementation. There, and on any capture the native engine cannot paint ( body and html roots, transformed or zoomed ancestors, clip , width / height , outerShadows , plugins with render hooks), SnapDOM runs the SVG engine on the same clone, so the option is safe to set without a feature check. A successful native capture is a bitmap: url / toRaw() lazily encode PNG, toSvg() returns a PNG-backed image, and toBlob() defaults to PNG unless a format was set. title: debug
text: SnapDOM logs nothing to the console by default. title: Automatic image downsampling
text: SnapDOM reduces oversized raster assets to the resolution the requested output needs, accounting for output size, transforms and DPR. It preserves aspect ratio and never upscales the source. This covers , captured canvas/video frames, non-repeating backgrounds and SVG . The benefit depends on the export: Raster exports decode smaller embedded images, which saves work when sources are much larger than their display size. SVG exports carry smaller image data. url and toRaw() return that serialized capture without rasterizing it. The SVG engine keeps the original asset data, so later exports at a larger resolution still have it. Images that already fit are left alone. A native-engine capture is a bitmap, so enlarging it scales the captured pixels.

title: Fallback image on load failure

The callback's width/height come from the original element (dataset, style/attrs, etc.) when available. The callback also gets src , so it can send only the images that failed through your own proxy: see Capture images without CORS .

title: Dimensions (scale, width, height)
text: width or height takes precedence over scale . dpr still multiplies raster pixels. Only width : height scales proportionally (and vice versa). Both width and height : exact size, may distort.
