title: SnapDOM plugins: lifecycle, hooks and custom exports
text:
Docs / Plugin API Documentation SnapDOM Plugins Plugins turn a capture into HTML, structured context, element maps, PDFs or recordings. Write hooks when you need to change the captured content or add an output. Build a plugin Browse plugins What is a SnapDOM plugin A plugin is a plain object with a unique name and lifecycle hooks. Capture hooks can change the cloned content; defineExports adds methods to the result. Hooks may be synchronous or async . The core exports images, canvas and blobs; see the plugin catalogue for other outputs. Official plugins Package Outputs Reference and demos @zumer/snapdom-plugins HTML, structured context, element maps, effects and recordings. Plugin toolbox @zumer/snapdom-pdf Searchable, paginated PDF with selectable text, links and optional form fields. PDF @zumer/snapdom-vector Editable SVG and Figma clipboard export. Vector @zumer/snapdom-stream A live element as a canvas, for WebGL textures and video overlays. Stream Install the toolbox alongside SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer (plugins 5.x): npm install @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest import { filter } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/filter'; import { timestampOverlay } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/timestamp-overlay'; PDF, Vector and Stream are separate packages. See community plugins for packages by other authors. Redact fields, blocks and attributes redactInputs() masks field values, hides or removes private blocks and strips named attributes from images, HTML and structured exports. The rules for fields, blocks and attributes, and their limits, are documented on the redact-inputs page . Build a plugin This plugin changes the heading in the captured copy. The live heading stays the same: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; const card = document.createElement('article'); card.innerHTML = '

Original title

'; document.body.appendChild(card); const titlePlugin = { name: 'capture-title', afterClone({ clone }) { clone.querySelector('h2').textContent = 'Shared copy'; } }; const result = await snapdom(card, { plugins: [titlePlugin] }); document.body.appendChild(await result.toPng()); For a packaged plugin, start from the project template: npx degit zumerlab/snapdom/packages/plugin-template my-plugin Read the plugin specification for hook contracts and the contribution guide for packaging and tests. Get listed: once your plugin is published, submit a PR adding it to community-plugins.md . Registering plugins Global registration (applies to all captures): import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; // Pass plugin objects, calling factories with their options. snapdom.plugins( myPluginInstance, myPluginFactory({ optionA: true }), anotherFactory({ level: 2 }) ); Per-capture registration (that call only): const out = await snapdom(element, { plugins: [ [overlayFilterPlugin, { color: 'rgba(0,0,0,0.25)' }], [myFullPlugin, { providePdf: true }] ] }); Execution order = registration order. Per-capture plugins run before global ones. Duplicates are skipped by name ; a per-capture plugin with the same name overrides its global version. Lifecycle hooks Hooks run in capture order (see the capture flow ): Hook Stage Purpose beforeSnap Start Adjust options before any work. beforeClone Pre-clone Before DOM clone (modify live DOM carefully). resolveNode Per node Replace or skip a node after the compiled exclusion policy. afterClone Post-clone Modify cloned tree safely (e.g. inject overlay). beforeRender Pre-render Right before the selected render engine runs. afterRender Post-render Inspect context.dataURL / context.meta , and svgString on the SVG path. defineExports Result setup After capture, add custom exporters (e.g. toPdf ). beforeExport Per export Before each toPng , toSvg , etc. afterExport Per export Observe the returned result. afterSnap Once After the first successful export; cleanup. Order: beforeSnap → beforeClone → resolveNode (per node) → afterClone → beforeRender → afterRender → defineExports → [beforeExport → exporter → afterExport] → afterSnap . The bracketed segment repeats per export; afterSnap fires once after the first successful one. Export-hook return values are ignored. Change an export's options in beforeExport , or use defineExports to produce a custom result. v2.x.x migration: an afterExport return used to become the next hook's payload (it never replaced the caller's output). V3 ignores those returns and gives every hook the same export payload, so remove return-value chaining. The TypeScript name PluginExportFacade is gone; ctx.exports remains available inside defineExports . Infer its type there or use NonNullable after importing CaptureContext . Context object Capture hooks share one context with normalized options and stage results. Export hooks get a view for that export: Input & normalized options: element ; the options self-reference; needs ; shouldExclude(element) ; and the public capture options such as scale , dpr , width , height , format , backgroundColor , quality , fonts, exclusion, clipping, selection, reconciliation, invalidation, caching, plugins, and engine. format is canonical; deprecated type stays synchronized with it, and changing either in beforeSnap is honored. Intermediate values (depending on stage): clone , classCSS , styleCache , nodeMap , fontsCSS , baseCSS , svgString , dataURL , and frozen meta . Large clone-stage fields are released after rendering. Result setup: artifacts = { classCSS, fontsCSS, baseCSS, scrollbarCSS } and exports , the hook-free core exporter facade available to defineExports . During export: context.export = { type, options, requestedOptions, url, svgString } . type is the exporter name; frozen requestedOptions is what the caller supplied; options is the merged bag passed to the exporter. url is the captured data URL: SVG normally, PNG after a successful native capture. svgString() lazily decodes an SVG capture and throws for a raster capture. Change capture options in beforeSnap , except plugins , needs , invalidate and cache , which are already resolved. In beforeExport(ctx, payload) , mutate payload.options ; the context view does not steer that export. Pipeline depth and memoization A per-capture plugin may declare needs: "clone" or needs: "render" (the default). SnapDOM runs to the deepest requested stage. A clone-only result can expose plugin outputs such as context or an element map, but reading url or calling an image exporter throws. It does not recapture on demand. Global plugins must use "render" . Clone/render-affecting hooks suspend automatic repeat memoization unless the plugin declares pure: true . Pure beforeRender / afterRender hooks may also use differential recapture, while hooks involved in clone construction still force a conservative full recapture after a change. A capture stopped at needs: "clone" is never memoized because it has no render artifact. Declare purity only for deterministic, idempotent hooks; export-only hooks and defineExports do not need it. context.shouldExclude(node) covers both exclude and filter , following updates made in beforeSnap . Content selection checks data-capture="exclude" , then exclude , then filter ; the first omission decides its independent excludeMode or filterMode . resolveNode(node, context) runs after those checks. Return a replacement Node , null to skip, or undefined to continue normal cloning. Custom exports via plugins Plugins add exports through defineExports(context) . Each key you return (e.g. "pdf" ) becomes a method on the capture result ( toPdf() ). Use several outputs from one capture: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { htmlExport, contextExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins'; const out = await snapdom(element, { plugins: [htmlExport(), contextExport()] }); Call the custom export: const png = await out.toPng(); const html = await out.toHtml(); const context = await out.toContext({ format: 'json' }); Example: overlay filter plugin This example dims the captured HTML with a translucent overlay. Only the clone changes; the live page stays untouched. /** * Overlay filter for captured HTML. * Inserts a full-size
overlay on the cloned root. * * @param {{ color?: string; blur?: number }} [options] * color: overlay color (rgba/hex/hsl). Default: 'rgba(0,0,0,0.25)' * blur: optional blur in px (default: 0) */ export function overlayFilterPlugin(options = {}) { const color = options.color ?? 'rgba(0,0,0,0.25)'; const blur = Math.max(0, options.blur ?? 0); return { name: 'overlay-filter', /** * Add a full-coverage overlay to the cloned HTML root. * @param {any} context */ async afterClone(context) { const root = context.clone; if (!(root instanceof HTMLElement)) return; // HTML-only // Ensure containing block so absolute overlay anchors to the root if (getComputedStyle(context.element).position === 'static') { root.style.position = 'relative'; } const overlay = document.createElement('div'); overlay.style.position = 'absolute'; overlay.style.left = '0'; overlay.style.top = '0'; overlay.style.right = '0'; overlay.style.bottom = '0'; overlay.style.background = color; overlay.style.pointerEvents = 'none'; if (blur) overlay.style.filter = `blur(${blur}px)`; root.appendChild(overlay); } }; } Usage: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; // Global registration snapdom.plugins(overlayFilterPlugin({ color: 'rgba(0,0,0,0.3)', blur: 2 })); // Per-capture const out = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#card'), { plugins: [[overlayFilterPlugin, { color: 'rgba(255,200,0,0.15)' }]] }); const png = await out.toPng(); document.body.appendChild(png); The source element supplies the live position value because the clone is detached. Full plugin template Use this as a starting point for custom logic or exporters. export function myPlugin(options = {}) { return { /** Unique name used for de-duplication/overrides */ name: 'my-plugin', /** Optional pipeline depth; global plugins must remain at "render". */ needs: 'render', /** Set true only for deterministic/idempotent clone or render hooks. */ pure: false, /** Early adjustments before any clone/style work. */ async beforeSnap(context) {}, /** Before subtree cloning (use sparingly if touching the live DOM). */ async beforeClone(context) {}, /** Per source node, after context.shouldExclude(node) has been applied. */ async resolveNode(node, context) {}, /** After subtree cloning (safe to modify the cloned tree). */ async afterClone(context) {}, /** Right before the selected renderer runs. */ async beforeRender(context) {}, /** After rendering; svgString exists only on the SVG path. */ async afterRender(context) {}, /** * Define custom exporters during result setup. * Return a map { [key: string]: (ctx:any, opts:any) => Promise }. */ async defineExports(context) { return {}; }, /** Before EACH export call (toPng/toSvg/toBlob/...). */ async beforeExport(context, { format, options }) {}, /** * After EACH export call. * Observes { format, options, result }; return values are ignored. */ async afterExport(context, { format, options, result }) {}, /** Runs ONCE after the FIRST successful export finishes (cleanup). */ async afterSnap(context) {} }; } Before using a plugin in production: Keep frozen data on the capture context, not a shared plugin closure. Test repeated exports and concurrent captures with the same plugin instance. Use the core exports facade from defineExports for raster work, so sizing, compressed originals and Safari handling stay consistent. Test in Chromium, Firefox and Safari, including scale: 2 and changes after the first capture. Original title

'; document.body.appendChild(card); const titlePlugin = { name: 'capture-title', afterClone({ clone }) { clone.querySelector('h2').textContent = 'Shared copy'; } }; const result = await snapdom(card, { plugins: [titlePlugin] }); document.body.appendChild(await result.toPng()); For a packaged plugin, start from the project template: npx degit zumerlab/snapdom/packages/plugin-template my-plugin Read the plugin specification for hook contracts and the contribution guide for packaging and tests. title: Registering plugins
text: Global registration (applies to all captures): import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; // Pass plugin objects, calling factories with their options. snapdom.plugins( myPluginInstance, myPluginFactory({ optionA: true }), anotherFactory({ level: 2 }) ); Per-capture registration (that call only): const out = await snapdom(element, { plugins: [ [overlayFilterPlugin, { color: 'rgba(0,0,0,0.25)' }], [myFullPlugin, { providePdf: true }] ] }); Execution order = registration order. Per-capture plugins run before global ones. Duplicates are skipped by name ; a per-capture plugin with the same name overrides its global version.

title: Lifecycle hooks
text: Hooks run in capture order (see the capture flow ): Hook Stage Purpose beforeSnap Start Adjust options before any work. beforeClone Pre-clone Before DOM clone (modify live DOM carefully). resolveNode Per node Replace or skip a node after the compiled exclusion policy. afterClone Post-clone Modify cloned tree safely (e.g. inject overlay). beforeRender Pre-render Right before the selected render engine runs. afterRender Post-render Inspect context.dataURL / context.meta , and svgString on the SVG path. defineExports Result setup After capture, add custom exporters (e.g. toPdf ). beforeExport Per export Before each toPng , toSvg , etc. afterExport Per export Observe the returned result. afterSnap Once After the first successful export; cleanup. Order: beforeSnap → beforeClone → resolveNode (per node) → afterClone → beforeRender → afterRender → defineExports → [beforeExport → exporter → afterExport] → afterSnap . The bracketed segment repeats per export; afterSnap fires once after the first successful one. Export-hook return values are ignored. Change an export's options in beforeExport , or use defineExports to produce a custom result. v2.x.x migration: an afterExport return used to become the next hook's payload (it never replaced the caller's output). V3 ignores those returns and gives every hook the same export payload, so remove return-value chaining. The TypeScript name PluginExportFacade is gone; ctx.exports remains available inside defineExports . Infer its type there or use NonNullable<CaptureContext['exports']> after importing CaptureContext .

title: Context object
text: Capture hooks share one context with normalized options and stage results. Export hooks get a view for that export: Input & normalized options: element ; the options self-reference; needs ; shouldExclude(element) ; and the public capture options such as scale , dpr , width , height , format , backgroundColor , quality , fonts, exclusion, clipping, selection, reconciliation, invalidation, caching, plugins, and engine. format is canonical; deprecated type stays synchronized with it, and changing either in beforeSnap is honored. Intermediate values (depending on stage): clone , classCSS , styleCache , nodeMap , fontsCSS , baseCSS , svgString , dataURL , and frozen meta . Large clone-stage fields are released after rendering. Result setup: artifacts = { classCSS, fontsCSS, baseCSS, scrollbarCSS } and exports , the hook-free core exporter facade available to defineExports . During export: context.export = { type, options, requestedOptions, url, svgString } . type is the exporter name; frozen requestedOptions is what the caller supplied; options is the merged bag passed to the exporter. url is the captured data URL: SVG normally, PNG after a successful native capture. svgString() lazily decodes an SVG capture and throws for a raster capture. Change capture options in beforeSnap , except plugins , needs , invalidate and cache , which are already resolved. In beforeExport(ctx, payload) , mutate payload.options ; the context view does not steer that export.

title: Pipeline depth and memoization
text: A per-capture plugin may declare needs: "clone" or needs: "render" (the default). SnapDOM runs to the deepest requested stage. A clone-only result can expose plugin outputs such as context or an element map, but reading url or calling an image exporter throws. It does not recapture on demand. Global plugins must use "render" . Clone/render-affecting hooks suspend automatic repeat memoization unless the plugin declares pure: true . Pure beforeRender / afterRender hooks may also use differential recapture, while hooks involved in clone construction still force a conservative full recapture after a change. A capture stopped at needs: "clone" is never memoized because it has no render artifact. Declare purity only for deterministic, idempotent hooks; export-only hooks and defineExports do not need it. context.shouldExclude(node) covers both exclude and filter , following updates made in beforeSnap . Content selection checks data-capture="exclude" , then exclude , then filter ; the first omission decides its independent excludeMode or filterMode . resolveNode(node, context) runs after those checks. Return a replacement Node , null to skip, or undefined to continue normal cloning.

text: Ecosystem Plugins · Tools Plugins and tools built on SnapDOM. Plugins add outputs and transforms to a capture. SnapDiff, SnapEye and SnapSurf use SnapDOM for visual testing and browser agents. PDF Plugin Vector Plugin Stream Plugin The toolbox 12 plugins SnapDiff Tool SnapEye Tool SnapSurf Experimental Choose by the job Job Use Export an element as an image SnapDOM core Make a PDF with selectable text and pages PDF Edit the result in Figma or an SVG tool Vector Feed a live element to WebGL or a video call Stream Redact, filter, record or map a capture The toolbox Check that nothing changed visually SnapDiff Give a coding agent before/after evidence SnapEye Let an agent reach a state and verify it SnapSurf (experimental) One settings panel, three kinds of checks 1 · Reach the state SnapSurf opens the page and clicks Settings. title: Capture an Angular Component as an Image — SnapDOM
text:
How-to / Frameworks / Angular Framework Guide · Angular 19+ Capture an Angular component Download a signal-driven Angular view after its next render, with a typed viewChild reference and asset readiness checks. TL;DR Use viewChild.required to select the rendered card and afterNextRender to capture after signal updates reach the DOM. Keep the export button outside the captured element. Install and use SnapDOM in Angular Install the capture library in your existing Angular project: npm install @zumer/snapdom Add this standalone component to your Angular view. import { Component, ElementRef, Injector, afterNextRender, inject, signal, viewChild } from '@angular/core' import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' @Component({ selector: 'app-export-card', standalone: true, template: `

{{ title() }}

Ready to share.

{{ error() }}

`, }) export class ExportCardComponent { card = viewChild.required>('card') title = signal('Monthly report') saving = signal(false) error = signal('') private injector = inject(Injector) save() { this.saving.set(true) this.error.set('') afterNextRender(async () => { try { const el = this.card().nativeElement await document.fonts.ready await Promise.all(Array.from(el.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())) await snapdom.download(el, { format: 'png', filename: 'angular-card' }) } catch (error) { this.error.set(error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Capture failed') } finally { this.saving.set(false) } }, { injector: this.injector }) } } Wait for Angular’s next render The click handler may change signals, fetch data or reveal an @if block. Reading the DOM immediately after that change can capture the previous view. Angular’s afterNextRender callback runs after the next application render; pass the component’s injector when registering it from an event handler. The example’s saving signal schedules that render. An optional viewChild can be undefined when its element is absent; use a required query only for a card that is always rendered. If the card is conditional, wait until it exists before enabling export. Wait for data, images and fonts Finish the application’s data request before scheduling capture. afterNextRender waits for Angular’s DOM work, not network responses. The example then waits for document.fonts.ready and decodes images inside the card; a broken image reaches the status message instead of silently producing an incomplete report. For an exportable chart, wait for its own animation or ready event too. When the output is destined for an upload instead of a download, follow the PNG Blob and FormData pattern . Angular SSR and hydration Keep the export attached to a browser click. Render callbacks do not run during server-side rendering, and a server cannot provide the live layout that SnapDOM captures. For a hydrated application, wait until the component is interactive and its data has settled; a render callback alone is not a blanket guarantee that every child has completed hydration. Frequently asked questions Why does the PNG show the previous signal value? The capture ran before Angular applied the signal change to the DOM. Register afterNextRender with the component injector, then capture from its callback. Can I capture an Angular component on the server? This recipe captures a view in the browser after it becomes interactive. Server-side screenshot jobs need a browser automation tool to load and render the route first. Related Choose the capture root HTML to PNG SnapDOM in React Export API

title: Capture a Lit Component as an Image — SnapDOM
text:
How-to / Frameworks / Lit Framework Guide · Lit 3 Capture a Lit component Export a Lit card from its open shadow root, wait for updateComplete, and choose whether the image includes the host or only the card. TL;DR Wait for this.updateComplete , select the card from this.renderRoot , then export it. SnapDOM can walk open shadow roots; document.querySelector cannot reach their internal nodes. Install and use SnapDOM in Lit Install the capture library in your existing Lit project: npm install @zumer/snapdom Load this module in your client entry, then place in your page. import { LitElement, html, css } from 'lit' import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' class ExportCard extends LitElement { static properties = { title: { type: String }, saving: { state: true }, error: { state: true }, } static styles = css` article { padding: 24px; background: #eef3ff; border-radius: 12px; } ` constructor() { super() this.title = 'Monthly report' this.saving = false this.error = '' } async save() { this.saving = true this.error = '' try { await this.updateComplete const card = this.renderRoot.querySelector('#card') await document.fonts.ready await Promise.all(Array.from(card.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())) await snapdom.download(card, { format: 'png', filename: 'lit-card' }) } catch (cause) { this.error = cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : 'Capture failed' } finally { this.saving = false } } render() { return html`

${this.title}

Ready to share.

${this.error}

` } } customElements.define('export-card', ExportCard) Wait for the right Lit element updateComplete resolves after this element finishes its update. It does not promise that every nested Lit component or asynchronous resource is ready. If a known child owns part of the report, await that child’s updateComplete before capture too: await this.updateComplete const chart = this.renderRoot.querySelector('report-chart') await chart.updateComplete await snapdom.download(this.renderRoot.querySelector('#card'), { format: 'png' }) For third-party charts, use their documented ready signal. Do not add a fixed timeout and assume the subtree has settled. Choose the host or the internal card Capturing this exports the custom element host, including its open shadow tree and host-level styles. Capturing this.renderRoot.querySelector('#card') exports only the card, leaving the form controls out of the image. The example uses the latter. A closed shadow root is inaccessible to code outside the component. Keep capture inside the component, where the render root reference is available, or provide an explicit export method. SnapDOM cannot bypass that browser boundary. See the Shadow DOM capture recipe for the open-root case. Assets and server-rendered Lit Lit’s update lifecycle does not wait for fonts or image downloads; the example waits for those resources explicitly and reports failures. If a child contains a same-origin iframe, also wait for the frame to load and use the iframe capture recipe . In a server-rendered application, invoke the export after the browser has upgraded and hydrated the relevant components. Run this module in the client entry and capture from an interaction, rather than from the server rendering pipeline. Frequently asked questions Why can document.querySelector not find my card? The card is inside the component’s shadow root. Select it with this.renderRoot.querySelector from the component, or capture the host to include its open shadow tree. Does updateComplete include child updates? Not by default. Wait for known child components’ updateComplete promises and for any separate data or asset readiness signals before capture. title: Capture HTML to PNG in Next.js with SnapDOM
text: How-to / Frameworks / Next.js Next.js Guide Capture HTML to PNG in Next.js Use a client component and a dynamic import to capture after hydration, loading SnapDOM when the user exports. TL;DR SnapDOM needs a browser DOM. Use a client component for the ref and event handler, then import SnapDOM inside the handler. This keeps capture code out of server rendering. 1. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Run the capture in a browser event handler after the component has hydrated. 2. App Router: client component Create a client component that owns the ref and capture logic. 'use client' defines a client boundary, but client components may still be prerendered. Importing SnapDOM inside the click handler keeps that import in the browser. // app/capture/CaptureCard.tsx 'use client' ; import { useRef } from 'react' ; export default function CaptureCard () { const cardRef = useRef <HTMLDivElement>( null ); async function handleCapture () { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const { snapdom } = await import ( '@zumer/snapdom' ); const img = await snapdom. toPng (cardRef.current, { scale: 2 }); document.body. appendChild (img); } return ( < div > < div ref={cardRef} className= "card" > < h3 >Hello SnapDOM</ h3 > < p >Captured from a Next.js client component.</ p > </ div > < button onClick={handleCapture}>Capture</ button > </ div > ); } Try it live This plain HTML demo uses the same capture call as the client component. A client-side capture alone does not update that page. For server-rendered cards, see the @vercel/og comparison below. Common gotchas "window is not defined" / "document is not defined" errors Import SnapDOM inside a browser event handler, as shown above, or load the capture component with dynamic(() => import('./CaptureCard'), { ssr: false }) from a client component. A 'use client' directive alone does not prevent prerendering. The captured image is blank in production but works in dev Check that the target is mounted, has a nonzero size and contains the expected data. Wait for layout-changing assets such as fonts. SnapDOM embeds used web fonts with embedFonts: 'auto' by default; a blank capture can have causes beyond font loading. Should I use SnapDOM or @vercel/og for OG images? Different tools. @vercel/og renders Satori-compatible JSX on the server (no real browser, no full CSS). SnapDOM captures rendered DOM in the browser, including the current component state and browser layout. Use @vercel/og when the card is fully described in JSX and you don't need real browser fidelity. Use SnapDOM when you want to capture a piece of your live UI with its current browser layout. Can I run SnapDOM in a server action? No. Server actions run in Node.js without a real DOM. Use Puppeteer or Playwright if you need server-side screenshots, and SnapDOM client-side. A configured proxy handles cross-origin asset requests; same-origin requests remain direct. Does it work with Turbopack? SnapDOM has an ES module entry and no native runtime dependencies. title: Capture HTML to PNG in React with SnapDOM
text:
How-to / Frameworks / React React Guide Capture HTML to PNG in React Integrate SnapDOM with React refs, display image previews with object URL cleanup, and reuse the capture logic across components. TL;DR Attach a useRef to the element you want to capture, install @zumer/snapdom , and call snapdom.toPng(ref.current) from a button handler. SnapDOM returns the HTMLImageElement ready to append. 1. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest SnapDOM ships an ES module with no runtime dependencies. For server-rendered apps, follow the Next.js guide to keep capture in the browser. 2. Minimal capture component import { useRef } from 'react' ; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; export function CaptureCard () { const cardRef = useRef ( null ); const handleCapture = async () => { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (cardRef.current, { scale: 2 }); document.body. appendChild (img); }; return ( < div > < div ref={cardRef} className= "card" > < h3 >Hello SnapDOM < p >This whole div will be captured. < button onClick={handleCapture}>Capture ); } The button appends the captured PNG to the document. Try it live This plain HTML demo runs the same capture call on a rendered card. In React, the component ref supplies that DOM element. Hello SnapDOM This whole div will be captured. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. 3. Download instead of appending Use download() to save the captured card as a file: const handleDownload = async () => { if (!cardRef.current) return ; const result = await snapdom (cardRef.current); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); }; 4. Keep the captured image in state If you want to render a preview inside your component, store the image as an object URL using toBlob + URL.createObjectURL : import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; export function CapturePreview() { const cardRef = useRef(null); const [previewUrl, setPreviewUrl] = useState(null); useEffect(() => () => { if (previewUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(previewUrl); }, [previewUrl]); const handleCapture = async () => { if (!cardRef.current) return; const blob = await snapdom.toBlob(cardRef.current, { format: 'png' }); setPreviewUrl(URL.createObjectURL(blob)); }; return ( <>
…
{previewUrl && } ); } The effect releases each object URL when the preview changes or the component unmounts. 5. Reusable React hook If you call SnapDOM from many components, extract a small hook: // useSnapdom.js import { useCallback, useRef } from 'react' ; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; export function useSnapdom (options = {}) { const ref = useRef ( null ); const capture = useCallback ( async (format = 'png' ) => { if (!ref.current) return null ; const result = await snapdom (ref.current, options); return result. to (format); }, [options]); return { ref, capture }; } Use it like this: const { ref, capture } = useSnapdom ({ scale: 2 , embedFonts: true }); return ( <> < div ref={ref}>… < button onClick={() => capture ( 'png' )}>Capture ); Export a real component For a minimal PNG download handler, use the React card download recipe . For several widgets together, use the dashboard recipe . For a file to upload, adapt the PNG Blob and FormData example after the ref’s content has finished rendering. Common gotchas My captured image is blank or empty Check these conditions: 1. You called snapdom before the ref was attached. Always trigger the capture from a user event (button click) or inside useEffect after mount, never directly inside the component body. 2. The captured element has display: none or is detached from the document. SnapDOM needs a rendered element in the live DOM tree. If the handler updates React state before capture, wait for that update to commit. Capturing immediately after a state setter can read the previous DOM. Data, chart animations, fonts and images have separate readiness checks. Web fonts render as Times New Roman SnapDOM defaults to embedFonts: 'auto' and embeds used web fonts when their files are accessible. Wait for application data and fonts to settle before capture if they can change the layout. Cross-origin images don't render SnapDOM fetches external images and inlines them as data URLs. If your CDN doesn't send Access-Control-Allow-Origin , configure a proxy with { useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' } . Does SnapDOM work with React 18 strict mode? Yes. SnapDOM doesn't subscribe to React lifecycle, so the double-invocation in development strict mode doesn't affect captures triggered from event handlers. Can I use SnapDOM in Next.js? Yes — use a client component ( 'use client' ) and a dynamic import. See the dedicated Next.js guide . Does SnapDOM work with React Native? No. SnapDOM is a browser-only library — it relies on DOM APIs and SVG foreignObject that don't exist in React Native. title: Capture a Svelte Component as an Image — SnapDOM
text:
How-to / Frameworks / Svelte Framework Guide · Svelte 5 Capture a Svelte component Export a Svelte 5 card using bind:this, reactive state and tick(), including the latest edit and a browser-only import. TL;DR Bind the card with bind:this , apply any state changes, then await tick() before export. In SvelteKit, load SnapDOM inside the click handler so capture runs only in the browser. Install and use SnapDOM in Svelte Install the capture library in your existing Svelte project: npm install @zumer/snapdom Save this as ExportCard.svelte and render it in your page.

{title}

Capture after a Svelte state update Svelte batches DOM updates. The example normalizes the title and then awaits tick() , so the downloaded card contains the normalized title rather than the previous value. tick() does not wait for a fetch, chart animation or image download; await those separately. The reference from bind:this becomes available after mount. If the card lives inside an {#if} block, keep the export button disabled while it is absent. Use a click handler rather than an effect that could export again whenever reactive state changes. Wait for assets without including the controls The card is the capture root; the title input, button and status message remain outside it. Image decoding and document.fonts.ready settle the card’s assets after the DOM update. Rejected image decoding is surfaced in the status message, so the user can retry after correcting the asset. Use snapdom.toBlob(card, { format: 'png' }) for an upload and the FormData recipe to send the file to your endpoint. For dashboard layouts containing graphs, use the dashboard export recipe . Use the same component in SvelteKit SvelteKit can render this component on the server. The dynamic import and every DOM read are inside save() , which the browser invokes from the button. Do not move capture into module initialization or a server load function. This example uses Svelte 5 runes and onclick . A legacy-mode component can use ordinary reactive variables, but still needs bind:this and the same wait for pending DOM updates. Frequently asked questions Does tick() wait for my API response? No. Await the application data request, update state, then await tick(). Fonts, image decoding and chart animations have their own readiness checks. Why is bind:this undefined? The element is not mounted yet or its conditional block is absent. Trigger export after mount, while the bound card is present. text: How-to / Frameworks / Vue Vue 3 Guide Capture HTML to PNG in Vue 3 Use a Vue template ref and nextTick() to capture the current DOM, then download the image or display a preview. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Zero runtime dependencies and an ES module entry. In Nuxt, keep imports and capture calls inside the browser boundary. 2. Minimal capture component (Composition API) The template ref name ( cardRef ) must match the variable declared in script setup . nextTick() waits for pending Vue DOM updates; wait separately for application data and layout-changing assets. Try it live This plain HTML demo captures a rendered card. In Vue, cardRef.value supplies the element to the same SnapDOM call. Hello SnapDOM This whole div will be captured. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. 3. Download instead of appending async function download() { await nextTick(); if (!cardRef.value) return; const result = await snapdom(cardRef.value); await result.download({ format: 'png', filename: 'card' }); } 4. Render a live preview Capture to a Blob and create an object URL to use as the preview source: The handler releases the previous preview URL; onUnmounted releases the final one. 5. Reusable composable // useSnapdom.js import { nextTick, ref } from 'vue'; import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; export function useSnapdom(options = {}) { const target = ref(null); async function capture(format = 'png') { await nextTick(); if (!target.value) return null; const result = await snapdom(target.value, options); return result.to(format); } return { target, capture }; } < script setup > import { useSnapdom } from './useSnapdom' ; const { target, capture } = useSnapdom ({ scale: 2 , embedFonts: true }); < template > < div ref= "target" > … < button @click= "capture('png')" > Capture Choose the Vue export target Keep the ref on the visible card, invoice or dashboard, and keep the export controls outside that root. Web fonts aren't being captured SnapDOM defaults to embedFonts: 'auto' and embeds used web fonts when their files are accessible. In Nuxt, load SnapDOM with a dynamic import inside that handler or inside onMounted ; can keep the capture UI out of server rendering. title: Capture images without CORS headers: placeholders, fallbackURL and a proxy
text: How-to / Special cases / Capture images without CORS How-To Recipe Capture images without CORS headers Handle map tiles and CDN images that the browser can display but scripts cannot read: inspect warnings, enable CORS or use a proxy you control. TL;DR An unreadable keeps its box and, by default, shows a grey placeholder with an image-fallback entry in result.warnings . To get the real pixels, serve the image with CORS headers, or send the images that fail through a small proxy of your own with fallbackURL . What a capture does with an image it cannot read The capture resolves as usual. Each image SnapDOM could not read keeps its size and position and shows a grey box marked "img"; with placeholders: false the box stays empty. With placeholders enabled, result.warnings lists the failed URL and debug: true logs it. placeholders: false leaves an empty box without this warning. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#map')) for (const w of result.warnings) console.log(w.code, w.message) // image-fallback image failed to inline, using placeholder: https://tiles.example.com/5/16/10.png Why the page shows it and the capture cannot SnapDOM renders the element as an SVG image, and an SVG image loads nothing from the network, so every image is read and embedded first. A browser displays an image from any site, but it hands the pixels to a script only when the image's server allows it with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. Without that header no script can read the image, SnapDOM included. Fix it at the source If you control the server, add the header to the image responses. Nothing else changes, in your code or in the capture: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * Send the images that fail through your own proxy When the images come from a server you do not control, put a proxy in between that fetches them and adds the header. Hand it to fallbackURL , which SnapDOM calls only for an it could not read: const PROXY = 'https://image-proxy.your-account.workers.dev/?url=' const result = await snapdom(map, { fallbackURL: ({ src }) => PROXY + encodeURIComponent(src) }) useProxy: PROXY works too, but it sends every request to another origin through the proxy: images that already allow CORS, CSS backgrounds, stylesheets and font files. Use it when the images you cannot read are CSS backgrounds or SVG , which fallbackURL does not cover. The proxy then has to accept your font hosts and their stylesheets and font files as well, or embedded fonts stop loading. A small image proxy This Cloudflare Worker does the job. It fetches only from the hosts you list, because an open proxy fetches anything for anyone, and it returns only images. Redirect responses are rejected so they cannot send the fetch to an unlisted host. // A CORS proxy for the images SnapDOM cannot read, as a Cloudflare Worker. // Only the hosts listed here: an open proxy fetches anything for anyone. const HOSTS = ['tiles.example.com', 'icons.example.com'] export default { async fetch(request) { let target try { target = new URL(new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('url')) } catch {} if (request.method !== 'GET' || !target || target.protocol !== 'https:' || !HOSTS.includes(target.hostname)) { return new Response('Not allowed', { status: 403 }) } const upstream = await fetch(target, { redirect: 'manual' }) const type = upstream.headers.get('content-type') || '' if (!upstream.ok || !type.startsWith('image/')) { return new Response('Not an image', { status: 502 }) } return new Response(upstream.body, { headers: { 'content-type': type, 'cache-control': 'public, max-age=86400', 'access-control-allow-origin': '*' } }) } } Create a Worker in the Cloudflare dashboard, paste the code, put your image hosts in HOSTS and deploy. Any server that adds the header does the same job. Maps drawn on a canvas OpenLayers paints its tiles into a , and so does any code that calls drawImage . A canvas that drew an image from a server without CORS headers is tainted: the browser blocks every read of it, from any script. The capture still resolves, the canvas comes out blank, and result.warnings holds a canvas-tainted entry. Nothing can read that canvas afterwards, so the fix is to load the tiles with CORS in the first place, from a server or a proxy that sends the header: import TileLayer from 'ol/layer/Tile' import XYZ from 'ol/source/XYZ' new TileLayer({ source: new XYZ({ // a tile URL without a query string of its own can follow ?url= as it is url: PROXY + 'https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png', crossOrigin: 'anonymous' }) }) In your own canvas code, set img.crossOrigin = 'anonymous' before img.src . Frequently asked questions Why does the image show on the page but not in the capture? The browser displays images from any site, but lets a script read one only when its server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin . SnapDOM has to read an image to embed it. Do I need a proxy if my images already send CORS headers? No. SnapDOM fetches them directly. Can SnapDOM capture a tainted canvas? No script can read a tainted canvas. Load the images it draws with crossOrigin from a server or proxy that allows it, and the canvas captures normally. Does this apply to the PDF plugin? Yes. The PDF pages come from the capture you hold, so fallbackURL and useProxy set on snapdom() fix the PDF too. Export a PDF with cross-origin images covers that case and the Content Security Policy that blocks the fetch while the page shows the image. title: Capture a DOM Element Without Puppeteer — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Special cases / Capture without Puppeteer How-To Recipe Capture an element without Puppeteer When the element already exists in the user’s browser, export it locally instead of sending HTML to a headless-browser service. TL;DR Use SnapDOM client-side when you need a user-triggered export of an existing DOM element. Capture the element in the page Install @zumer/snapdom , select the rendered element, and capture it: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const element = document.querySelector('#shareable') await snapdom.download(element, { format: 'png', filename: 'shareable', scale: 2, }) The user’s browser does the work No browser process needs to be launched because the page’s existing browser performs the capture. This removes a server round trip and avoids operating a Chromium worker for user-facing exports. Capture locally, no screenshot server Click capture: the element is processed in this page without sending its DOM to a screenshot server. JS Client-side capture No Puppeteer · no Playwright · no upload Capture in browser Create local Blob The captured result will appear here. Limits and common mistakes Use Puppeteer or Playwright when rendering must happen without a user browser, must use a controlled engine, or must capture arbitrary external pages. SnapDOM captures accessible DOM, not remote URLs. Frequently asked questions Is SnapDOM a replacement for every Puppeteer screenshot? No. It replaces client-side element export, not server-side URL rendering or browser automation. Does it work offline? The capture can work offline once the page and required assets are locally available; uncached remote fonts or images cannot be fetched without a network. title: How to Capture a Full Web Page in the Browser — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Special cases / Capture a full page How-To Recipe Capture a full web page Snapshot the document’s rendered DOM rather than only the visible viewport. TL;DR Pass document.documentElement or a dedicated page wrapper to SnapDOM. Capture the whole document Install @zumer/snapdom , select the rendered element, and capture it: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const page = document.documentElement const capture = await snapdom(page, { embedFonts: true, outerShadows: true, }) await capture.download({ format: 'png', filename: 'full-page' }) The root includes content beyond the viewport Capturing the root includes the document’s layout beyond the current viewport. A dedicated content wrapper is often preferable when fixed navigation or overlays should be excluded. Capture content beyond a viewport This scrollable preview is intentionally tall; capture exports the complete selected DOM subtree. Long-form page 01 Hero section Content rendered below the initial visible area remains part of this DOM element. 02 Features Content rendered below the initial visible area remains part of this DOM element. 03 Customer story Content rendered below the initial visible area remains part of this DOM element. 04 Pricing Content rendered below the initial visible area remains part of this DOM element. 05 Final call to action Content rendered below the initial visible area remains part of this DOM element. Capture full element Download full element The captured result will appear here. Pages taller than the canvas limit With the default SVG engine, PNG and JPEG file exports automatically preserve the requested resolution beyond canvas limits. SnapDOM renders the frozen capture in windows and encodes one file: const capture = await snapdom(page) await capture.download({ format: 'png', scale: 2 }) // Or get a file to upload/store: const blob = await capture.toBlob({ format: 'png', scale: 2, dpr: 1 }) // JPEG works the same way, up to 65,535px per side: await capture.download({ format: 'jpg', scale: 2, quality: 0.9 }) download() always uses DPR 1. For PNG this automatic path requires CompressionStream ; older browsers keep the existing downscale and warning, as does a JPEG past 65,535px per side. WebP cannot go past 16,383px per side. Large files still need encoding time and memory, and image viewers have their own limits. toCanvas() , toPng() , toJpg() and WebP exports keep the single-canvas size guards: 16,384px per side in Safari, 32,767px in Chrome/Firefox, plus an area limit. If you need separate canvases, export pieces with crop : const capture = await snapdom(page) const { contentX, contentY, w0, h0 } = capture.meta const pieceHeight = 4000 // CSS px for (let y = 0; y < h0; y += pieceHeight) { const canvas = await capture.toCanvas({ scale: 2, dpr: 1, crop: { x: contentX, y: contentY + y, width: w0, height: Math.min(pieceHeight, h0 - y) } }) // save or upload this piece, then move on } crop uses SVG viewBox coordinates, including bleed and padding; contentX / contentY locate the content. Each call returns one canvas. The capture runs once; only the rasterization repeats. Keep pieceHeight × scale × dpr under the limit. How tiling works . Limits and common mistakes Very large pages create large SVG and bitmap surfaces. For huge or virtualized documents, capture logical sections or render hidden items before capture. Frequently asked questions Is this the same as a viewport screenshot? No. A viewport screenshot captures visible screen pixels; this captures the selected DOM subtree and its layout extent. Will lazy content be included? Only content that exists and has resolved. Load or render lazy sections before starting capture. title: How to Capture an Iframe as an Image — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Special cases / Capture an iframe How-To Recipe Capture an iframe as an image Include a same-origin iframe in an element capture while preserving the frame’s visible viewport and surrounding styles. TL;DR Capture the parent container normally. Same-origin iframe documents are accessible; cross-origin iframe contents are not. Capture the panel with its iframe Install @zumer/snapdom , select the rendered element, and capture it: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const panel = document.querySelector('#panel-with-frame') const image = await snapdom.toPng(panel, { placeholders: true, embedFonts: true, }) document.body.appendChild(image) Same-origin frames are inlined, cross-origin frames become placeholders SnapDOM reads an accessible iframe document, captures its visible content and places the result back into the parent snapshot. A cross-origin frame cannot be read, so it is drawn as a striped placeholder of the same size (the default) and result.warnings records iframe-cross-origin . Enable debug: true to log it; the parent layout keeps the frame's space. Capture a same-origin iframe The embedded srcdoc frame is same-origin and can be included in the parent capture. SAME-ORIGIN FRAME Inside iframe This document can be read and captured. " style="display:block;width:100%;height:120px;border:0"> Capture iframe panel Download panel The captured result will appear here. Limits and common mistakes Wait for the frame to load before capturing its parent. They become a striped placeholder the size of the frame, so the surrounding layout is unchanged and the unavailable content is explicit. The button below downloads only the article; it stays outside the captured root: import { useRef } from 'react' import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' export function ShareCard() { const cardRef = useRef(null) const save = async () => { const capture = await snapdom(cardRef.current, { embedFonts: true }) await capture.download({ format: 'png', filename: 'share-card' }) } return <> <article ref={cardRef}>Your component</article> <button onClick={save}>Download PNG</button> </> } React renders, SnapDOM captures the DOM SnapDOM is framework-agnostic: React renders the component and SnapDOM captures the resulting DOM. title: Generate a Social or Open Graph Card from HTML — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Real content / Generate a social card How-To Recipe Generate a social card from HTML Design the card with ordinary HTML and CSS, preview it live, then export the rendered component as a shareable image. TL;DR Give the card its intended CSS dimensions, wait for fonts and images, then export a PNG. Export width / height resize the output without reflowing the card. Render the card to PNG Install @zumer/snapdom , select the rendered element, and capture it: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' await document.fonts.ready const card = document.querySelector('#social-card') await Promise.all(Array.from(card.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())) const image = await snapdom.toPng(card, { width: 1200, height: 630, dpr: 1, embedFonts: true, backgroundColor: '#ffffff', }) document.querySelector('#preview').appendChild(image) The image matches the card the user saw This pattern works well for user-created share cards inside browser apps because the exported image matches the card preview. For an upload, call snapdom.toBlob(card, { format: 'png', width: 1200, height: 630, dpr: 1 }) ; the preview above returns an image element. title: How to Capture a DOM Element in High Resolution — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Basics / Capture in high resolution How-To Recipe Capture an element in high resolution Control pixel density and output size without changing the live component’s CSS. TL;DR Use dpr for raster pixel density and scale to multiply the output dimensions. Downloads use DPR 1, so use scale for higher-resolution files. Export at a higher pixel density Install @zumer/snapdom , select the rendered element, and capture it: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const image = await snapdom.toPng(element, { dpr: 2, scale: 1.5, backgroundColor: '#ffffff', embedFonts: true, }) Size and sharpness are separate settings dpr changes raster pixel density. scale changes output dimensions when neither width nor height is set. Explicit dimensions take precedence over scale; use the smallest output that meets your destination requirement. Compare normal and 2× output Capture the same target with the default settings or fixed DPR 2 and compare pixel dimensions. 2× Resolution test Fine text and one-pixel rules reveal the output density. Default capture Capture at DPR 2 The captured result will appear here. Limits and common mistakes Doubling width and height produces four times as many pixels. Very high DPR values can exceed canvas limits for image previews and canvas exports. For large PNG or JPEG files, use the automatic file-export path . download() always uses DPR 1, so pass scale (for example scale: devicePixelRatio ) for a sharper downloaded file. Frequently asked questions Should I use DPR or scale? Use DPR for sharper raster output at the same CSS size; use scale to enlarge the capture itself. Downloads always use DPR 1, so use scale for a sharper downloaded file. Does SVG need a high DPR? SVG preserves scalable content, but embedded images and canvas snapshots retain their source resolution. DPR affects raster exports such as PNG, JPEG, WebP and Canvas. title: Capture with html-in-canvas: Chrome's drawElementImage as a SnapDOM engine
text:
How-to / Special cases / Capture with html-in-canvas How-To Recipe Capture with html-in-canvas Use Chrome’s drawElementImage() through SnapDOM’s optional engine. Unsupported browsers or capture geometry fall back to SVG; native captures produce a bitmap. TL;DR snapdom(el, { engine: 'html-in-canvas' }) . In Chrome 157 and newer the capture is painted by Chrome's own renderer, so scrollbars and native controls come out as the page draws them, with the exceptions under Limits. In Firefox, Safari, older Chrome, and on any capture the engine cannot paint, SnapDOM runs the SVG engine on the same clone and you get the same result object. Keep the default for speed; pick this engine when scrollbars, or anything else the SVG image draws differently, have to match the page. Turn it on Set the engine at capture time. Export methods keep the same signatures; the limits below explain native output and SVG fallback. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#card'), { engine: 'html-in-canvas' }) const png = await result.toPng() document.body.appendChild(png) A native capture is a bitmap, so its raw form is a PNG data URL; an SVG capture is an SVG one. That is also how you tell which engine ran: const native = result.toRaw().startsWith('data:image/png') console.log(native ? 'painted by Chrome' : 'SVG engine') Unsupported browsers and captures use the SVG engine automatically. What Chrome 157 gives you html-in-canvas is a WICG specification that Chrome ships without a flag since version 157. You mark a canvas as content="drawable" , put the element inside it with the drawable attribute, and once the browser has painted it, draw it into the 2D context:
…
 The browser paints with its own renderer, so everything it can draw on a page it can draw into the canvas, native controls included. Two things shape the design. The element must be a descendant of that canvas, so the DOM is built around the capture. And the paint is "read-back allowed": content the page is not allowed to read, such as a cross-origin image without CORS headers or a url() reference to one, is left out of the picture instead of tainting the canvas. What SnapDOM adds around that call SnapDOM does not replace the native paint. It prepares what gets painted and takes care of what comes after. Capture any element where it is The native call draws only an element that lives inside a drawable canvas. SnapDOM clones the element you point at, resolves its computed styles, turns pseudo-elements into real nodes, inlines images and fonts, and mounts that finished clone into a canvas of its own behind the page. The source element stays in place. The same call in every browser Firefox and Safari have no html-in-canvas. There, and in Chrome before 157, the same option gives you the SVG engine, with the same result object and the same exports. One code path, no feature check, no second library for the browsers that are not Chrome. What the native paint leaves out, the clone carries By the time the engine draws, the clone holds its images and fonts as data URLs, so a cross-origin image the page can read through CORS is in the picture instead of being withheld. An image no script can read still needs a header or a proxy; that guide covers it. Everything before the paint still happens exclude and filter , password masking, plugins that edit the clone (redact fields, replace text, stamp a timestamp), shadow DOM, iframes, lazy image resolution: the native paint sees the finished clone, not the raw page. Everything after the paint too toPng() , toJpg() , toWebp() , toBlob() and download() at your scale and dpr ; GIF, video and live-stream plugins frame by frame; agent context. The painted bitmap goes straight to the pixel exports, so nothing is PNG-encoded until you ask for a string. A capture the engine cannot paint still comes out Captures of body or html , transformed or zoomed roots, clip , width / height , outerShadows and plugins with render hooks go through the SVG engine on their own. Unsupported geometry takes the SVG path automatically. Which engine, when SVG stays the default because it is faster. The native engine waits for a rendering update before it can draw, which costs about a frame per capture; the SVG engine serializes the clone and draws it as an image. These are warm recaptures from BENCHMARKS.md , measured September 4, 2026 with prerelease SnapDOM, Chrome 152 with the canvas drawing flag enabled, Apple M5 and DPR 1: SVG engine (default) html-in-canvas Browsers All Chrome 157 and newer; SVG elsewhere Form controls, scrollbars, text shaping Drawn as an SVG image, close to the page The page's own renderer Card, 480×240, to canvas 2.7 ms 35.5 ms Table, 250 rows, to canvas 52.6 ms 70.9 ms Unchanged element, repeated capture Under 1 ms Under 1 ms SVG output: toSvg() as SVG, html-export, vector, PDF text layer Yes No, it is a bitmap; those plugins switch the capture to SVG Full page, clip , transformed root Yes The SVG engine runs Pick html-in-canvas for a settings panel or a data grid with its own scrollbars, anything where a native part drawn slightly differently would be noticed. Keep the default for dashboards, cards and social images, where speed matters more and the SVG engine already matches the page. The demo makes a separate capture for each engine; each call prepares its own clone from the current DOM. The second button runs a tiny plugin that edits the clone before the paint, to show that the native engine draws the prepared clone, not the live element. In a browser without the API both columns say so and come from the SVG engine. The lab runs every official plugin through this engine and reports which ones use SVG. title: Limits
text: The engine paints the clone SnapDOM built, so a control the clone already draws differently from the page looks the same as with the SVG engine: <audio controls> becomes a drawn player, and a bare <progress> or <meter> loses Chrome's native look. Selects, date, range, color and number inputs, checkboxes, radios and buttons match the page with either engine. The engine paints one plain element box. It does not do document roots, transformed or zoomed ancestors, bleed for outer shadows, region clips or capture-level sizing; those captures take the SVG engine, where that geometry lives. A plugin with a beforeRender or afterRender hook makes the capture use SVG too, because it works at that boundary: html-export, pdf, vector, and redact-inputs with blocks or attributes . A paint that comes back blank or unreadable also falls back, so a successful native capture is always a readable bitmap. Chromium browsers still on the origin-trial builds (Chrome 148 to 156 with the flag, and forks on those versions) want the older layoutsubtree canvas attribute; SnapDOM sets both names, so they work too.

title: Frequently asked questions
text: Do I need a feature check before setting engine: 'html-in-canvas' ? No. In a browser without the API, and on any capture the native engine cannot paint, SnapDOM runs the SVG engine on the same clone and returns the same result object. Is html-in-canvas faster than the SVG engine? In the cited small-card benchmark, the native capture took 35.5 ms and SVG took 2.7 ms. The native path waits for a rendering update. Eligible unchanged captures can be reused on both engines. Does it work in Firefox or Safari? They have no implementation of html-in-canvas. The same call gives you the SVG engine there, with the same result object. Can I get an SVG from an html-in-canvas capture? No. A native capture is a bitmap: url and toRaw() give a PNG data URL, toSvg() returns a PNG-backed image, and an SVG Blob request rejects. Plugins that need the SVG, such as pdf, vector and html-export, make the capture use the SVG engine on their own. title: How to Convert HTML to PNG in JavaScript — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Basics / Convert HTML to PNG How-To Recipe How to convert HTML to PNG in JavaScript Append a PNG preview, download a file, or create a PNG Blob for upload. Each pattern starts from a rendered DOM element. TL;DR Use toPng() for a preview image, download() for a file, or toBlob(element, { format: 'png' }) for an upload. Step 1: Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest Or load it from a CDN if you don't use a bundler: < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; </ script > Pattern 1: Append the PNG to the page Useful for quick previews and demos. snapdom.toPng returns an HTMLImageElement , ready to insert anywhere in the DOM: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); Pattern 2: Download the PNG as a file Use the built-in download method: const result = await snapdom (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); Pattern 3: Upload the PNG to a server Capture the element to a Blob, wrap it in FormData , and POST it to your endpoint: const blob = await snapdom.toBlob(document.querySelector('#card'), { format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData(); form.append('file', blob, 'card.png'); const response = await fetch('/api/upload', { method: 'POST', body: form, }); if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Image upload failed'); const { url } = await response.json(); console.log('Uploaded to', url); This is the same pattern you'd use to generate dynamic og:image share cards — capture the rendered card client-side, upload to a CDN, return the URL. Try the three patterns live Same element, three buttons: append the PNG, download it, or produce the upload-ready Blob: HTML PNG Gradients, borders & shadows Rounded corners, a dashed border, a gradient, ready to capture together. ⚡ Even this shadow Append PNG Download Get Blob The result will appear here. Bonus: Get a Base64 / data URL If you specifically need a base64 string (e.g. to email or embed inline), call toPng and read the src of the returned image: const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. querySelector ( '#card' )); const dataUrl = img.src; // "data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo…" High-DPI / retina output SnapDOM picks up the device's devicePixelRatio automatically through the dpr option, so retina screens already get sharp output without configuration. Override it with dpr when you want a fixed pixel density (e.g. exporting a 2× asset on a non-retina machine): const img = await snapdom. toPng (el, { dpr: 2 }); scale multiplies the captured size when no explicit width or height is set. Use scale when you want a larger image; use dpr when you want the same logical size at higher pixel density. They can be combined: const img = await snapdom. toPng (el, { dpr: 2 , // retina pixel density scale: 1.5 , // zoom 1.5× backgroundColor: '#ffffff' , }); Frequently asked questions Can I convert HTML to PNG without a server? Yes. SnapDOM runs in the browser and does not need a screenshot server. Its SVG foreignObject pipeline uses the browser's renderer; fonts and images may still require network requests. What if I need JPG or WebP instead of PNG? Use snapdom.toJpg(el, { quality: 0.9 }) or snapdom.toWebp(el, { quality: 0.9 }) . The API surface is identical, only the output format changes. How do I render custom fonts correctly? SnapDOM defaults to embedFonts: 'auto' , which embeds used web fonts when their files are accessible. Use localFonts or excludeFonts when you need more control. Can I exclude some elements from the capture? Yes. Pass { exclude: ['.skip-me'] } with a list of CSS selectors, or { exclude: node => … } for a predicate that returns true for nodes to omit. What about converting HTML to PDF? Use the MIT pdf plugin. Its toPdf() method returns a PDF Blob with selectable text, pagination and links. The plugin is on npm as @zumer/snapdom-pdf ; see the PDF reference for installation and examples. Does it handle Shadow DOM and Web Components? Open shadow roots need no extra setup. See Capture Shadow DOM . Related How to screenshot a div SnapDOM in React SnapDOM in Next.js SnapDOM vs html2canvas

title: How to Convert HTML to SVG in JavaScript — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Basics / Convert HTML to SVG How-To Recipe How to convert HTML to SVG Capture a DOM element as a scalable, self-contained SVG image without a server or headless browser. TL;DR Use snapdom.toSvg(element) for an SVG image, or snapdom.toRaw(element) when you need the SVG data URL. Export the element as SVG Install @zumer/snapdom , select the rendered element, and capture it: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const element = document.querySelector('#card') const svg = await snapdom.toSvg(element, { embedFonts: true }) document.body.appendChild(svg) The SVG wraps the rendered HTML SnapDOM clones the selected DOM subtree, inlines its rendered styles and assets, then serializes it inside SVG <foreignObject> . The browser remains responsible for painting the HTML. Use toRaw() when you need the underlying data URL for storage or transport. Try HTML SVG live Capture this styled HTML card as an SVG image. The result stays sharp when resized. SVG foreignObject HTML stays HTML The result stays sharp at any size. Capture SVG Download SVG The captured result will appear here. Limits and common mistakes The output is an SVG container around styled HTML; it is not a conversion to SVG paths. Use it for browser display. For editable SVG geometry in Figma or Illustrator, use the Vector plugin ; embedded images and canvas content remain raster. Frequently asked questions Is the result true vector artwork? Not with toSvg() : text and HTML stay inside SVG foreignObject. For real paths editable in Figma or Illustrator, use the Vector plugin . Can I get the SVG source? Use snapdom.toRaw(element) to get the SVG data URL, or fetch and decode that URL when XML text is required. Related Convert HTML to Canvas Convert HTML to PNG Export API SnapDOM vs html-to-image

title: Migrate from html2canvas to SnapDOM: options, code and pitfalls
text: How-to / Migrate / Migrate from html2canvas Migration guide Migrate from html2canvas to SnapDOM Map html2canvas options and Canvas consumers to SnapDOM, replace onclone with a plugin, and check return types, sizing and resource access. TL;DR html2canvas(el, { scale: 2 }) becomes snapdom.toCanvas(el, { dpr: 2 }) . Most apps change three lines: the import, the call, and what they do with the result. What changes, in one block Install @zumer/snapdom and replace the call. The canvas consumer is the closest match to what you have: // Before import html2canvas from 'html2canvas' const canvas = await html2canvas(el, { scale: 2, useCORS: true }) const dataURL = canvas.toDataURL('image/png') // After import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const canvas = await snapdom.toCanvas(el, { dpr: 2 }) const dataURL = canvas.toDataURL('image/png') If the canvas only existed to get a PNG, skip it: const img = await snapdom.toPng(el) returns an HTMLImageElement whose src is the data URL. The return value is a capture, not a canvas html2canvas resolves to a canvas and leaves the encoding to you. snapdom(el) resolves to a capture object that already holds the frozen SVG and exports it on demand, so one capture can feed several outputs without re-walking the DOM: const capture = await snapdom(el, { dpr: 2 }) const img = await capture.toPng() // HTMLImageElement const canvas = await capture.toCanvas() // HTMLCanvasElement const blob = await capture.toBlob({ format: 'png' }) // Blob for upload await capture.download({ format: 'jpg', filename: 'card' }) // file to disk The shortcuts snapdom.toPng , snapdom.toJpg , snapdom.toWebp , snapdom.toSvg , snapdom.toCanvas and snapdom.toBlob do the capture and one export in a single call, which is what most html2canvas call sites want. Option by option Every html2canvas option you may have set, and what to write instead. Options not listed here ( removeContainer , windowWidth , windowHeight , scrollX , scrollY , letterRendering ) have no equivalent because SnapDOM captures the element's own box and never scrolls the page. html2canvas SnapDOM Notes scale: 2 dpr: 2 html2canvas scale is a pixel density. SnapDOM also has a scale option, but it multiplies the output size in CSS pixels. Writing scale: 2 out of habit gives you double-sized output on top of the default device DPR. Set dpr: 2 for a fixed pixel density. backgroundColor: '#fff' backgroundColor: '#fff' Same name. The default differs: html2canvas fills white, SnapDOM keeps PNG and SVG transparent and only fills white for JPEG and WebP. A PNG that used to come out white needs the option. useCORS: true allowTaint: true proxy: url nothing, or useProxy: base SnapDOM fetches and inlines images itself. An image served without CORS headers still cannot be read; pass useProxy with the base URL of a proxy for those. There is no tainted mode to opt into. ignoreElements: (el) => bool exclude: [...] or filter: fn exclude takes selectors and predicates; a predicate that returns true drops the node. filter is the inverse: true keeps. By default an excluded node leaves an invisible box so layout holds; excludeMode: 'remove' collapses it. A data-capture="exclude" attribute works without any option. onclone: (doc, el) => {} a plugin with afterClone The clone is handed to plugin hooks. An inline plugin needs a name and edits ctx.clone ; see the example below. width , height width , height Output size in pixels. Setting one keeps the aspect ratio. x , y clip: { x, y, width, height } A rectangle in page coordinates. clip: 'viewport' captures what is on screen. canvas: existing canvas: existing Same: reuse a canvas you already own as the raster target. logging: true debug: true With it off, SnapDOM logs nothing. imageTimeout none A resource that fails shows a placeholder ( placeholders: true by default) or the fallbackURL you provide. foreignObjectRendering none SnapDOM’s default SVG engine uses foreignObject. An optional native canvas engine is also available. Replacing onclone The onclone callback edited the cloned document before html2canvas drew it. The same work goes in a plugin hook, inline for a one-off or registered globally with snapdom.plugins() when several call sites need it: const img = await snapdom.toPng(el, { plugins: [{ name: 'strip-controls', afterClone(ctx) { ctx.clone.querySelectorAll('.no-capture, button').forEach(n => n.remove()) } }] }) Two differences from onclone : the hook receives the clone of the element, not a whole document, and beforeClone exists for changes to the live DOM that you undo in afterClone . The plugin API lists every hook. Fonts come along html2canvas drew text with whatever fonts the page had loaded. SnapDOM renders the clone inside an SVG image, which is an isolated document, so it embeds the web fonts the element uses on its own ( embedFonts: 'auto' ). Font files must be accessible. Two cases need attention: Icon fonts are matched by name; add yours with iconFonts if glyphs come out as boxes. A font stylesheet served without CORS headers cannot be read from any site. Enable debug: true and check resource access, CORS and CSP before changing font options. What renders now that did not before html2canvas reimplements CSS painting, so its own documentation lists what it skips: box-shadow , filter , mix-blend-mode , object-fit , border-image , background-blend-mode , box-decoration-break , writing-mode , repeating-linear-gradient() and zoom . title: What changes, in one block
text: Install @zumer/snapdom and replace the call. The canvas consumer is the closest match to what you have: // Before import html2canvas from 'html2canvas' const canvas = await html2canvas(el, { scale: 2, useCORS: true }) const dataURL = canvas.toDataURL('image/png') // After import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const canvas = await snapdom.toCanvas(el, { dpr: 2 }) const dataURL = canvas.toDataURL('image/png') If the canvas only existed to get a PNG, skip it: const img = await snapdom.toPng(el) returns an HTMLImageElement whose src is the data URL.

title: The return value is a capture, not a canvas
text: html2canvas resolves to a canvas and leaves the encoding to you. snapdom(el) resolves to a capture object that already holds the frozen SVG and exports it on demand, so one capture can feed several outputs without re-walking the DOM: const capture = await snapdom(el, { dpr: 2 }) const img = await capture.toPng() // HTMLImageElement const canvas = await capture.toCanvas() // HTMLCanvasElement const blob = await capture.toBlob({ format: 'png' }) // Blob for upload await capture.download({ format: 'jpg', filename: 'card' }) // file to disk The shortcuts snapdom.toPng , snapdom.toJpg , snapdom.toWebp , snapdom.toSvg , snapdom.toCanvas and snapdom.toBlob do the capture and one export in a single call, which is what most html2canvas call sites want.

title: Option by option
text: Every html2canvas option you may have set, and what to write instead. Options not listed here ( removeContainer , windowWidth , windowHeight , scrollX , scrollY , letterRendering ) have no equivalent because SnapDOM captures the element's own box and never scrolls the page. html2canvas SnapDOM Notes scale: 2 dpr: 2 html2canvas scale is a pixel density. SnapDOM also has a scale option, but it multiplies the output size in CSS pixels. Writing scale: 2 out of habit gives you double-sized output on top of the default device DPR. Set dpr: 2 for a fixed pixel density. backgroundColor: '#fff' backgroundColor: '#fff' Same name. The default differs: html2canvas fills white, SnapDOM keeps PNG and SVG transparent and only fills white for JPEG and WebP. A PNG that used to come out white needs the option. useCORS: true allowTaint: true proxy: url nothing, or useProxy: base SnapDOM fetches and inlines images itself. An image served without CORS headers still cannot be read; pass useProxy with the base URL of a proxy for those. There is no tainted mode to opt into. ignoreElements: (el) => bool exclude: [...] or filter: fn exclude takes selectors and predicates; a predicate that returns true drops the node. filter is the inverse: true keeps. By default an excluded node leaves an invisible box so layout holds; excludeMode: 'remove' collapses it. A data-capture="exclude" attribute works without any option. onclone: (doc, el) => {} a plugin with afterClone The clone is handed to plugin hooks. An inline plugin needs a name and edits ctx.clone ; see the example below. width , height width , height Output size in pixels. Setting one keeps the aspect ratio. x , y clip: { x, y, width, height } A rectangle in page coordinates. clip: 'viewport' captures what is on screen. canvas: existing canvas: existing Same: reuse a canvas you already own as the raster target. logging: true debug: true With it off, SnapDOM logs nothing. imageTimeout none A resource that fails shows a placeholder ( placeholders: true by default) or the fallbackURL you provide. foreignObjectRendering none SnapDOM’s default SVG engine uses foreignObject. An optional native canvas engine is also available.

title: Replacing onclone
