title: Export a PDF with cross-origin images: warnings, CSP and a proxy
text: How-to / Real content / PDF with cross-origin images How-To Recipe Export a PDF with cross-origin images Fix missing CDN images and map tiles in a PDF: inspect capture warnings, check CSP and CORS, or configure a proxy you control. TL;DR With the default placeholders, an unreadable keeps its box, shows a grey placeholder and adds image-fallback to result.warnings . Read the warnings before you call toPdf() . Then let the fetch through your Content Security Policy ( connect-src , not img-src ), add CORS headers to the images you serve, and send the rest through a proxy of your own with fallbackURL or useProxy . Both options reach the captures toPdf() runs. Check result.warnings first The capture you hold already knows what it could not read. The PDF pages are drawn from that capture, so a grey box in the result is a grey box in the PDF. Log the warnings before you export: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { pdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-pdf' const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#report'), { plugins: [pdf()] }) for (const w of result.warnings) console.log(w.code, w.message) // image-fallback image failed to inline, using placeholder: https://cdn.example.com/avatars/42.png const blob = await result.toPdf({ page: 'a4' }) Each entry includes code and message , and debug: true prints the same lines to the console. Keep placeholders on while you look: with placeholders: false the box stays empty and nothing is recorded. A CSS background or an SVG the capture cannot read is dropped without a warning. Your own CSP: connect-src, not img-src SnapDOM reads every image it embeds with fetch() , and a Content Security Policy governs that read through connect-src . img-src only decides what the page may display. A policy that lists your CDN under img-src and not under connect-src shows the avatars on the page and exports grey boxes, with no CORS problem anywhere. The same rule covers the proxy origin from the section below, and the stylesheet and font hosts when fonts are embedded ( embedFonts , 'auto' by default, fetches the webfonts the element uses). Content-Security-Policy: img-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; connect-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com https://image-proxy.example.com https://fonts.googleapis.com https://fonts.gstatic.com List the hosts. connect-src * makes the images load, and it also lets any script on the page talk to any server, which is what the policy was there to prevent. Fix it at the source If you control the image server, add the header to the image responses and nothing else changes, in your code or in the export. Your own origin needs nothing: a same-origin image is read directly, cookies included. Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * A proxy for hosts you do not control When the images come from a server you cannot change, put a proxy of your own in between that fetches them and adds the header. The CORS guide includes an image proxy , a Cloudflare Worker with a host allowlist; any server that adds the header does the same job. Then hand it to the capture: const PROXY = 'https://image-proxy.example.com/?url=' const result = await snapdom(report, { plugins: [pdf()], // only the the capture could not read, fetched again through the proxy fallbackURL: ({ src }) => PROXY + encodeURIComponent(src) }) const blob = await result.toPdf({ page: 'a4' }) fallbackURL is called only for an SnapDOM could not read. useProxy: PROXY instead sends every cross-origin request through the proxy: images that already allow CORS, CSS backgrounds, SVG , stylesheets and font files. Use it when the missing images are backgrounds or SVG , which fallbackURL does not cover, and let the proxy accept your font hosts too. It takes a base ending in ?url= or / , or a template with {url} ; any other base gets ?url= appended. Both are capture options: set them on snapdom() , not on toPdf() . The pages come from that capture, and the elements the export captures on its own (an element header or footer, a watermark element, cover and back pages) get the same useProxy , fallbackURL , placeholders and exclude . Add the proxy origin to connect-src , and note that the proxied request carries no cookies: the proxy has to fetch the image on its own. Large PDFs Each image URL is fetched once per capture: identical requests in flight share one response, a failure is remembered for eight seconds so a broken URL is not retried per node, and the data URL stays in a cache that later captures reuse. Images are fetched six at a time and each request has 3000 ms. A proxy that answers in two seconds adds about two seconds per six uncached images; one that does not answer in time gives a placeholder and an image-fallback warning, the same as a CORS failure. Give the proxy a cache (the Worker in the CORS guide sets cache-control: public, max-age=86400 ), and when result.warnings is not empty, show the warnings before you offer the download. Frequently asked questions The image shows on the page but not in the PDF. Why? The browser displays an image from any host; a script may read one only when the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin and the page's Content Security Policy lets fetch() reach it through connect-src . SnapDOM has to read an image to embed it, and result.warnings names the one it could not. My avatars come from a CDN that needs the user's cookies. SnapDOM sends cookies only to your own origin: a same-origin image is fetched with credentials: 'include' , everything else with 'omit' , and no option changes that. A host that needs a cookie answers with a login page or a 401 and the avatar becomes a placeholder. Serve the avatars from your origin, or through a proxy that fetches them with a credential of its own. Can I skip the images entirely? exclude: 'img' leaves them out of the capture; an invisible spacer keeps the layout, and excludeMode: 'remove' drops the box as well. placeholders: false keeps the box of an image that failed and leaves it empty, without a warning. Both reach the captures toPdf() runs. Related Capture images without CORS PDF plugin Capture before a PDF Capture options

title: How to Save a Chart.js Chart as a PNG — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Real content / Save a Chart.js chart How-To Recipe How to save a Chart.js chart as a PNG Chart.js draws to a <canvas> , so its built-in toBase64Image() exports the chart canvas, including its built-in labels. When you want the title, HTML legend and container in the picture too, capture the whole component with SnapDOM. TL;DR Wrap the chart, wait for it to finish drawing, then const img = await snapdom.toPng(wrapper) . You get one PNG with the canvas and everything around it. The problem Chart.js renders inside a <canvas> element. Its native chart.toBase64Image() exports exactly that canvas and drops anything you laid out in HTML around it: a heading, a custom legend, annotations, the card background. If your export needs to look like the chart your users actually see on the page, you need to capture the surrounding DOM as well. SnapDOM captures a DOM subtree — including live <canvas> pixels — into a single image, so the chart and its frame come out as one composited PNG. Step 1: Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest chart.js Without a bundler, load both from a CDN: import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; import Chart from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js/auto/+esm" ; Step 2: Wrap the chart in a capture target Put the canvas inside an element that also holds whatever you want in the exported image: < div id= "chart-card" style= "padding:20px;background:#fff;border-radius:12px;" > < h3 > Monthly revenue </ h3 > < canvas id= "chart" ></ canvas > </ div > Step 3: Wait for the draw, then capture A canvas only holds pixels once Chart.js has painted them. Capturing during the entry animation gives you a blank or half-drawn plot. The reliable fix is to capture from the animation's onComplete callback: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; import Chart from 'chart.js/auto' ; const chart = new Chart (document. getElementById ( 'chart' ), { type: 'bar' , data: { labels: [ 'Jan' , 'Feb' , 'Mar' , 'Apr' ], datasets: [{ label: 'Revenue' , data: [12, 19, 9, 22] }] }, options: { animation: { onComplete : async () => { const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. getElementById ( 'chart-card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); } } } }); Prefer a static export with no timing games? Set options.animation = false and capture right after new Chart(...) returns. Step 4: Download it as a file const result = await snapdom (document. getElementById ( 'chart-card' )); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'revenue-chart' }); Or get a Blob to upload: const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (document. getElementById ( 'chart-card' ), { format: 'png' }); Expected result A single PNG that matches what's on screen: the <h3> heading, the card's white background and rounded corners, and the fully rendered bar chart — all in one image at your device pixel ratio. Pass { scale: 2 } to toPng for a sharper, higher-resolution export. Try it live A real Chart.js bar chart, in a card with an HTML heading. Capture it and compare: the exported PNG includes the heading and the card frame — exactly what toBase64Image() would drop: Monthly revenue Capture chart card Download The captured PNG will appear here. Going further Capture the wrapper when you need the chart together with surrounding HTML labels and card styling. For an animation, the optional GIF export plugin can capture a sequence of frames; see the plugins page . Frequently asked questions My exported chart is blank — why? You captured before Chart.js finished drawing. Capture inside options.animation.onComplete , or set options.animation = false so the chart paints synchronously. Can I export just the canvas without the surrounding HTML? Use chart.toBase64Image() when the canvas alone is the output you need, including Chart.js titles or legends drawn inside it. Capture the wrapper with SnapDOM when you also need surrounding HTML, custom legends or container styling. How do I get a higher-resolution image? Pass { scale: 2 } (or higher) to snapdom.toPng . SnapDOM also respects window.devicePixelRatio automatically. Does this work with react-chartjs-2? Yes. Put a ref on the wrapping element and call snapdom.toPng(ref.current) from the chart's onComplete option. The wrapper is just a DOM node — SnapDOM doesn't care how it was rendered. title: How to Screenshot a Div in JavaScript — SnapDOM
text: How-to / Basics / Screenshot a div How-To Recipe How to screenshot a div in JavaScript Select the rendered element, call snapdom.toPng , and use the returned image in a preview or download. TL;DR snapdom.toPng(element) returns an HTMLImageElement for a preview. Use download() for a file or toBlob() for upload; examples follow. Step 1: Install SnapDOM npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest If you don't use a bundler, you can also use the CDN build: < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; </ script > Step 2: Pick the div you want to screenshot Select the rendered element you want to export: const el = document. querySelector ( '#card' ); It doesn't need to be inside the viewport, but it must be attached to the document and not display: none . If it loads web fonts or images, wait for them first: await document.fonts.ready; await Promise.all(Array.from(el.querySelectorAll('img'), img => img.decode())); For an iframe or a web component, see the iframe and Shadow DOM recipes. Step 3: Capture it One line: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' ; const img = await snapdom. toPng (el); The returned img is a real HTMLImageElement with the captured content as its src (a PNG data URL). Step 4: Do something with the image Append it to the page const img = await snapdom. toPng (el); document.body. appendChild (img); Download it as a file const result = await snapdom (el); await result. download ({ format: 'png' , filename: 'card' }); Get a Blob to upload to a server const blob = await snapdom. toBlob (el, { format: 'png' }); const form = new FormData (); form. append ( 'file' , blob, 'screenshot.png' ); await fetch ( '/api/upload' , { method: 'POST' , body: form }); Full working example Drop this into a fresh HTML file and open it in a browser: <! DOCTYPE html > < html > < body > < div id= "card" style= "padding:24px;background:#4f46e5;color:#fff;border-radius:12px;" > < h2 > Hello SnapDOM </ h2 > < p > This entire div is about to become a PNG. </ p > </ div > < button id= "go" > Capture </ button > < script type= "module" > import { snapdom } from "https://unpkg.com/@zumer/snapdom@latest/dist/snapdom.mjs" ; document. getElementById ( 'go' ). addEventListener ( 'click' , async () => { const img = await snapdom. toPng (document. getElementById ( 'card' )); document.body. appendChild (img); }); </ script > </ body > </ html > Or try it right here The example above, running on this page — same div, same snapdom.toPng call: Hello SnapDOM This entire div is about to become a PNG. Capture Download The captured PNG will appear here. Useful options dpr: 2 — pixel density (auto-detects window.devicePixelRatio for retina; override here when you need a fixed value). scale: 2 — multiply the captured size (zoom). Different from dpr : scale makes the output bigger, dpr makes it sharper at the same logical size. backgroundColor: '#fff' — fill transparent areas with a colour. embedFonts: 'auto' — the v3 default embeds used web fonts. exclude: ['.skip'] — skip any element matching the selector. useProxy: 'https://your-proxy.example.com/' — fetch cross-origin images through a CORS proxy. Frequently asked questions Why not use the browser's built-in screenshot API? Chrome 157+ has drawElementImage() , with restrictions on where drawable elements live; SnapDOM’s native engine guide explains it. The Screen Capture API ( getDisplayMedia ) captures a user-selected tab or screen and requires permission; it does not target an arbitrary DOM element. Does this work with web fonts? Yes. SnapDOM embeds used web fonts by default with embedFonts: 'auto' , provided their files are accessible. Can I screenshot something inside an iframe? Same-origin iframes are supported out of the box. Cross-origin iframes are not: the browser blocks access to their content. What about Shadow DOM? Open shadow roots need no extra setup. See Capture Shadow DOM . How big is the library? SnapDOM has zero runtime dependencies. Check the distributed build you import for its current bundle size; official plugins are separate imports. title: ASCII Mirror: a live element as text | SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / ASCII mirror Labs Experiment A live element, as text A card with text and a spinning CSS cube. The right side is the same element redrawn as ASCII art on every frame, through the stream plugin. TL;DR Two calls. stream() keeps a canvas in step with the card, and asciiFromCanvas() , the function behind the ascii-export plugin, turns each frame into characters. No capture result in between: the canvas goes straight from one to the other. What you're looking at The left card is editable HTML on a white background with solid-colored boxes, the shape the stream plugin patches best. The right pane is a <pre> . On every frame the plugin hands over its canvas, the text is recomputed and replaced. Pick a character set, change the width, or switch to color to see each character carry the pixel it came from. Try it Charset Classic Blocks Dots Binary Width 90 Color Invert Editable DOM contenteditable + CSS 3D Hello, text Keystrokes and the spinning cube become patched frames, then characters. S N A P D O ASCII output stream() + asciiFromCanvas() starting… Loading the stream plugin… How it works stream() watches the card The first frame is a full SnapDOM capture. After that, a keystroke is traced to the nearest box with a solid background and only that subtree is captured and drawn into its rectangle. The cube spins under a 3D transform, which no box of its own can hold, so each turn repaints the white card around it: still a patch, capped here at 15 fps, and the stats count it as one. asciiFromCanvas() does the pixel work On each repaint it downsamples the canvas to one pixel per character, maps luminance to the charset and returns a string, or colored HTML when format: 'html' . It is the same code the toAscii() export uses, exported on its own so it runs on any drawable: a stream frame, a video, your own canvas. One handler joins them onFrame receives every repaint with its canvas; the handler runs asciiFromCanvas() on it and writes the string. The handle exposes the live canvas , a ready promise, stats and stop() . The <pre> is replaced textContent for plain text, innerHTML for the colored version. Nothing else on the page is touched. Copy-paste example import { stream } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' import { asciiFromCanvas } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/ascii-export' const out = document.querySelector('pre') const live = stream(document.querySelector('#card'), { fps: 15, onFrame: frame => { out.textContent = asciiFromCanvas(frame.canvas, { width: 90 }) } }) await live.ready // later: live.stop() The same shape works for any pixel-level step on a frame, or for a video element instead of a stream: asciiFromCanvas() takes anything drawImage accepts. Limits and things to watch On a gradient card, the plugin can repaint a window of the enclosing card. Resizing, removing nodes, overlapping effects or large dirty regions can require a full frame. More columns increase conversion work; color mode also creates one <span> per character. Lower the width if updates lag. title: html-in-canvas: the browser paints the capture | SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / html-in-canvas Labs Experiment The browser paints the capture SnapDOM's second engine hands the captured clone to Chrome's own renderer through the html-in-canvas API. Compare it with the SVG engine and see which plugins run on it. TL;DR snapdom(el, { engine: 'html-in-canvas' }) paints the clone SnapDOM already built, styles resolved and images and fonts inlined, with Chrome's own renderer instead of an SVG image. It runs in Chrome 157 and newer, where the API ships without a flag. Anywhere else, or on a capture this engine cannot paint, SnapDOM uses the SVG engine and you get the same result object. The guide explains when to pick it and what SnapDOM adds on top of the raw API. Try it Checking this browser… Live element Quarterly report Revenue grew 12% this quarter. Email Plan Pro Free Subscribed Send SVG engine Not captured yet html-in-canvas engine Not captured yet Capture with both engines Type in the field or change the plan, then capture again. Each column captures the same card separately, using the same preparation pipeline and a different render engine. Plugins A plugin that works on the clone runs as it is: by the time the browser paints, its change is already in the clone. A plugin with a render hook, beforeRender or afterRender , gets the SVG engine on purpose, because it reads the SVG or does its work at that boundary. Those captures still succeed, through SVG. Plugin Engine Why This browser timestamp-overlay html-in-canvas Adds its label to the clone replace-text html-in-canvas Edits text in the clone filter html-in-canvas CSS filter on the clone color-tint html-in-canvas Overlay on the clone redact-inputs html-in-canvas Masks values in the clone. With blocks or attributes it uses SVG: its final pass runs in beforeRender agent-map html-in-canvas Reads the clone, draws on the pixels context-export html-in-canvas Reads the live page ascii-export html-in-canvas Reads the pixels gif-export html-in-canvas, every frame Recaptures with the same options video-export html-in-canvas, every frame Recaptures with the same options stream html-in-canvas Full frames come from the engine html-export SVG Serializes the clone in afterRender pdf SVG Its text layer measures the SVG vector SVG Takes the clone in beforeRender Check them in this browser How it works The same clone Everything up to the render is the normal pipeline: computed styles become classes, pseudo-elements become real nodes, images and fonts become data URLs, and clone plugins run. The engine choice comes after all of that. A mount the browser can paint The clone goes into a shadow root under <canvas content="drawable"> , behind the page. Chrome lays it out like any element, with the page's own form controls, scrollbars and text shaping. Two frames, one draw After one full rendering update the browser holds a snapshot of the mount, and drawElementImage() paints it at your scale and dpr . A blank or unreadable result sends the capture to the SVG engine instead. The bitmap goes straight to the exports toCanvas() , toPng() and the rest draw from the painted canvas. result.url is a PNG data URL, made the first time you read it. Copy-paste example npm install @zumer/snapdom import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' const result = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#card'), { engine: 'html-in-canvas' }) const png = await result.toPng() The engine is part of the default build and falls back to SVG when unavailable. A successful native capture is a bitmap: url returns PNG, toSvg() returns a PNG-backed image, and an SVG Blob request rejects. Use engine: 'svg' for serialized SVG; see the export contracts . What stays on the SVG engine This engine paints one plain element box. Captures of body or html , a scrolled root, a root or ancestor with a transform or zoom , a root with a filter , and the outerShadows , clip , width and height options all go through SVG, where that geometry is handled. So do captures in browsers without the API. html-in-canvas is a WICG specification. Chrome 157 ships it without a flag; before that it was an origin trial and chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element , and Chromium browsers still on those builds want the older layoutsubtree canvas attribute, which is why SnapDOM sets both names. Firefox and Safari have no implementation, so there every capture uses the SVG engine. title: Into the dock: a panel painted by Chrome, folded in WebGL | SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / Into the dock Labs Experiment A settings panel, into the dock One capture with the html-in-canvas engine becomes a WebGL texture that folds into the dock. The same frame from the raw API and from the SVG engine shows where each one differs. TL;DR snapdom(panel, { engine: 'html-in-canvas' }) gives one canvas painted by Chrome's own renderer, with the cross-origin avatar already in it. A vertex shader folds that canvas into the dock tile and unfolds it back. In Firefox, Safari and Chrome before 157 the same call gives you the SVG engine, and the fold works the same. Try it Checking this browser… Zumerlab Team settings Plan Pro Team Free Renews Volume Accent Seats Email me Weekly Daily Invoice #1048 $420 Invoice #1047 $420 Invoice #1046 $380 Invoice #1045 $380 Invoice #1044 $380 Invoice #1043 $310 Invoice #1042 $310 Invoice #1041 $290 Cancel Save Minimize to the dock Raw drawElementImage() Minimize once to fill this SnapDOM, SVG engine Minimize once to fill this SnapDOM, html-in-canvas Minimize once to fill this Change the plan, move the slider, scroll the invoices, then minimize. Click the tile in the dock to bring the panel back. What the three frames show The raw API draws a copy of the panel that lives inside a <canvas content="drawable"> , because that is the only place drawElementImage() can draw from. The avatar and the cover pattern come from another origin, so Chrome leaves them out of the paint, even though that server allows CORS. The SVG engine has the avatar, because SnapDOM fetched it and wrote it into the clone as a data URL. It draws the clone as an SVG image, so the invoice list can get a scrollbar the page does not show. The html-in-canvas engine prepares a clone through the same pipeline, then paints it with Chrome's renderer. The avatar is there and the list looks like the page. This is the frame the dock animation uses. How it works One capture snapdom(panel, { engine: 'html-in-canvas' }) , then toCanvas() . The canvas becomes a texture texImage2D uploads it once, and the live panel hides. Nothing is captured again while it moves. A grid of vertices folds it An 8 by 60 vertex grid starts on the panel's box. As one progress uniform goes from 0 to 1, the lower rows narrow toward the dock tile first, then the whole grid slides down the funnel and lands inside the tile. The tile is the same capture The dock tile shows the canvas at thumbnail size. Clicking it runs the shader backward and shows the live panel again, with your changes still in it. title: Paint Canvas — The PNG Is the Canvas — SnapDOM Labs
text:
Showcase / Labs / Paint on a capture Labs Experiment The PNG is the canvas A paint app with no element. The board is an that SnapDOM re-exports as a PNG after every stroke. TL;DR A plugin's afterRender hook saves the rendered clone; afterClone swaps it back in on the next capture and appends the newest stroke. SnapDOM uses Canvas only for the raster export. What you're looking at Pick a color and brush size, then drag across the board. The page keeps no bitmap buffer; the drawing state lives in the plugin. Try it Draw on the board below. The line under the cursor is a local SVG path; the PNG underneath catches up about every 120ms. Brush Clear Download painting How it works A hidden source element A 420×420
off-screen holds one empty replaces the board The PNG goes into the board. The download button points at the same .src . Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM 3 can reuse eligible captures, but stateful hooks run on fresh captures and the accumulated drawing belongs to the plugin. afterClone and afterRender share one closure: afterClone adds the new mark to savedClone , afterRender saves the result for the next call, independent of capture reuse. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. Swap in your own persistence logic for any "keep building on the last capture" case: function createPaintPlugin (sourceEl) { let savedClone = null let skipNext = false let pendingStroke = null function makePath (stroke) { const path = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'path') path.setAttribute('data-stroke-id', stroke.id) path.setAttribute('d', stroke.d) path.setAttribute('fill', 'none') path.setAttribute('stroke', stroke.color) path.setAttribute('stroke-width', stroke.size) path.setAttribute('stroke-linecap', 'round') path.setAttribute('stroke-linejoin', 'round') return path } return { name: 'paint', recordStroke (stroke) { pendingStroke = stroke }, afterClone (ctx) { if (skipNext) { skipNext = false; pendingStroke = null; return } if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) if (!pendingStroke) return const layer = ctx.clone.querySelector('.strokes') const existing = layer.querySelector(`[data-stroke-id="${pendingStroke.id}"]`) if (existing) existing.setAttribute('d', pendingStroke.d) else layer.append(makePath(pendingStroke)) }, afterRender (ctx) { savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) pendingStroke = null }, clear () { skipNext = true } } } The usage: capture again on every stroke update, plugin included: const plugin = createPaintPlugin(canvasSource) async function render (stroke) { if (stroke) plugin.recordStroke(stroke) const img = await snapdom.toPng(canvasSource, { plugins: [plugin] }) board.replaceChildren(img) } // on clear: plugin.clear() then render() again — skipNext lets SnapDOM // clone the pristine live element once, instead of hand-building an // empty replacement clone that might miss pipeline setup. stroke recordStroke() snapdom.toPng() afterClone (restore + append) afterRender (checkpoint) Limits and things to watch Every stroke update is a full capture, so the render loop is throttled (120ms here) rather than running on every pointermove . The live path keeps the drawing instant while the PNG catches up. The skipNext flag lets clear() hand the first render after a clear to SnapDOM's own cloning pipeline; a hand-built empty clone would miss pipeline behavior added later (pseudo-elements, SVG defs inlining). title: Stop Motion — You Choose the Frames — SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / Stop motion Labs Experiment You choose the frames Pose an actor, press the shutter, move on. The sequence is the poses you kept, like a physical stop-motion rig. TL;DR A small plugin's afterRender hook fires once per capture and hands back ctx.dataURL . The plugin collects those URLs into an ordered array; the player sets the rhythm. What you're looking at Three sliders pose an actor on a small stage. Capture pose captures the stage and appends it to a filmstrip. Play flips through the filmstrip at a fixed interval. Try it Pose the actor, capture a few poses, then press Play. Each thumbnail is a separate SVG snapshot. Horizontal Vertical Rotation + Capture pose Play Capture at least two poses. How it works The plugin factory closes over a counter frameCollector(onFrame) returns a plugin with one private index : the frame count, no clone or DOM reference. Moving a slider captures nothing The sliders update inline styles and a CSS custom property on the live #actor . SnapDOM is not involved yet. Capture pose runs one capture The button calls snapdom(poseScene, { plugins: [collector] }) against the live stage, in whatever pose the sliders show. afterRender fires with the finished context Once SnapDOM renders the SVG, afterRender(ctx) increments the counter and calls back with { index, url: ctx.dataURL } . The page pushes the URL into an array capturedFrames.push(frame.url) , plus a thumbnail in the filmstrip. The plugin knows nothing about the filmstrip. Play iterates the array on a timer Play walks capturedFrames for a few loops, swapping .src on an interval. The plugin is not involved. Why this needed a plugin In the paint-canvas and target-range labs a plugin mutates ctx.clone and persists it, so each capture builds on the last. Here ctx.clone is left alone and each pose is a self-contained render. The afterRender hook centralizes frame collection via ctx.dataURL . An application could instead read result.url after awaiting snapdom() ; the callback keeps the bookkeeping in one place. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. It collects dataURLs and nothing else: function frameCollector (onFrame) { let index = 0 return { name: 'frame-collector', afterRender (ctx) { index += 1 onFrame({ index, url: ctx.dataURL }) }, reset () { index = 0 } } } The usage: capture a pose, read the frame back through the callback: const capturedFrames = [] const collector = frameCollector(frame => { capturedFrames.push(frame.url) }) // runs once per "Capture pose" click, against whatever // pose the sliders are showing at that moment await snapdom(poseScene, { plugins: [collector] }) slider input live style change (no capture) Capture pose snapdom() afterRender (ctx.dataURL) capturedFrames.push() Limits and things to watch The collector's afterRender hook is stateful, so in v3 each pose runs a fresh capture; resource caches can still be reused. Each SVG data URL stays in memory, so the filmstrip grows with frame count and content. title: Target Range — Every Shot Hits the Clone — SnapDOM Labs
text:
Showcase / Labs / Target range Labs Experiment Every shot hits the clone A shooting gallery where the board is a PNG. Each shot re-captures on top of the shots before it; the live target in the DOM stays clean. TL;DR A plugin's afterRender hook saves the rendered clone; afterClone swaps it back in on the next capture with a new bullet hole appended. The accumulation lives in the plugin's closure. What you're looking at Ten shots, a swaying crosshair, a ring-scored target. The board is one , replaced after every shot with a new snapdom.toPng() result. Try it Aim, click to fire. The reticle drifts and kicks after every shot, and the drift grows as ammo runs out. The marker that appears is the exported PNG. 0 Score 10 Shots 0 Best Ready? 10 shots. The reticle sways and kicks with every shot, so compensate for the drift. Start Restart Download target The download button uses the returned by the last snapdom.toPng() call; no second capture. How it works A hidden source element A 340×340
off-screen holds one SVG target built from a ring definition. SnapDOM captures this element, not the visible board. The shot is scored locally On click, the reticle's position after sway and recoil (not the raw mouse position) is converted to a percentage and scored against the ring radii. The resulting { xPct, yPct, color } goes to plugin.addHit() . addHit() appends a marker to the saved clone On the first shot the plugin clones the live source once. Each call appends a jagged, randomized torn-paper hole, positioned in percentage coordinates so it survives the render round trip. snapdom.toPng() runs again, plugin included The demo calls snapdom.toPng(target, { plugins: [plugin] }) again, same as the first shot. afterClone swaps in the saved clone The plugin replaces ctx.clone with the clone it has been building, holes included, instead of the hole-free source. afterRender checkpoints the result The plugin clones the rendered result as the baseline for the next shot. The output replaces the board The PNG goes into the board. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM 3 can reuse eligible captures, but stateful hooks run on fresh captures and the accumulated holes belong to the plugin. afterClone and afterRender share one closure with addHit() : it adds the mark to savedClone , afterClone swaps that clone in, afterRender saves the result for the next call, independent of capture reuse. Copy-paste example The plugin factory, usable for any "keep building on the last capture" case: function createHitboardPlugin (sourceEl) { let savedClone = null return { name: 'hitboard', afterClone (ctx) { if (savedClone) ctx.clone = savedClone.cloneNode(true) }, afterRender (ctx) { savedClone = ctx.clone.cloneNode(true) }, addHit (xPct, yPct, color) { if (!savedClone) savedClone = sourceEl.cloneNode(true) if (getComputedStyle(savedClone).position === 'static') { savedClone.style.position = 'relative' } const hit = document.createElement('div') hit.style.cssText = ` position: absolute; left: ${xPct}%; top: ${yPct}%; width: 24px; height: 24px; margin: -12px 0 0 -12px; pointer-events: none; ` hit.innerHTML = bulletHoleMarkup(color) savedClone.appendChild(hit) }, reset () { savedClone = null } } } The usage: score the shot, tell the plugin, capture again: const plugin = createHitboardPlugin(target) function shoot (xPct, yPct) { const { color } = scoreAt(xPct, yPct) plugin.addHit(xPct, yPct, color) return snapdom.toPng(target, { plugins: [plugin] }) } // on restart: plugin = createHitboardPlugin(target) — a fresh closure, // not plugin.reset(), so a stale reference from the finished game can't // leak a hole into the new one. shot addHit() snapdom.toPng() afterClone (restore + append) afterRender (checkpoint) Limits and things to watch addHit() initializes savedClone from the live source on first call, so the plugin needs no priming. reset() sets it back to null and the next capture re-clones the pristine source. Simpler than Paint Canvas 's skipNext flag: a restart is a hard reset, not a stroke boundary to detect mid-stream. title: Live Video Overlays from Plain HTML — SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / Video overlay Labs Experiment Live video overlays from plain HTML A scoreboard, a lower third, a stream chat: HTML and CSS composited over live video in the browser, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari. No OBS, no server. TL;DR The stream plugin keeps the overlay as a canvas that repaints only the boxes that changed; streamTexture uploads those rectangles to WebGL, where a shader composites them over the video and gives the look: clean, shine, CRT, hologram, glitch, or liquid glass refracting the footage under each panel. The output is a canvas. No browser flag. Try it Sports TV runs a broadcast package over a simulated match; press Goal or wait for one. Streamer uses your camera; Share screen puts your game behind the overlay, you in a circle. Change the look, drag the pieces, record a clip, or press Edit for the HTML and CSS. Sports TV Streamer Clean Liquid glass Shine CRT Hologram Glitch Goal! Camera Share screen Record Edit starting Liquid Refraction Bevel Frost Dispersion HTML CSS The overlay is this HTML and CSS. Panels with class glass paint var(--panel) , which the Liquid glass look turns into refracting glass shaped by the box and its border-radius ; give them position: absolute to drag them. data-clock shows a clock, data-rotate="one|two" cycles its text. The stage below is 960 by 540 pixels. How it works The HTML is a real DOM element Your markup goes into a 960 by 540 stage on this page, with your CSS nested under it. stream() turns it into a canvas that repaints only what changed The first frame is a full SnapDOM capture. After that, a change is traced to the nearest box that can repaint on its own, and only that subtree is captured. When the change cannot be isolated, the stream captures a wider region or a full frame. streamTexture() uploads the dirty rectangles On WebGL2, only the changed rectangles are uploaded. A full repaint uploads the full texture. The shader composites the video and the overlay Most looks read only the overlay texture: a light sweep, scanlines and glow, a hologram tint, glitch slices on a goal. Liquid glass also reads the layout: each frame, every .glass panel's box and border-radius become a rounded-rectangle distance field, joined by a smooth minimum with the drop under the pointer, so nearby shapes melt together. A spring makes each shape trail its box, so moving pieces stretch and wobble. Inside, the footage is sampled through a lens: pulled inward at the rim, frosted, colour-split, darkened over bright backgrounds so white text stays legible. The streamed HTML goes on top. The program output is a canvas It records to MP4 or WebM with recordCanvas() , or goes out as a WebRTC track with captureStream() , overlay included. The code The SnapDOM part is short. The rest is a full-screen fragment shader. import { stream, streamTexture } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl2') const overlay = streamTexture(gl) stream(stage, { embedFonts: false, onFrame: (frame) => overlay.update(frame), // uploads frame.rects only }) // every animation frame: upload the video, pass each .glass box to the shader, draw for (const el of stage.querySelectorAll('.glass')) { const r = el.getBoundingClientRect() // relative to the stage rects.push(r.left - base.left, r.top - base.top, r.width, r.height) } Limits The glass shape is the box and its border-radius , one radius per box; other shapes need their own distance function in the shader. The texture is pixels: links and buttons in it are not clickable. A box over a translucent background ( rgba() with alpha below 1) cannot repaint alone and forces a full repaint. Keep glass boxes free of background colour. Footage from another origin needs CORS.

The texture is pixels: links and buttons in it are not clickable. A box over a translucent background ( rgba() with alpha below 1) cannot repaint alone and forces a full repaint. Keep glass boxes free of background colour. Footage from another origin needs CORS.

title: WebGL Live Mirror — DOM, Live on the GPU — SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / Live mirror Labs Experiment DOM, live on the GPU Edit the card on the left. SnapDOM captures the latest state and uploads it to the WebGL texture on the right; rapid edits are combined into the next capture. TL;DR A defineExports plugin adds a webgl export that feeds the captured SVG into an existing WebGL texture. A dirty / working loop collapses fast typing into one trailing capture, so stale captures never queue up. What you're looking at The right panel updates after each capture. It is a SnapDOM capture of the live element, decoded into an and uploaded as a WebGL TEXTURE_2D . The theme buttons change a CSS custom property the element reads, so a theme switch takes the same capture path. The shader dropdown only changes how the fragment shader samples the texture on the GPU. Try it Edit the text, switch the accent color or swap shaders while typing. The right pane is a WebGL canvas with its own render loop; SnapDOM only refreshes its texture. Theme Shader Faithful Hologram Pixelate Editable DOM contenteditable Live signal Type here Every edit becomes a WebGL texture through SnapDOM. EDITABLE DOM_ WebGL texture idle GPU texture input updateMirror() snapdom() capture.toWebgl() GPU texture How it works Typing fires an input listener Each keystroke in the contenteditable element fires a native input event, whose one listener calls updateMirror() . updateMirror() sets a dirty flag If a capture is running, it marks the work dirty and returns. Otherwise it enters a while (dirty) loop and captures the element with { plugins: [mirrorPlugin] } . The plugin's defineExports(ctx) adds a webgl export SnapDOM wires it up as capture.toWebgl() , which passes the capture's context, including ctx.export.url , the rendered SVG data URL. The export loads that SVG into the existing texture It creates an Image from ctx.export.url . Once decoded, the WebGLMirror instance's update() uploads it as a new TEXTURE_2D and returns the canvas. An independent render loop keeps drawing it The mirror's own requestAnimationFrame loop, started once outside SnapDOM, redraws the texture every frame with the selected shader. The dirty re-check collapses bursts of keystrokes dirty is re-checked after each capture, so a fast-typed sentence yields one trailing capture of the latest DOM state. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM's core exports ( toPng , toCanvas and the rest) return a finished image or canvas. An existing WebGL texture is a destination the caller invents. defineExports is the seam for that: a plugin returns named async functions that get the capture's context and are wired up as capture.to() . beforeSnap / afterRender here only time each round trip for the readout. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. It needs only ctx.export.url , so it fits any WebGL renderer with an update(url) method: function webglMirror (renderer) { let started = 0 let elapsed = 0 return { name: 'webgl-live-mirror', beforeSnap () { started = performance.now() }, afterRender () { elapsed = performance.now() - started }, defineExports () { return { webgl: async ctx => { const canvas = await renderer.update(ctx.export.url) statsEl.textContent = `${elapsed.toFixed(0)} ms · GPU updated` return canvas } } } } } The usage. The dirty / working loop collapses a burst of edits into one trailing capture: const mirrorPlugin = webglMirror(renderer) let dirty = false let working = false async function updateMirror () { dirty = true if (working) return working = true while (dirty) { dirty = false const capture = await snapdom(editable, { plugins: [mirrorPlugin] }) await capture.toWebgl() } working = false } editable.addEventListener('input', updateMirror) Limits and things to watch A keystroke can trigger a fresh capture and upload: keep the element small, or debounce the handler for heavier content. SnapDOM 3 reuses eligible work automatically, but this demo's timing hooks are stateful and force a fresh capture; resource caches are still reused. title: Seamless DOM WebGL: text that isn't text — SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / Seamless DOM Labs Experiment The text you see isn't text Click into the box below and type. Every glyph is a WebGL texture rendered from the last SnapDOM capture. The editable DOM is invisible, and updates cross-fade in. TL;DR A transparent contenteditable proxy gives the browser a real caret and keystrokes; a hidden source element mirrors the text and is what SnapDOM captures. A defineExports plugin feeds each capture into a WebGL renderer that double-buffers two textures and cross-fades between them. What you're looking at You get a blinking caret and text selection. The glyphs are pixels in a WebGL texture captured from a hidden DOM element and mixed into the canvas under your cursor. The shader dropdown changes only what the fragment shader does with the finished frame. Try it Type, paste or press Enter. The browser handles the caret and selection; WebGL paints the captured letters. Shader Faithful Hologram CRT Liquid Kaleidoscope Melt Datamosh Neon Edge Live DOM signal Type here This text is real DOM, but you're seeing it as a WebGL texture kept in sync by SnapDOM. LIVE GPU Hidden DOM double-buffered texture starting… How it works A transparent proxy owns the caret The .input-layer sits on top of the WebGL canvas with transparent text and background. It gives the browser somewhere to place a caret and receives keyboard and paste events; the caret and selection stay visible. Every edit is mirrored to a hidden element On every input event, paste, and Enter (a beforeinput override inserts a literal newline instead of letting contenteditable create a new <div> ), the proxy's text is copied into the hidden #dom-source element and refresh() runs. refresh() coalesces bursts Same dirty / working loop as the live-mirror demo: input during a capture is flagged dirty and picked up by the running loop. It captures #dom-source with the seamlessWebgl plugin. The plugin exports into the renderer The plugin's defineExports returns a webgl export that hands the capture's URL to renderer.update(ctx.export.url) instead of returning an image. The idle texture is loaded, not the visible one SeamlessRenderer.update() loads the new capture into whichever of its two textures ( current or next ) is off screen, then starts a roughly 110ms blend toward it. The shader mixes, then the effect applies The fragment shader mixes beforeImage and afterImage by a blend uniform that ramps 0 1 over that window; the selected shader runs on the result. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM's core exports return a finished image. defineExports lets a plugin register a named export (here webgl ) that does something else with the render, such as pushing it into one of two alternating GPU textures. The difference from the live-mirror demo is architectural. Splitting the caret owner from the capture source makes the transition seamless: the canvas never waits on a capture, it is always mid-blend between two textures it already has while the hidden source is captured again. Copy-paste example The plugin factory forwards a capture's URL to the renderer you hand it: function seamlessWebgl (renderer) { let started = 0 let elapsed = 0 return { name: 'seamless-webgl', beforeSnap () { started = performance.now() }, afterRender () { elapsed = performance.now() - started }, defineExports () { return { webgl: async ctx => { const canvas = await renderer.update(ctx.export.url) perfLabel.textContent = `${elapsed.toFixed(0)} ms · texture swapped` return canvas } } } } } The usage calls the export through the generic capture.to('webgl') rather than capture.toWebgl() . Both work; .to(name) invokes a plugin-defined export without SnapDOM knowing its name ahead of time: const plugin = seamlessWebgl(renderer) let dirty = false let working = false async function refresh () { dirty = true if (working) return working = true while (dirty) { dirty = false const capture = await snapdom(source, { plugins: [plugin] }) await capture.to('webgl') } working = false } input sync #dom-source refresh() capture.to('webgl') renderer.update() blend 0 1 shader Limits and things to watch The transparent-proxy trick works for plain text only; rich text and IME composition edge cases need more care. This proxy reduces Enter to a literal newline and paste to plain text. Double-buffering costs one extra WebGL texture of GPU memory over the live-mirror demo, worth it only when the crossfade is the point. title: WebGL Shatter — A Capture, Shattered — SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / Shattered capture Labs Experiment A capture, shattered Five WebGL shaders, one starting point: a SnapDOM capture of a live, editable card, turned into a WebGL texture. TL;DR A defineExports plugin ( shatterExport ) adds result.toShatter() , which gets a canvas through the silent ctx.exports.canvas() facade (no re-triggered beforeExport / afterExport hooks) and slices it into a grid of small canvases used as WebGL textures. Ripple, glitch, dissolve and metal need no plugin: the whole card is one texture via plain snapdom.toCanvas() . What you're looking at The card's heading and paragraph are contenteditable . SnapDOM captures the card as it renders (your text, font metrics, gradient, shadow), so the effects run on your own words. Try it Edit the card, pick an effect, press the button (it relabels per effect). Ripple and Glitch settle on their own; Dissolve ends empty and needs Reset. Metal tracks your pointer until you exit it. Shatter Ripple Glitch Dissolve Metal Live DOM Try me! This text is editable HTML. SnapDOM captures it as it renders, font, gradient and shadow included, and turns it into a WebGL texture. 100% SnapDOM Shatter Reset Edit the card's text before applying an effect: you'll see your own text, not a canned image. How it works Ripple, Glitch, Dissolve, Metal: one texture, one shader snapdom.toCanvas(card, { scale: 2 }) captures the card as one canvas, uploaded with texImage2D . A per-effect fragment shader distorts or reveals it over a fixed duration (Metal: indefinitely, tracking the pointer). The card hides while the effect plays The card's CSS visibility is set to hidden after the capture and restored when the effect finishes. Metal stays hidden until you exit it. Shatter needs more than one texture shatterExport 's defineExports(ctx) returns a shatter export. result.toShatter({ cols, rows }) first gets a canvas via ctx.exports.canvas(opts) , the core exporter called directly. That canvas is sliced into a grid The canvas is cut into cols × rows small canvases with drawImage ; each becomes its own WebGL texture at its origin cell. Physics takes over Each piece spawns with a random velocity and rotation; gravity applies every frame and pieces fade out until none are left. Why this needed a plugin SnapDOM's built-in exports ( toPng , toCanvas , toSvg , toBlob ) return one complete image. Slicing into tiles is a shatter concern, not a capture concern. defineExports adds the custom shatter output. The shatter export still needs canvas pixels, so it calls the silent ctx.exports.{img,svg,canvas,blob,png,jpeg,webp} facade, which reuses the core exporters without re-running the plugin's beforeExport / afterExport hooks: no recursion, no duplicate firing. The other four effects use no plugin; most creative uses of a capture need none. defineExports is for a new output shape ; reach for toCanvas() first. Copy-paste example The plugin factory. cols / rows set the grid: function shatterExport (options = {}) { const { cols: defaultCols = 14, rows: defaultRows = 9 } = options return { name: 'shatter', defineExports (ctx) { return { shatter: async (_ctx2, opts = {}) => { const cols = opts.cols || defaultCols const rows = opts.rows || defaultRows // Reuse the core canvas exporter directly — this does NOT // re-run beforeExport/afterExport, so it's safe to call from // inside another export. const canvas = await ctx.exports.canvas(opts) const pw = canvas.width / cols const ph = canvas.height / rows const pieces = [] for (let ry = 0; ry Usage. The plugin is local to this capture; toShatter() appears on the result beside toPng / toCanvas : const result = await snapdom(card, { plugins: [shatterExport({ cols: 16, rows: 11 })] }) const { pieces } = await result.toShatter() // pieces[i] = { u, v, du, dv, canvas } — grid position (0..1) plus a // small <canvas>, ready to hand to texImage2D as its own WebGL texture The other four effects skip the plugin: one capture, one texture: const canvas = await snapdom.toCanvas(card, { scale: 2 }) const tex = makeTexture(canvas) // gl.texImage2D(..., canvas) card snapdom(plugins) result.toShatter() ctx.exports.canvas() slice into pieces WebGL textures Limits and things to watch The ctx.exports.canvas() facade is documented in PLUGIN_SPEC.md . A 16×11 grid makes 176 pieces; finer grids add draw calls, textures and memory. title: HTML Overlay over WebRTC — SnapDOM Labs
text: Showcase / Labs / WebRTC overlay Labs Experiment An HTML overlay, sent over WebRTC Left: video with an HTML scorebug composited on top. Right: the same picture received as a WebRTC track. No OBS, no server. TL;DR The stream plugin keeps the overlay as a canvas. A program canvas draws it over the footage, captureStream() turns that into a video track, and WebRTC carries it. Try it Change the score, slide the lower third, or put your camera behind the graphics. The right side follows a few frames later. Open a viewer tab to add a receiver. Program output (sender) canvas Received over WebRTC video +1 Home +1 Away Lower third Camera Open a viewer tab starting How it works The overlay is HTML Scoreboard, live badge and lower third are plain DOM on a transparent 960×540 stage. The lower third slides with left , not transform , so the stream patches a strip instead of repainting the frame. stream() keeps it as a canvas After the first full capture, isolated changes are patched in; other changes trigger a wider or full repaint. The stats line shows the median repaint cost. A program canvas composites it Each frame draws the footage, then the overlay canvas on top. captureStream() makes it a track The program canvas becomes a MediaStreamTrack . contentHint: 'detail' asks the encoder to favor detail; bandwidth and receiver scaling still affect legibility. WebRTC carries it Both peers run in your browser; viewer tabs find the sender through a BroadcastChannel . A real app does the offer/answer through its own signalling server. The media path is the same. The code import { stream } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const overlay = stream(stage, { embedFonts: false }) function frame() { ctx.drawImage(footage, 0, 0, 960, 540) ctx.drawImage(overlay.canvas, 0, 0, 960, 540) requestAnimationFrame(frame) } requestAnimationFrame(frame) const track = program.captureStream(30).getVideoTracks()[0] track.contentHint = 'detail' peerConnection.addTrack(track)

title: Agent map plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Context / Agent map @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Map interactive elements for agents. Adds toAgentMap() : an image with numbered badges on interactive elements and a JSON map of their names, roles, bounds and state. This format is often called Set-of-Mark. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { agentMap } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/agent-map'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [agentMap()] }); const { image, map, dimensions } = await result.toAgentMap(); // image: data URL of the screenshot with numbered red badges overlaid // map: [{ i, n, r, b, s? }, …]: index, name, role, bbox, state // Agent says "click element 2" → map[2].b gives [x, y, w, h] Map entry shape (default fields: 'minimal' ): Key Type Description i number Index matching the badge drawn on the image n string Accessible name: aria-label, then labelledby, then alt, then title, then labels, then textContent. The textContent fallback is capped at 60 characters r string Explicit role or an implicit role such as button , link , checkbox , radio , textbox , combobox , slider or heading b [x, y, w, h] Bounding box in output pixels, scaled with the image and maxImageWidth s object? Meaningful state: checked , disabled , focus , expanded , pressed , selected , value , hasValue , open , selectedText , covered isSemanticOnly true? Structural entry added by semantic: true ; no badge is drawn for it Example map for a checkout form: [ { i: 0, n: 'Email', r: 'textbox', b: [28, 80, 280, 34] }, { i: 1, n: 'Send product updates', r: 'checkbox', b: [28, 134, 13, 13], s: { checked: true } }, { i: 2, n: 'Apply coupon', r: 'button', b: [28, 176, 114, 38], s: { expanded: false } }, { i: 3, n: 'Remove coupon', r: 'button', b: [150, 176, 140, 38], s: { disabled: true } }, { i: 4, n: 'Pay $53.90', r: 'button', b: [28, 220, 97, 38] } ] Options Option Type Default Description image 'annotated' | 'raw' | false 'annotated' Annotated image, raw image or map only. false skips this export's image generation; see needs to skip capture rendering too fields 'minimal' | 'full' 'minimal' 'full' adds t (raw text content) and a (meaningful attributes) per entry. semantic boolean false Include structural elements such as headings, paragraphs and landmarks maxImageWidth number 1024 Downscale target for the image; bboxes rescale to match. imageFormat 'png' | 'jpg' | 'webp' 'png' Image format (only used when image is rendered). imageQuality number 0.8 Quality for lossy formats. interactiveSelector string see below CSS selector for interactive elements. semanticSelector string see below CSS selector for semantic elements (used when semantic: true ). labelStyle object {} Override badge styles. needs 'clone' | 'render' 'render' Use 'clone' with image: false to skip rendering; only valid on a per-capture plugin Defaults: Interactive elements: links with href , buttons, inputs, selects, textareas, summaries, [contenteditable="true"] , and elements with tabindex other than -1 . Also matches roles button , link , tab , menuitem , checkbox , radio , switch , slider , combobox , textbox . Structural elements: h1 – h6 , nav , main , article , section , header , footer , figcaption , blockquote , legend , p . Per-call overrides: image , imageFormat , imageQuality , maxImageWidth , plus image sizing ( width , height , scale , dpr ) and backgroundColor . Selectors, fields, semantics and badge styles are frozen during capture. For a map without rendering: const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [agentMap({ image: false, needs: 'clone' })] }); const { map, dimensions } = await result.toAgentMap(); Such a result has no image; result.url and image exports throw. The map includes open shadow roots and slotted content and respects core's exclusion policy. Sensitive input values are omitted; other input/textarea values become up to 12 bullets. This does not redact the image. Badges are applied only to toAgentMap({ image: 'annotated' }) ; raw images and other exports keep the captured page. Bounding boxes are not exact with perspective, rotated ancestors, or a root rotation stripped by outerTransforms: false . When to use Use it for visual agents that need element coordinates, visual QA, or image/map datasets. It runs inside the web app, including browser extensions and Electron pages, without requiring an external browser automation process.

title: ASCII export plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Export / ASCII export @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Export the capture as ASCII art. Adds a toAscii() export method that converts captures to ASCII art. Plain text remains the default. Use toAscii({ format: 'html', contrast: 0.8 }) for a colored, compact HTML preview; contrast defaults to zero and does not change existing text exports. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { asciiExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/ascii-export'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [asciiExport({ width: 100 })] }); const art = await result.toAscii(); console.log(art); Options Option Type Default Description width number 80 Character width of output charset string ' .:-=+*#%@' Characters from lightest to darkest invert boolean false Invert luminance mapping format 'text' | 'html' 'text' Plain text, or colored HTML in a <pre> contrast number 0 Non-negative luminance contrast boost toAscii({ width, charset, invert, format, contrast }) overrides any of them per call. The conversion is also exported on its own. asciiFromCanvas(source, options) turns any drawable (a canvas, an image, a video frame) into ASCII with the same options. Run it on every frame of a @zumer/snapdom-stream stream for a live ASCII mirror: import { stream } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream'; import { asciiFromCanvas } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/ascii-export'; const live = stream(el, { fps: 15, onFrame: (frame) => (pre.textContent = asciiFromCanvas(frame.canvas, { width: 100 })) }); await live.ready; live.stop();

title: Export DOM as text or JSON for agents — SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Context / Context export @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Export the UI as text for agents. Adds toContext() : the captured UI as a text outline or JSON tree containing structure, roles, visible text, state and optional bounds. It skips hidden content and collapses wrappers that add no information. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { contextExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/context-export'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [contextExport()] }); const outline = await result.toContext(); const { root, truncated, nodes } = await result.toContext({ format: 'json' }); Options Option Type Default Description format 'outline' | 'json' 'outline' Text outline or { root, truncated, nodes } maxTextLength number 120 Per-node text limit; longer text ends with an ellipsis maxNodes number 800 Node limit; output reports truncation geometry boolean true Include [x, y, width, height] relative to the capture root needs 'clone' | 'render' 'render' 'clone' skips rendering; only valid on a per-capture plugin The tree is frozen during capture. Per-call options can change format , maxTextLength , or omit captured geometry. They cannot increase maxNodes or restore geometry that was not captured. Open shadow roots and slots follow core's exclusion policy. Sensitive input values are omitted; other input/textarea values are masked. Ordinary page text and attributes remain in the output. Use contextExport({ needs: 'clone' }) when you only need structured output. That result has no image, so result.url and image exports throw.

title: GIF export plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Record / GIF export @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Record the element as a GIF. Adds toGif() , which records the live element and returns an image/gif Blob. Its built-in GIF89a encoder uses median-cut quantization and LZW, with no encoding dependency. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { gifExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/gif-export'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [gifExport({ fps: 12, duration: 3000 })] }); const blob = await result.toGif(); // Or download directly: await result.toGif({ download: 'animation.gif' }); Options Option Type Default Description fps number 10 Frames per second duration number 2000 Total duration in ms (ignored if frames is set) frames number none Explicit frame count (overrides duration ) maxColors number 256 Palette size per frame (2–256) background string '#ffffff' Color composited under transparent pixels scale number capture's scale Capture scale repeat number 0 Loop count ( 0 = forever, -1 = play once) filename string 'capture.gif' Download filename Per-call opts override constructor options and accept download ( boolean | string ). Recording starts when toGif() runs, including its first frame. It preserves the original capture policy, including exclusions and plugins. Frame capture speed limits the sampling rate.

title: HTML export plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Export / HTML export @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Export the frozen HTML. Adds toHtml() , which returns the frozen clone with its captured styles and fonts as an HTML document. You can reopen the captured layout without exporting it as a bitmap. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { htmlExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/html-export'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [htmlExport()] }); const html = await result.toHtml(); // full <!DOCTYPE html> string // Or download a .html file: await result.toHtml({ download: 'snapshot.html' }); Options Option Type Default Description fullDocument boolean true Wrap output in <!DOCTYPE html>… ; if false , return just <style> + the fragment filename string 'capture.html' Download filename when opts.download is true title string 'Captured interface' Escaped document title lang string 'en' Escaped document language Per-call opts accepts fullDocument , filename and download . Set download: true to download, or pass a filename string. The method returns the HTML string either way. The document retains source markup, including event-handler attributes; it is not sanitized.

title: SnapDOM plugins: PDF, Vector, Stream and the toolbox
text: Plugins 15 official plugins · MIT Plugins for SnapDOM. Choose a plugin by its output or by what it changes in the capture. PDF, Vector and Stream have their own packages; the other twelve ship as the toolbox. All are MIT-licensed. Source npm Plugin demos Install npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest This installs SnapDOM and the toolbox. For PDF, Vector or Stream, install its package instead of the toolbox; its page has the command. All official plugins need SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer within 3.x. For example, install @zumer/snapdom-pdf alongside the toolbox to redact a report before exporting it: npm install @zumer/snapdom-pdf import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { redactInputs } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/redact-inputs' import { pdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-pdf' const el = document.querySelector('#report') const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs(), pdf()] }) const blob = await result.toPdf({ page: 'a4' }) Plugins by job Prepare plugins change the clone before it renders; the others add an export method to the result, and Stream keeps a canvas in step with the element. Prepare Change what the capture shows. The live page is never touched. Redact inputs Mask field values, hide blocks, drop attributes Replace text Strings or regular expressions, in the clone only Filter Grayscale, sepia, blur or any filter string Color tint A blend-mode overlay with its own opacity Timestamp overlay Date, time or a custom formatter in a corner Export Other outputs from the same capture. PDF Documents with selectable text, links and pages Vector Editable SVG and the Figma clipboard HTML export The clone with its styles and fonts as a document ASCII export Text or colored HTML, also frame by frame JPEG XL Exact text and lossy photos in one file Record Record the live element over time. Stream A live element as a canvas that repaints what changed GIF export A built-in GIF89a encoder, no dependency Video export MP4 or WebM through MediaRecorder Context Structured output for coding agents and visual QA. Agent map Badges on the image plus a JSON element map Context export An outline or JSON tree of structure, text and state Community plugins Maintained by their authors. Check the supported SnapDOM versions before using one with 3.x. To add yours, open a pull request with a row in community-plugins.md ; CONTRIBUTING_PLUGINS.md says what a row needs. Plugin What it does Category npm Author snapdom-html2pdf-plugin Exports a webpage to PDF through html2pdf.js export snapdom-html2pdf-plugin jswhisperer figma-restoration-mcp-vue-tools Figma component restoration MCP kit with SnapDOM-powered screenshots and diff analysis integration Yujie Wu Build your own A plugin is an object with hooks. The plugin guide walks through one, and PLUGIN_SPEC.md is the contract: hook order, what each hook receives, and what it may change.

For PDF, Vector or Stream, install its package instead of the toolbox; its page has the command. All official plugins need SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer within 3.x. For example, install @zumer/snapdom-pdf alongside the toolbox to redact a report before exporting it: npm install @zumer/snapdom-pdf import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { redactInputs } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/redact-inputs' import { pdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-pdf' const el = document.querySelector('#report') const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs(), pdf()] }) const blob = await result.toPdf({ page: 'a4' })

Redact inputs Mask field values, hide blocks, drop attributes Replace text Strings or regular expressions, in the clone only Filter Grayscale, sepia, blur or any filter string Color tint A blend-mode overlay with its own opacity Timestamp overlay Date, time or a custom formatter in a corner

title: Export
text: Other outputs from the same capture. PDF Documents with selectable text, links and pages Vector Editable SVG and the Figma clipboard HTML export The clone with its styles and fonts as a document ASCII export Text or colored HTML, also frame by frame JPEG XL Exact text and lossy photos in one file

title: Record
text: Record the live element over time. Stream A live element as a canvas that repaints what changed GIF export A built-in GIF89a encoder, no dependency Video export MP4 or WebM through MediaRecorder

title: Context
text: Structured output for coding agents and visual QA. Agent map Badges on the image plus a JSON element map Context export An outline or JSON tree of structure, text and state

title: JPEG XL plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Export / JPEG XL @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Export the capture as JPEG XL. Adds toJxl() , toBlob({ format: 'jxl' }) and download({ format: 'jxl' }) . Text and interface stay exact while photos take the quality, in one JPEG XL file. The encoder is rapier-jxl (MIT), an optional peer: the text measurement loads at the first capture, the encoder at the first export. Source · MIT Changelog npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest npm install rapier-jxl Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { jxl } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/jxl'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [jxl()] }); const img = await result.toJxl({ quality: 0.8 }); const blob = await result.toBlob({ format: 'jxl' }); await result.download({ format: 'jxl', filename: 'card' }); Options Option Type Default Description module string 'rapier-jxl/capture-complete' With your codec : 'rapier-jxl/capture' (every pixel exact) or 'rapier-jxl/upload' (photographic) codec object none Your own encoder with prepare and capture decoder object none createCodec() from rapier-jxl/codec/decode , for toJxl() where JPEG XL does not show effort number 3 Default effort, 1-9 webgpu false | 'required' none Disable WebGPU, or require a device helpers boolean | object none Helper workers for the encoder the plugin creates Exports take toWebp() 's options, plus effort , signal , onProgress (0 to 1) and onEncoded (once). quality: 1 is exact. The plugin's own encoder takes up to 40 megapixels; plugin.close() ends its workers. Encoding works in every browser: toBlob() and download() give image/jxl . Where the browser cannot show JPEG XL (Edge, for one), toJxl() shows the decoder 's pixels, or rejects with JXL_NOT_SHOWN without one.
