title: HTML to searchable PDF in JavaScript — SnapDOM PDF
text: Plugins / PDF Official plugin · MIT Export a searchable PDF. Capture a live element, add selectable text and links, and paginate it into a PDF in your browser. Install npm install @zumer/snapdom @zumer/snapdom-pdf Requires SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer within 3.x. Source and MIT license . Without a bundler, map both packages in an import map and serve the whole @zumer/snapdom-pdf folder, because its index.js imports files from src/ . <script type="importmap"> { "imports": { "@zumer/snapdom": "/vendor/snapdom.mjs", "@zumer/snapdom-pdf": "/vendor/snapdom-pdf/index.js" } } </script> Quick start import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { pdf } from '@zumer/snapdom-pdf' snapdom.plugins(pdf()) const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#report')) const blob = await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4', download: 'report.pdf' }) Register the plugin before you capture. A capture made without it has no toPdf() . To use it on one capture only, pass it there: snapdom(el, { plugins: [pdf()] }) . toPdf() returns a PDF Blob . download also saves the file. shot.to('pdf', options) does the same as toPdf(options) . How it works The page image plus a PDF text layer The page image is SnapDOM's capture. The plugin places a second, invisible text layer over it using positions derived from SnapDOM's final serialized clone. No headless browser or separate layout engine rebuilds the page. By default, the image preserves the capture’s appearance while the text layer adds selection, search and copy. Paper sizes add pagination; optional fields keep supported controls fillable. Vector text , headers and footers , encryption and structured reports are configured below. Options on pdf() Set these options on pdf() : they decide which text, controls and pagination hints the plugin reads from the captured artifact. A later toPdf() call cannot change them. Option Default What it does formValues true Include the values typed in inputs and the selected option. Passwords become bullets. shadow true Read text inside open shadow roots. breakAvoid true Measure blocks so page breaks avoid cutting them. outline true Turn headings into bookmarks. A selector string picks other elements; false turns it off. forms true Measure form controls so the PDF can have fillable fields. Every other option works in either place. On pdf() it becomes the default for every export; in toPdf() it applies to that export and wins. Pages Option Default What it does page 'fit' 'fit' makes one page the size of the capture. Paper sizes: 'a3' to 'a6' , 'b4' , 'b5' , 'letter' , 'legal' , 'tabloid' , 'executive' , or [width, height] in points. orientation 'portrait' 'portrait' or 'landscape' . margin 24 Margin on every side, in points. Ignored on page: 'fit' . repeatHeaders true Repeat a table's <thead> on each page the table continues to. Page breaks avoid table rows, list items, figures, quotes, images and anything with break-inside: avoid . CSS page breaks are respected. A block taller than a page still has to split. Image and file size What you see in the PDF is an image of the capture, with invisible text on top so it can be selected and searched. Option Default What it does image true Draw the captured image. With false , only PDF text and annotations remain; use vectorText: true with embedded fonts to make eligible text visible. codec 'auto' Try JPEG and lossless and keep the smaller file, per image. 'jpeg' or 'flate' forces one. quality 0.92 JPEG quality. It only matters when JPEG wins, which on normal pages is rare. backgroundColor none Fill transparent areas with a colour. Usually makes the file smaller. Sharpness and size come from the capture: snapdom(el, { scale, dpr }) . Both multiply the image's pixels and leave the page layout alone. The image keeps that many pixels per CSS pixel at the size it is printed. A capture enlarged to fill the paper is drawn at the enlarged size, so it stays as sharp as on screen. dpr defaults to the screen of the machine that exports, so set it, for example to 2 , to get the same file everywhere. Text and links Option Default What it does text true Add the invisible text layer, so the text can be selected, searched and copied. links true Make links clickable. Same-page anchors jump inside the PDF. debugText false Paint the text layer red, to check where it sits. Links work for http: , https: , mailto: and tel: . Any other link is left out with a warning. Covering something with a box or a blur hides the pixels, not the text: it can still be selected in the PDF. To keep data out, remove or replace it before the capture. Fonts and sharp text Option Default What it does embedFonts true Embed the page's web fonts, only the letters the document uses. 'full' embeds whole fonts; false none. vectorText false Draw the text as real letters instead of pixels: sharp at any zoom. The PDF can only embed fonts the capture carries, so capture with snapdom(el, { embedFonts: true }) . System fonts have no file to embed. Copying text works the same with or without embedded fonts. vectorText needs embedded fonts. Right-to-left and complex scripts stay as image. With image: false it gives a very small text-only PDF, without borders, backgrounds or pictures. Bookmarks and accessibility Option Default What it does outline true Bookmarks from headings. Set it on pdf() . tagged true Tag headings, paragraphs, lists, tables and figures for screen readers. lang from the page Document language, for example 'en' or 'es-MX' . The PDF is marked accessible (PDF/UA-1) only when it qualifies: every font embedded, a language, a meta.title , alt text on every image and fields: false . There is no option to force it. When something is missing, the report says what. Fillable forms Option Default What it does fields true Turn form controls into fields you can fill in the PDF. false keeps their values as plain text. Text inputs, textareas, checkboxes, radio buttons and selects become fields with their name, value and label. Read-only, disabled, required and maxlength carry over. Password fields are written empty. Buttons, sliders, colour pickers and file inputs stay as image. The PDF never contains scripts or submit actions. Header, footer and page numbers Option Default What it does header none Text, a function, { left, center, right, size, font, color, rule, gap } or an element. footer none The same, at the bottom. pageNumbers false true writes "1 / 4". { format, align, size, font, color } changes it. await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4', header: { left: 'North Studio', right: 'Delivery report' }, pageNumbers: { format: (page, pages) => `Page ${page} of ${pages}` }, }) These need a paper size and do nothing on page: 'fit' . Text is real PDF text. An element is captured as an image, so its text cannot be selected. Cover, contents, back page and watermark Option Default What it does cover none An element captured as the first page. toc none A table of contents from the headings. true , a title, or { title, levels, size, font, indent, dots, label, color, leaderColor } . back none An element captured as the last page. watermark none Text or an element over every page. { text, opacity, angle, size, font, color } or { element, opacity, angle, fit } . Cover, contents and back page need a paper size. The watermark also works on page: 'fit' . Metadata Option Default What it does meta none { title, author, subject, keywords, creator, created, modified } . Viewers show the title instead of the file name. Dates are written only when you pass them. Pass new Date() when you want today. The same captured state with the same options produces identical unencrypted bytes. Encryption uses fresh randomness for each export. Password await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4', encrypt: { userPassword: 'ada-1815', ownerPassword: 'owner-key' }, }) encrypt protects the file with AES-256. userPassword is required. ownerPassword defaults to it. permissions takes print , modify , copy , annotate , fillForms , assemble and printHighRes , all true by default. Only the password protects the file. Permissions are requests that a viewer may ignore. Encryption needs https or localhost, and an encrypted export is different every time. Output Option Default What it does download false A file name, or true for snapdom.pdf . The Blob is still returned. deflate true Compress the PDF's internal streams. Progress, cancel and report Option Default What it does onProgress none Called with { phase, done, total } as pages are made. total is null until the page count is known. signal none An AbortSignal . Aborting stops the export with an AbortError . onReport none Called once the PDF is done, with what happened: pages, size, fields, fonts and warnings. await shot.toPdf({ page: 'a4', onProgress: ({ done, total }) => bar.update(done, total), signal: controller.signal, onReport: (report) => console.log(report.pages, report.warnings), }) Each warning in the report has a code , such as link-unresolved or text-clipped , so a test can check for them without reading messages. When something looks wrong The plugin warns in the console with a [snapdom-pdf] prefix: a block split across pages, a link without a target, text cut off. The same warnings arrive in the report. A grey box where an image should be means the capture could not read that image. It shows up in the capture's result.warnings as image-fallback . Export a PDF with cross-origin images explains the fix. If the PDF does not match the page, report a small example with the capture options, browser and warning codes. Limits Text is an image unless you use vectorText , so a deep zoom shows the capture's resolution. Closed shadow roots cannot be read. Date inputs are written in ISO format, not as the browser shows them. An element used as header, footer or watermark has no selectable text. A repeated table header has no links. The full test suite runs in Chromium. Firefox and WebKit are checked for the main features. Questions Is the text really selectable, or is it OCR? It is selectable without OCR. Eligible text is placed from browser geometry in SnapDOM's final serialized clone, so structural exclusions and geometry-preserving replacements stay aligned with the capture. Ambiguous paint effects are omitted fail-safe. Download a sample and copy a paragraph. Does it need a server? The exporter itself runs in the browser and returns a Blob ; it does not upload the PDF. SnapDOM may still fetch resources used by the page, or use a proxy if your application configured one. Which browsers? The complete fixture suite is Chromium-only. Both plugin builds must also pass the release artifact smoke in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. That supports the plugin/API contract in all three; it does not pretend every complex layout has the same three-engine coverage.

title: Redact inputs plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Prepare / Redact inputs @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Redact fields before sharing. Masks input and textarea values, excludes selected blocks, and removes named attributes from captured outputs. Core already masks password fields to match their visible bullets; other field values remain visible unless you redact them. The live page stays unchanged. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { redactInputs } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/redact-inputs'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); // Defaults: email, tel, and the cc-* / current-password / new-password / one-time-code // autocomplete tokens. snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs()] }); // Everything, including textareas: snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs({ all: true })] }); // App-specific fields, blanked rather than bulleted: snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs({ selector: '[data-private]', mask: () => '' })] }); // Exclude whole blocks and remove metadata attributes: const redaction = redactInputs({ blocks: ['.private-panel', '[data-private-block]'], attributes: [ { selector: '[data-token]', names: ['data-token'] }, { selector: '.customer', names: ['title', 'aria-label'] } ] }); snapdom(el, { plugins: [redaction] }); // Remove those blocks from the layout as well: snapdom(el, { excludeMode: 'remove', plugins: [redaction] }); The default mask keeps the string's length. Glyph widths can differ, so wrapping and truncation may change. A <select> is not masked (its visible option label stays); hide it with a blocks rule instead. Options Option Type Default Description types string[] ['email', 'tel'] Input type attribute values to redact autocomplete string[] ['cc-*', 'current-password', 'new-password', 'one-time-code'] Autocomplete tokens; a trailing * matches by prefix selector string '' Extra CSS selector for inputs and textareas all boolean false Redact every input and textarea, regardless of types , autocomplete or selector mask (value, el) => string same-length bullets Custom masker blocks string | string[] [] CSS selectors for whole subtrees to exclude; uses the capture's excludeMode attributes Array<{ selector: string, names: string[] }> [] Remove exact named attributes from clones of matching source elements and their semantic projections; names are not wildcard patterns blocks keeps an invisible space by default ( excludeMode: 'hide' ); 'remove' drops the subtree from the captured layout. It combines with the capture's existing exclude rules. If the capture root itself belongs to a blocked subtree, 'remove' throws; use 'hide' for that capture. Selectors match source elements, including nodes in open shadow trees. attributes removes the listed DOM attributes and their projections in agent-map and context-export , such as accessible names or structured state. It does not erase copies of those values already materialized as visible text, CSS content , or bitmap pixels. Use blocks to hide the subtree that paints visible content. A value attribute rule on an input or textarea clears its displayed value and omits its structured state.value . Existing default field masks still apply when you add block or attribute rules. HTML exports use the prepared clone with the selected redaction rules. agent-map and context-export apply the same block, attribute and field rules to their source-derived data, regardless of official plugin order. The rules do not search arbitrary text or images for sensitive content. The built-in mask without custom selectors permits reuse of unchanged captures. Custom masks and nonempty selector , blocks or attributes rules run on every capture. Changed content runs the full pipeline so no field skips redaction. Nonempty blocks or attributes rules add a final beforeRender pass, which makes a capture requested with engine: 'html-in-canvas' use the SVG renderer. Field-only redaction does not add this pass. agent-map and context-export omit sensitive values and mask other typed values in their structured state fields. Ordinary page text and labels remain. An attached image still follows core's capture policy; use this plugin to mask its visible fields too.

title: Usage
text: import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { redactInputs } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/redact-inputs'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); // Defaults: email, tel, and the cc-* / current-password / new-password / one-time-code // autocomplete tokens. snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs()] }); // Everything, including textareas: snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs({ all: true })] }); // App-specific fields, blanked rather than bulleted: snapdom(el, { plugins: [redactInputs({ selector: '[data-private]', mask: () => '' })] }); // Exclude whole blocks and remove metadata attributes: const redaction = redactInputs({ blocks: ['.private-panel', '[data-private-block]'], attributes: [ { selector: '[data-token]', names: ['data-token'] }, { selector: '.customer', names: ['title', 'aria-label'] } ] }); snapdom(el, { plugins: [redaction] }); // Remove those blocks from the layout as well: snapdom(el, { excludeMode: 'remove', plugins: [redaction] }); The default mask keeps the string's length. Glyph widths can differ, so wrapping and truncation may change. A <select> is not masked (its visible option label stays); hide it with a blocks rule instead.

title: Options
text: Option Type Default Description types string[] ['email', 'tel'] Input type attribute values to redact autocomplete string[] ['cc-*', 'current-password', 'new-password', 'one-time-code'] Autocomplete tokens; a trailing * matches by prefix selector string '' Extra CSS selector for inputs and textareas all boolean false Redact every input and textarea, regardless of types , autocomplete or selector mask (value, el) => string same-length bullets Custom masker blocks string | string[] [] CSS selectors for whole subtrees to exclude; uses the capture's excludeMode attributes Array<{ selector: string, names: string[] }> [] Remove exact named attributes from clones of matching source elements and their semantic projections; names are not wildcard patterns blocks keeps an invisible space by default ( excludeMode: 'hide' ); 'remove' drops the subtree from the captured layout. It combines with the capture's existing exclude rules. If the capture root itself belongs to a blocked subtree, 'remove' throws; use 'hide' for that capture. Selectors match source elements, including nodes in open shadow trees. attributes removes the listed DOM attributes and their projections in agent-map and context-export , such as accessible names or structured state. It does not erase copies of those values already materialized as visible text, CSS content , or bitmap pixels. Use blocks to hide the subtree that paints visible content. A value attribute rule on an input or textarea clears its displayed value and omits its structured state.value . Existing default field masks still apply when you add block or attribute rules. HTML exports use the prepared clone with the selected redaction rules. agent-map and context-export apply the same block, attribute and field rules to their source-derived data, regardless of official plugin order. The rules do not search arbitrary text or images for sensitive content. The built-in mask without custom selectors permits reuse of unchanged captures. Custom masks and nonempty selector , blocks or attributes rules run on every capture. Changed content runs the full pipeline so no field skips redaction. Nonempty blocks or attributes rules add a final beforeRender pass, which makes a capture requested with engine: 'html-in-canvas' use the SVG renderer. Field-only redaction does not add this pass. agent-map and context-export omit sensitive values and mask other typed values in their structured state fields. Ordinary page text and labels remain. An attached image still follows core's capture policy; use this plugin to mask its visible fields too.

title: Stream DOM to canvas for WebGL and video — SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Stream Official plugin · MIT Stream a live element as a canvas. Use a canvas that follows DOM changes as a WebGL texture, video overlay or live preview. Unchanged areas keep their pixels. Quick start Add Stream to a page Requires SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer within 3.x. Source and MIT license . npm install @zumer/snapdom @zumer/snapdom-stream stream(element, options) returns the canvas, ready (a promise for the first full frame), stats and stop() . The canvas is updated in place and onFrame gets each repaint. Every capture option applies ( scale , dpr , embedFonts , exclude and the rest). import { stream } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const live = stream(panel, { scale: 2, onFrame(frame) { // frame.canvas is updated in place; frame.rects lists what changed, in canvas pixels. }, }) await live.ready document.body.append(live.canvas) // Call live.stop() when you remove the preview. How it works One full frame, then patches The first frame is a full capture. After that, every change (mutations, typing, focus, hover, running animations) is traced to the nearest box that can be repainted on its own, and only that subtree is captured and drawn into its rect. Patches A changed card costs the capture of that card, not of the page. frame.rects lists the boxes a frame redrew, in canvas pixels, so a consumer can upload or copy just those. Clip windows A change in a box that cannot be repainted on its own (a value on a translucent card, a row under a badge) repaints a window of the element instead: a clip capture of that box, with everything that paints there. Hover The pointer repaints only what a :hover rule restyles. Idle keyframes A keyframe in idle time heals anything the change tracking could not see, at most every 2 s and never more than 2% of the main thread. Full frames and frame.reason A frame that cannot be patched exactly is a full frame, and frame.reason says why: 'root resized' , 'no host for <div.x>' and so on. patches: false repaints full frames only, for comparison. Pixel for pixel Every patched frame is meant to match a full capture of the same DOM state pixel for pixel. The test suite checks exactly that on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Measured on a 1000px grid with one card changing per frame, median per frame, as full capture / patch: Cards Chromium full / patch Firefox full / patch WebKit full / patch 400 11.7 / 4.2 ms 28 / 4 ms 20 / 4 ms 2000 52.9 / 4.9 ms 119 / 5 ms 90 / 4 ms The whole API One function, and the pieces around it Everything below is exported from @zumer/snapdom-stream . stream(element, options) The entry. Returns { canvas, ready, stats, stop() } ; the options are the capture options plus the four listed further down. streamExport() and toStream() The plugin form. Register streamExport() on a capture and the result gains toStream(options) . It streams the element using that capture’s options. GIF and video recording methods require their own plugins. import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { streamExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const result = await snapdom(panel, { plugins: [streamExport()] }) const live = await result.toStream() await live.ready document.body.append(live.canvas) streamTexture(gl) Keeps a WebGL texture in step with the stream. On WebGL2 it uploads only the changed rects: 4% of the texture per frame in the WebGL demo, against 100%. import { stream, streamTexture } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const tex = streamTexture(gl) stream(panel, { onFrame: (frame) => tex.update(frame) }) // draw with tex.texture recordCanvas(canvas, options) Composite live.canvas over anything with drawImage , and record the result. rec.done resolves to an MP4 or WebM Blob, whichever the browser records. import { recordCanvas } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const rec = recordCanvas(output, { fps: 30, duration: 10000 }) const blob = await rec.done // MP4 or WebM, whichever the browser records WebRTC The composited canvas is a video track like a camera's, so an HTML overlay travels inside the video to every viewer, with no desktop software and no server-side render. const track = output.captureStream(30).getVideoTracks()[0] track.contentHint = 'detail' // graphics are text: keep the resolution peerConnection.addTrack(track, new MediaStream([track])) Overlay templates overlayStage , scoreboard , lowerThird , ticker and liveBadge : a stage and four broadcast graphics, as plain DOM with a small controller each. Every box that changes is opaque and the lower third slides with left , so a score, a clock tick or a slide costs a patch, not a full frame. Theme through CSS variables on the stage: accent , panel , panel-2 , text , ink , live , font . import { stream, overlayStage, scoreboard, lowerThird, ticker, liveBadge } from '@zumer/snapdom-stream' const stage = overlayStage({ width: 1920, height: 1080, theme: { accent: '#facc15' } }) const score = scoreboard({ home: 'HOME', away: 'AWAY' }) const lower = lowerThird({ name: 'Alex Morgan', role: 'Commentator' }) stage.append(score.el, liveBadge().el, lower.el, ticker({ items: ['Kick-off at 18:00'] }).el) document.body.append(stage) score.clock.start() score.add('home') lower.set({ name: 'Jamie Rivera' }) lower.hide() const live = stream(stage) await live.ready document.body.append(live.canvas) Options Options and limits All capture options apply ( scale , dpr , embedFonts , exclude and the rest), plus these four. onFrame(frame) Called after each repaint with { full, reason, rects, ms, busyMs, canvas } . ms is wall time; busyMs is the part the stream held the main thread, the one to budget on. fps Upper bound on repaints per second. Default: every animation frame. patches true . false repaints full frames only, for comparison. animations true . false stops following running animations and transitions: an animated box keeps the pixels it was last drawn with until a patch over it, a full frame or the keyframe. For a still of the page, where a spinner's angle does not matter but its full frames would. Limits Full frames A change with no box that can be repainted standalone repaints a window of the enclosing box that kept its rect, with everything that paints there. It is a full frame only when nothing kept its rect (the root resized), a node was removed, a blur, drop-shadow or url() filter above the change spreads it, a backdrop-filter box overlaps it, a positioned box overlaps a host that cannot be a window, or the patches would cover more than half of the canvas. CSSOM edits Programmatic CSSOM edits ( insertRule , rule.style ) produce no signal; the keyframe heals them. Spilled ink Text ink that spills past a box edge onto a pixel shared with a neighbour waits for the keyframe. Core version Requires SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer for pixel-aligned patches at fractional positions. Questions Is the canvas a video of the element? No. It is a capture, redrawn where the element changed. The first frame is a full capture; after that only the changed boxes are captured and drawn into their rects, and a keyframe in idle time heals anything the tracking could not see. How do I know whether a frame was patched? frame.full is false and frame.rects lists the boxes that were redrawn, in canvas pixels. A full frame carries frame.reason : 'root resized' , 'no host for <div.x>' and so on. Which engines are covered? The test suite compares every patched frame against a full capture of the same DOM state on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and the per-frame numbers above were measured on the three. Can I record it, or send it over WebRTC? Yes. recordCanvas() records any canvas a stream feeds, as MP4 or WebM, whichever the browser records. canvas.captureStream() turns the composited canvas into a video track for a peer connection, overlay included. Where can I see it running? Three labs are built on it: the video overlay , the WebRTC overlay and the ASCII mirror , which is the demo below. The showcase has a stream demo too.

title: HTML to editable SVG and Figma — SnapDOM Vector
text: Plugins / Vector Official plugin · MIT Export editable vector artwork. Reconstruct supported text and shapes as SVG artwork or copy the captured result into Figma. Getting started Requires SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer within 3.x. Source and MIT license . npm install @zumer/snapdom @zumer/snapdom-vector import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import vector from '@zumer/snapdom-vector' const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#plan-card'), { plugins: [vector()] }) const svg = await shot.toVector() // a standalone SVG string const copyButton = document.querySelector('#copy-to-figma') copyButton.addEventListener('click', () => shot.toFigma()) // HTTPS or localhost The exporter builds the artwork in the browser. It does not upload the capture; SnapDOM may fetch images and fonts used by the page. Fidelity See what changes in each format Browsers, SVG and Figma do not support the same effects. The plugin tells you when it had to adapt, rasterize or omit something, and identifies the affected layer. You can review those changes before handing the file to a designer or a client. Exact The destination can reproduce the layer as editable vector content. Adapted The layer remains vector, but an effect was translated to the closest available equivalent. Rasterized or omitted The effect has no usable vector equivalent. The report names the layer and explains what happened. The clearest case is backdrop-filter : frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and SVG has no way to express that, so the panel arrives as a flat colour. The report names the layer, and the limits list it. Read about fidelity reports How it works Built from the browser's resolved layout Grid, flexbox, sticky positioning and container queries are already resolved on screen. The plugin measures that result instead of trying to implement another CSS layout engine. Editable output Text remains text. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, images and DOM hierarchy become vector paint and usable layers. Browser layout Boxes, text lines and baselines are measured from the rendered page, including grid, flexbox, pseudo-elements and open shadow DOM. Private by design The plugin runs in the browser, including authenticated and staging pages. Captures are not uploaded to a server. Tested output Fixtures are rendered and compared against captures of the live elements in Chromium. Registering Register it per capture to avoid running the vector hook on unrelated image exports: // This capture only await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector()] }) // every capture in the page snapdom.plugins(vector()) The vector hook suspends automatic capture memoization because it needs the resolved clone. Global registration applies that work to every capture, including PNG exports. Keep the source element connected and laid out until export finishes. An element with display: none has no layout box to measure and causes an error. Everything about the capture stays on the snapdom() call. scale , dpr , backgroundColor and the rest are read before the plugin runs, so there is no second set of names for them here. exclude Option Default exclude none A CSS selector, a predicate (element) => boolean , or an array of either. Matching elements and their subtrees are left out of the vector output, text and layer names included. It is the only option. Give it to vector({ exclude }) as the default for every export from that capture, or to a single toVector() or toFigma() call, where it wins for that call. const shot = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector({ exclude: '.no-print' })] }) const svg = await shot.toVector({ exclude: ['.no-print', (node) => node.dataset.private === 'true'] }) SnapDOM's own exclude on the snapdom() call also applies: anything it leaves out of the capture never reaches the vector output. toVector() shot.toVector(options?) → Promise<string> Returns SVG shapes and text without foreignObject : a rectangle becomes a <rect> and a line of text becomes a <text> . Open the file in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot, Figma or a browser. Unsupported effects are listed in the diagnostics. The browser breaks the lines and the SVG only draws them. A block that occupies more than one line becomes one <text> per visual line, each at its measured baseline, so no editor re-wraps your paragraph differently. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, clips and images become native SVG paint. -webkit-text-stroke is a real stroke, and background-clip: text becomes the text's own fill. textLength is written only when a font binary travels with the file. Pinning a line to a width measured with your font, in a viewer that substituted another one, squeezes the glyphs. Native form controls are reconstructed at Chromium's measured proportions from their kind, state and accent colour, and each one is declared as a reconstruction. The SVG includes its approximation report in an XML comment beneath the <svg> tag. For the difference from core toSvg() , see how SVG foreignObject keeps HTML inside the capture . toFigma() shot.toFigma(options?) → Promise<void> Puts the capture on the clipboard in Figma's own paste format. Paste into a Figma file and you get frames, editable text, gradients, shadows, borders and images, with nothing installed. It resolves once the clipboard holds the copy. button.addEventListener('click', async () => { await shot.toFigma() toast('Copied. Paste it into Figma.') }) The Figma handoff example walks through copying a product card and checking its layers and fonts. Call it from a user action, on https or localhost. It uses the async clipboard API, and browsers only let a page the user is interacting with write to the clipboard. Outside a secure context it rejects with a message that says so. letter-spacing survives , which Figma's SVG importer cannot do: measured, a 376.8px line of text arrives at 449px through the SVG route, 50px of that from ignored tracking. Nodes whose paint the paste format cannot spell are drawn as vector artwork and carried as an image, unless they hold text, which stays editable. Effects that read what is underneath a node ( mix-blend-mode , backdrop-filter ) arrive unblended. The format is Figma's, and it is undocumented. Figma can change it in any release, with no error; the only symptom is a paste that does nothing. If that happens, toVector() and Figma's SVG import keep working while we update. Diagnostics Every approximation (a conic gradient drawn as wedges, a shadow spread folded into a blur, a filter a destination cannot run) is printed to the console under [snapdom-vector] , grouped by code with a count and up to three distinct messages, so four hundred identical warnings come out as one line and a count. The codes are stable and greppable, and toVector() also writes the list into the SVG. A diagnostic that says something will be lost in the destination (the SVG is exactly right in a browser, and Figma runs only part of it) is a warning about where the file is going, not a degradation of the file. What reaches the output, and what does not The engine walks the clone SnapDOM already resolved, which is why membership in the tree is not an argument here. In: Pseudo-elements ( ::before , ::after , ::first-letter ) as real nodes with real boxes, with counters and quotes resolved. Shadow DOM , flattened, so slotted content appears once, at the slot. Icon fonts resolved by ligature, and inline <svg> carried as vector with its element ids namespaced per instance. Images from currentSrc , so srcset resolves to what was actually shown, with object-fit and object-position applied. An SVG source is inlined as vector, not rasterized. Scroll offsets , applied, and overflow clipping as a real clip. <canvas> and <video> , as bitmaps. A tainted canvas is omitted with a reason rather than throwing. In-flight animations , at the values of the frame that was captured. Out: Anything exclude named, and anything SnapDOM itself excludes. display: none , visibility: hidden , and content clipped away by an overflow ancestor. The value inside a native control. The text in an <input> , the chosen <option> of a <select> and a placeholder are painted by the browser itself and no CSS property describes them. The widget's frame, border and background are drawn. Cross-origin iframes. The frame becomes a placeholder. Closed shadow roots , which are unreadable by anyone. Limits Review these limits before handing an export to another editor: Chromium. Everything is measured there and the pixel baselines were recorded there. Other engines are not tested, and we do not claim them. Fonts. The SVG embeds readable webfont files when it can. System and locally installed fonts have no file the page can provide; missing or uncovered faces are diagnosed. Editable text in Figma needs a font available there. A system font keyword is not a font name. Text painted by -apple-system or system-ui cannot tell any destination which face to load. Auto Layout is not inferred. Exported frames keep measured positions; they do not reflow when you resize them. backdrop-filter does not survive. Frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and neither SVG nor Figma can say that about an arbitrary backdrop. The panel arrives as a flat colour, and the diagnostics name it. A conic gradient becomes 128 flat wedges plus a small disc capping the apex. SVG has no conic paint server. Shadow spread is approximate. feMorphology 's kernel is rectangular, so the spread corners are. 3D transforms are flattened to their 2D projection, with a diagnostic. Figma has no colour-matrix effect , so filter: saturate(…) and its relatives have no equivalent there. They are named, with the CSS verbatim, rather than dropped quietly. The capture is one subtree, one viewport, one moment. No page-wide capture, no responsive variants, no component variants inferred from a static picture. Questions Is this a tracer? Does it vectorise the pixels? No. Nothing is traced and nothing is recognised. Every box, line and baseline is read from the live layout, and every fill is parsed from the CSS that produced it. A tracer cannot tell you the second stop of a gradient; this hands you its colour and position. Will my page come into Figma perfect? title: Getting started
text: Requires SnapDOM 3.4.0 or newer within 3.x. Source and MIT license . npm install @zumer/snapdom @zumer/snapdom-vector import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import vector from '@zumer/snapdom-vector' const shot = await snapdom(document.querySelector('#plan-card'), { plugins: [vector()] }) const svg = await shot.toVector() // a standalone SVG string const copyButton = document.querySelector('#copy-to-figma') copyButton.addEventListener('click', () => shot.toFigma()) // HTTPS or localhost The exporter builds the artwork in the browser. It does not upload the capture; SnapDOM may fetch images and fonts used by the page. Fidelity

title: See what changes in each format
text: Browsers, SVG and Figma do not support the same effects. The plugin tells you when it had to adapt, rasterize or omit something, and identifies the affected layer. You can review those changes before handing the file to a designer or a client. Exact The destination can reproduce the layer as editable vector content. Adapted The layer remains vector, but an effect was translated to the closest available equivalent. Rasterized or omitted The effect has no usable vector equivalent. The report names the layer and explains what happened. The clearest case is backdrop-filter : frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and SVG has no way to express that, so the panel arrives as a flat colour. The report names the layer, and the limits list it. Read about fidelity reports How it works

title: Built from the browser's resolved layout
text: Grid, flexbox, sticky positioning and container queries are already resolved on screen. The plugin measures that result instead of trying to implement another CSS layout engine. Editable output Text remains text. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, images and DOM hierarchy become vector paint and usable layers. Browser layout Boxes, text lines and baselines are measured from the rendered page, including grid, flexbox, pseudo-elements and open shadow DOM. Private by design The plugin runs in the browser, including authenticated and staging pages. Captures are not uploaded to a server. Tested output Fixtures are rendered and compared against captures of the live elements in Chromium.

title: Registering
text: Register it per capture to avoid running the vector hook on unrelated image exports: // This capture only await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector()] }) // every capture in the page snapdom.plugins(vector()) The vector hook suspends automatic capture memoization because it needs the resolved clone. Global registration applies that work to every capture, including PNG exports. Keep the source element connected and laid out until export finishes. An element with display: none has no layout box to measure and causes an error. Everything about the capture stays on the snapdom() call. scale , dpr , backgroundColor and the rest are read before the plugin runs, so there is no second set of names for them here.

title: exclude
text: Option Default exclude none A CSS selector, a predicate (element) => boolean , or an array of either. Matching elements and their subtrees are left out of the vector output, text and layer names included. It is the only option. Give it to vector({ exclude }) as the default for every export from that capture, or to a single toVector() or toFigma() call, where it wins for that call. const shot = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [vector({ exclude: '.no-print' })] }) const svg = await shot.toVector({ exclude: ['.no-print', (node) => node.dataset.private === 'true'] }) SnapDOM's own exclude on the snapdom() call also applies: anything it leaves out of the capture never reaches the vector output.

title: toVector()
text: shot.toVector(options?) → Promise<string> Returns SVG shapes and text without foreignObject : a rectangle becomes a <rect> and a line of text becomes a <text> . Open the file in Illustrator, Inkscape, Penpot, Figma or a browser. Unsupported effects are listed in the diagnostics. The browser breaks the lines and the SVG only draws them. A block that occupies more than one line becomes one <text> per visual line, each at its measured baseline, so no editor re-wraps your paragraph differently. Gradients, borders, radii, shadows, transforms, clips and images become native SVG paint. -webkit-text-stroke is a real stroke, and background-clip: text becomes the text's own fill. textLength is written only when a font binary travels with the file. Pinning a line to a width measured with your font, in a viewer that substituted another one, squeezes the glyphs. Native form controls are reconstructed at Chromium's measured proportions from their kind, state and accent colour, and each one is declared as a reconstruction. The SVG includes its approximation report in an XML comment beneath the <svg> tag. For the difference from core toSvg() , see how SVG foreignObject keeps HTML inside the capture .

title: toFigma()
text: shot.toFigma(options?) → Promise<void> Puts the capture on the clipboard in Figma's own paste format. Paste into a Figma file and you get frames, editable text, gradients, shadows, borders and images, with nothing installed. It resolves once the clipboard holds the copy. button.addEventListener('click', async () => { await shot.toFigma() toast('Copied. Paste it into Figma.') }) The Figma handoff example walks through copying a product card and checking its layers and fonts. Call it from a user action, on https or localhost. It uses the async clipboard API, and browsers only let a page the user is interacting with write to the clipboard. Outside a secure context it rejects with a message that says so. letter-spacing survives , which Figma's SVG importer cannot do: measured, a 376.8px line of text arrives at 449px through the SVG route, 50px of that from ignored tracking. Nodes whose paint the paste format cannot spell are drawn as vector artwork and carried as an image, unless they hold text, which stays editable. Effects that read what is underneath a node ( mix-blend-mode , backdrop-filter ) arrive unblended. The format is Figma's, and it is undocumented. Figma can change it in any release, with no error; the only symptom is a paste that does nothing. If that happens, toVector() and Figma's SVG import keep working while we update.

title: Diagnostics
text: Every approximation (a conic gradient drawn as wedges, a shadow spread folded into a blur, a filter a destination cannot run) is printed to the console under [snapdom-vector] , grouped by code with a count and up to three distinct messages, so four hundred identical warnings come out as one line and a count. The codes are stable and greppable, and toVector() also writes the list into the SVG. A diagnostic that says something will be lost in the destination (the SVG is exactly right in a browser, and Figma runs only part of it) is a warning about where the file is going, not a degradation of the file.

title: What reaches the output, and what does not
text: The engine walks the clone SnapDOM already resolved, which is why membership in the tree is not an argument here. In: Pseudo-elements ( ::before , ::after , ::first-letter ) as real nodes with real boxes, with counters and quotes resolved. Shadow DOM , flattened, so slotted content appears once, at the slot. Icon fonts resolved by ligature, and inline <svg> carried as vector with its element ids namespaced per instance. Images from currentSrc , so srcset resolves to what was actually shown, with object-fit and object-position applied. An SVG source is inlined as vector, not rasterized. Scroll offsets , applied, and overflow clipping as a real clip. <canvas> and <video> , as bitmaps. A tainted canvas is omitted with a reason rather than throwing. In-flight animations , at the values of the frame that was captured. Out: Anything exclude named, and anything SnapDOM itself excludes. display: none , visibility: hidden , and content clipped away by an overflow ancestor. The value inside a native control. The text in an <input> , the chosen <option> of a <select> and a placeholder are painted by the browser itself and no CSS property describes them. The widget's frame, border and background are drawn. Cross-origin iframes. The frame becomes a placeholder. Closed shadow roots , which are unreadable by anyone.

title: Limits
text: Review these limits before handing an export to another editor: Chromium. Everything is measured there and the pixel baselines were recorded there. Other engines are not tested, and we do not claim them. Fonts. The SVG embeds readable webfont files when it can. System and locally installed fonts have no file the page can provide; missing or uncovered faces are diagnosed. Editable text in Figma needs a font available there. A system font keyword is not a font name. Text painted by -apple-system or system-ui cannot tell any destination which face to load. Auto Layout is not inferred. Exported frames keep measured positions; they do not reflow when you resize them. backdrop-filter does not survive. Frosted glass is a blur of whatever sits behind the panel, and neither SVG nor Figma can say that about an arbitrary backdrop. The panel arrives as a flat colour, and the diagnostics name it. A conic gradient becomes 128 flat wedges plus a small disc capping the apex. SVG has no conic paint server. Shadow spread is approximate. feMorphology 's kernel is rectangular, so the spread corners are. 3D transforms are flattened to their 2D projection, with a diagnostic. Figma has no colour-matrix effect , so filter: saturate(…) and its relatives have no equivalent there. They are named, with the CSS verbatim, rather than dropped quietly. The capture is one subtree, one viewport, one moment. No page-wide capture, no responsive variants, no component variants inferred from a static picture.

title: Video export plugin for SnapDOM
text: Plugins / Record / Video export @zumer/snapdom-plugins · MIT Record the element as video. Adds toMp4() , which records the live element through MediaRecorder . The returned Blob's type identifies the recorded container. Source · MIT Changelog Showcase demo npm install @zumer/snapdom@latest @zumer/snapdom-plugins@latest Usage import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom'; import { videoExport } from '@zumer/snapdom-plugins/video-export'; const el = document.querySelector('#target'); const result = await snapdom(el, { plugins: [videoExport({ fps: 30, duration: 4000 })] }); const blob = await result.toMp4(); // Or download directly: await result.toMp4({ download: true }); The plugin tries supported MP4 codecs first, then WebM. A WebM fallback logs a warning; the default download filename matches the recorded .mp4 or .webm container. Explicit filenames and download strings are used as supplied. Options Option Type Default Description fps number 10 Frames per second duration number 2000 Total duration in ms (ignored if frames is set) frames number none Explicit frame count (overrides duration ) background string '#ffffff' Color composited under transparent pixels scale number capture's scale Capture scale bitrate number none videoBitsPerSecond passed to MediaRecorder filename string none Download filename; the default follows the recorded .mp4 / .webm container Requires MediaRecorder and canvas.captureStream() , which may be unavailable in headless environments. Per-call opts override constructor options and accept download ( boolean | string ). Recording starts at the call and preserves capture options as GIF recording does. MediaRecorder uses a real-time clock, so slow captures can stretch duration.

title: SnapDiff: Visual regression testing that runs in the browser
text: Ecosystem / Tools / SnapDiff @zumer/snapdiff 0.3.1 Visual regression testing that runs in the browser. SnapDiff captures DOM elements with SnapDOM, compares them to saved baselines, and shows what changed. Capture, diff, storage and review happen in the page; the Vitest suite adds disk baselines and tests that fail when visuals drift. GitHub npm Project site Built on SnapDOM, released from its own repository. Separate project What it does A script tag with data-snap attributes: baselines in IndexedDB, a badge to review changes. snapdiff-stale flags baselines older than their source files, with no rendering. defineDemoSuite turns each demo into a Vitest browser test with disk baselines. Install npm install --save-dev @zumer/snapdiff @zumer/snapdom@latest Use it import { snapdom } from '@zumer/snapdom' import { createRunner, Reporter } from '@zumer/snapdiff' const runner = createRunner({ snapdom, namespace: 'my-app', threshold: 0.1, failureRatio: 0 }) runner.test('homepage hero', () => document.querySelector('.hero')) const reporter = new Reporter(runner) reporter.mount() await reporter.runAndShow() Where it fits SnapDiff captures a DOM subtree rather than the browser window. Browser chrome is excluded; native controls can render differently from the live page. SnapEye and SnapDiff both compare pixels. Choose SnapEye for an agent’s capture-and-inspect task; choose SnapDiff for a maintained set of visual tests and baseline reviews. Works with SnapDOM 2.x and 3.x. Ways to use it Vitest browser suite Staleness check Determinism

title: SnapEye: Capture, compare and record for coding agents
text: Ecosystem / Tools / SnapEye @zumer/snapeye 0.4.0 Capture, compare and record for coding agents. SnapEye is a visual toolbelt built on SnapDOM for coding agents. The agent runs one command, gets a JSON answer, and only opens an image when the JSON says it should. GitHub npm Built on SnapDOM, released from its own repository. Separate project What it does capture records a baseline PNG of one target under .snapeye/baselines . diff compares the current render against it and reports changed regions as JSON. record captures a target for a fixed duration as GIF, video and filmstrip. Install npm install --save-dev @zumer/snapeye @zumer/snapdom@latest // vite.config.js import { defineConfig } from 'vite' import { snapeye } from '@zumer/snapeye/vite' export default defineConfig({ plugins: [snapeye()] }) Add the plugin to your Vite config, then start the dev server with npm run dev . In Astro, Nuxt or SvelteKit, add it to the framework’s Vite plugin list. For a static HTML file, use --serve instead. Use it npx snapeye capture header-desktop --target '#site-header' npx snapeye diff header-desktop --target '#site-header' --fail-on-change npx snapeye record menu --target '.menu' --duration 3000 --fps 10 --format gif # A route in the running app (capture its baseline before diffing) npx snapeye diff dashboard --url 'http://localhost:5173/settings?tab=billing' # A standalone HTML fixture npx snapeye capture issue --serve repro/issue.html --snapdom ../snapdom/dist --target '#test' Where it fits SnapEye does not navigate, click, reason, call a model or orchestrate an agent; getting the app into the right state stays the agent’s job. A browser driver reaches interactive states; SnapEye measures their appearance. Its visual comparison uses SnapDiff’s diff engine. The CLI talks to the app through the Vite plugin, or serves a page itself with --serve . Works with SnapDOM 2.24.10 or newer, including 3.x. title: SnapSurf: Web navigation and verification for agents
text:
Ecosystem / Tools / SnapSurf @zumer/snapsurf 0.1.2 · experimental Web navigation and verification for agents. SnapSurf tells an agent what its last action changed: a compact semantic digest of the page, a typed diff after each action, and assertions over that exact diff. It runs locally as an MCP server or CLI with its own Chromium session. GitHub npm Built on SnapDOM, released from its own repository. Separate project Experimental Status SnapSurf is at 0.1.2 and calls itself experimental: the CLI, the MCP tools and the diff format can change between releases. What it does browser_open returns a compact semantic digest of the page with element ids. browser_verify returns a typed diff after each action: content, state, layout, clickability. browser_assert checks that exact diff by its id, including changes beyond the displayed list. Add it to your MCP client { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "-p", "@zumer/snapsurf@latest", "snapsurf-mcp"] } Requires Node.js 22 or newer. The first launch installs Playwright’s Chromium. The server uses its own browser session; it does not inherit your browser’s logins. Use it # terminal 1: the daemon npx -y @zumer/snapsurf serve # terminal 2: a local smoke check npx -y @zumer/snapsurf open 'data:text/html,

Local%20check

' npx -y @zumer/snapsurf assert '{"exists":"Local check"}' npx -y @zumer/snapsurf stop Where it fits A semantic diff answers whether the observed page changed. It does not replace a pixel comparison against a saved visual baseline. SnapSurf runs its own Chromium session with its own cookies and storage, so it cannot use your everyday browser’s sign-ins. Its observation code also works as an in-page library built on SnapDOM. Bundles its own SnapDOM runtime; installing another SnapDOM version does not replace it.
